title: Determinants of Food Delivery Mobile Application Adoption among University Students in Malaysia: An Integrated UTAUT2–DOI Perspective
affiliations: Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia and Universiti Putra Malaysia

detail.title: Determinants of Food Delivery Mobile Application Adoption among University Students in Malaysia: An Integrated UTAUT2–DOI Perspective
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of online food delivery (OFD) platforms has transformed consumer purchasing behaviour, particularly among digitally native populations such as university students. This study investigates the key determinants influencing behavioural intention to adopt food delivery mobile applications in Selangor, Malaysia. Drawing upon an integrated framework combining the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) and Diffusion of Innovation (DOI), four key factors—convenience, price value, trust, and application design—are examined. A quantitative approach was employed using structured questionnaires distributed to 400 university students, with 379 valid responses analysed using SPSS. The findings reveal that all four factors significantly influence behavioural intention (p < 0.05), with application design emerging as the strongest predictor, followed by convenience, trust, and price. The results highlight the increasing importance of user experience (UX) and interface design in shaping digital consumption behaviour in the food service industry. This study contributes to the growing body of literature on OFD adoption in emerging markets and provides practical insights for platform developers and food service operators to enhance user engagement strategies. The study also extends existing technology adoption models by contextualising them within the Malaysian food service ecosystem. Future research is recommended to incorporate additional constructs such as hedonic motivation, perceived risk, and digital payment integration.

title: When Do Platform Attributes Drive Loyalty? The Contingent Role of Last-mile Delivery Speed in Emerging E-commerce Markets
affiliations: Dong-A University, Dong-A University and Dong-A University

detail.title: When Do Platform Attributes Drive Loyalty? The Contingent Role of Last-mile Delivery Speed in Emerging E-commerce Markets
detail.abstract: This study investigates the structural mechanism through which platform attributes translate into customer loyalty in e-commerce retailing within emerging markets. While the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) has been widely used to explain digital adoption, prior research has paid limited attention to how favorable cognitive evaluations are converted into sustained loyalty when consumption involves physical fulfillment. To address this gap, we extend TAM by integrating last-mile delivery performance as a critical boundary condition for value realization.Specifically, we conceptualize product quality and e-payment systems as key platform attributes that shape consumers’ cognitive beliefs—perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU). We further propose delivery speed as a pivotal last-mile delivery factor that conditions whether these cognitive evaluations translate into long-term customer loyalty. Using survey data from 273 online shoppers in Uzbekistan, we employ structural equation modeling (SEM) and multi-group analysis (MGA) to test the proposed framework.The results show that product quality and e-payment systems significantly enhance PU and PEOU, which in turn positively affect customer loyalty. Importantly, these relationships are contingent on delivery speed: the positive effects of platform attributes on loyalty are observed only under conditions of high delivery speed, whereas slow delivery substantially weakens these effects. This pattern highlights a conditional value realization process in which technological advantages are realized only when supported by effective physical fulfillment.The findings contribute to the e-commerce and technology acceptance literature by demonstrating how last-mile delivery functions as a value enabler in emerging markets. For practitioners, the results underscore that investments in digital platforms must be closely aligned with robust logistics capabilities to ensure sustainable competitive advantage in rapidly evolving e-commerce environments.

title: Capturing Latent Situational Influence in Offline Retail: An Embedding-Based Recommendation Framework
affiliations: Yunnan University of Finance and Economics, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Shenzhen University, Southwest University of Finance and Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Capturing Latent Situational Influence in Offline Retail: An Embedding-Based Recommendation Framework
detail.abstract: As offline retail environments undergo digital transformation, delivering personalized and data-driven services has become increasingly essential for improving customer engagement and operational performance. However, unlike online settings where user behaviours are continuously tracked, offline retail suffers from limited visibility into customers’ situational contexts, constraining the effectiveness of traditional recommendation systems. To address this challenge, this study proposes Store2Vec, an embedding-based framework that enhances collaborative filtering for intelligent offline retail. By representing stores as dense vectors derived from customer transaction sequences, Store2Vec captures latent situational similarities, reflecting how shoppers’ contextual choices link different stores. These embeddings are then integrated into an item-based collaborative filtering (ItemCF) model to generate store-to-store recommendations that operate efficiently without requiring individual-level behavioural data. Using large-scale transaction records from a leading retail group in Mainland China, the results demonstrate that Store2Vec significantly improves recommendation accuracy and scalability compared with traditional models. The study contributes theoretically by offering a data-driven approach to operationalize latent situational influence in consumer behaviour and methodologically by extending embedding-based techniques to the offline retail domain. Practically, the findings provide actionable insights for retailers and mall managers seeking to implement personalized recommendation strategies, optimize cross-store collaboration, and advance the intelligence of brick-and-mortar retail environments.

title: Does Excessive Autonomy Undermine Trust? The Influence of AI Agent Autonomy on User Trust and Continuance Usage Intention
affiliations: Wuhan University of Science and Technology, Wuhan University of Science and Technology and Wuhan University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Does Excessive Autonomy Undermine Trust? The Influence of AI Agent Autonomy on User Trust and Continuance Usage Intention
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of exercise and health management, this study examines the underlying mechanism through which AI agent autonomy affects user trust and continuance usage intention. A nonlinear model was developed and tested to investigate the effect of AI agent autonomy on user trust based on the theories of human-machine trust, value theory, and the theory of perceived control. These research findings reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between AI agent autonomy and user trust, with a trust threshold. Perceived value plays a curvilinear mediating role in this inverted U-shaped relationship, while perceived control plays a negative linear mediating role between AI agent autonomy and trust. Additionally, privacy risk perception strengthens the inverted U-shaped impact of AI agent autonomy on perceived value while amplifying its negative effect on perceived control. In the context of exercise and health management, this study demonstrates the dual mediation process by which AI agent autonomy influences user trust. It offers a theoretical foundation for optimizing autonomy levels and privacy communication tactics of health-related applications, as well as promoting long-term user retention.

detail.abstract: Generative AI has made educational content abundant, yet it has intensified three socio technical frictions: (1) reliable knowledge signals are difficult to identify and reward; (2) ranking and revenue sharing rules are often opaque, weakening trust and increasing acquisition costs; (3) referral and revenue share based learning platforms can collapse when cash outflows peak and exceed liquidity. This paper proposes AISIE (AI driven Shared Intelligence Education), a governance oriented artifact that integrates an identity ladder, auditable contribution accounting, and a cashflow safety valve that converts unpaid obligations into managed deferred liabilities. Using Design Science Research, we specify the artifact components and evaluate their financial resilience through 36 month Monte Carlo stress testing with 10000 runs, comparing scenarios with and without the safety valve. Results indicate that the safety valve significantly reduces the probability of negative cash balance under volatility and payout peaks, at the cost of bounded deferred liabilities governed by explicit repayment rules. AISIE contributes a reproducible blueprint for platform governance in AI mediated learning communities, with emphasis on auditability, incentive compatibility, and liquidity resilience. This manuscript is a research preprint describing a governance and evaluation proposal associated with the AI Shared Intelligence Education platform (AI Ho Wis).

title: Medical Firms' Online Q&A Interactions: Effect of Language Style on Investor Engagement
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU), Singapore Management University and Harbin Institute of Technology

detail.title: Medical Firms' Online Q&A Interactions: Effect of Language Style on Investor Engagement
detail.abstract: Purpose-This study investigates how language styles used by medical firms on digital Q&A platforms influence investor engagement. It examines the linguistic characteristics of managerial responses and compares their effects across industries, with a focus on the distinctive demands of medical communication. Design/methodology/approach-We analyze a panel dataset of 1,223 firm-month observations, constructed from 13,549 individual responses provided by 70 medical firms on a major Chinese web-based firm-investor Q&A platform over a 24-month period (2020-2021). Content analysis is used to assess linguistic features, such as first-person usage, uncertainty, understandability, and concreteness. A two-way fixed effects model with clustered robust standard errors is employed. We also perform subgroup and crossindustry analyses to validate the findings and highlight the distinct linguistic patterns in medical firms. Findings-Managerial responses featuring first-person pronouns, uncertainty, understandability, and similarity significantly enhance the number of investor engagements in the medical sector. Using language with higher uncertainty, achievement orientation, and lower concreteness encourages more detailed investor questions. Additionally, while some linguistic traits (e.g., achievement-related terms, understandability) positively influence engagement across industries, the effects of firstperson language, uncertainty, and concreteness are uniquely strong in medical firms. Originality-This study analyzes how specific language styles affect investor engagement in medical firm communications via digital Q&A platforms. It provides empirical evidence on the need for tailored language strategies in health-sector investor communication.

title: Machine Epistemic Singularity (MES) by Jalal Khawaldeh: A Structural Diagnosis of Scientific Integrity (SDSI) Framework

detail.title: Machine Epistemic Singularity (MES) by Jalal Khawaldeh: A Structural Diagnosis of Scientific Integrity (SDSI) Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

Experimental components consisted exclusively of controlled interactions with publicly accessible AI systems in accordance with their terms of service. Ethics committee approval was not required under standard guidelines. All analyses are based on published literature, publicly available AI outputs, and established philosophical frameworks.
declarations.funderStatement: No financial support was received. The work was conducted independently and self-funded.

detail.abstract:
This study introduces the Structural Diagnosis of Scientific Integrity (SDSI) framework, a multi-layer analytical architecture examining how algorithmic mediation may reconfigure the epistemic infrastructure of science. The framework integrates philosophical analysis, metascientific insights, and qualitative observation of generative AI systems.

At its centre lies Machine Epistemic Singularity (MES)—a diagnostic horizon clarifying what is at stake when algorithmic systems become embedded in scientific practice. MES denotes a hypothetical regime where empirical correction becomes marginal, recursive closure self-sustaining, and institutional mechanisms lose capacity to maintain material accountability: the property of epistemic systems whose outputs remain corrigible through empirical engagement.

The framework comprises: (1) a diagnostic grammar identifying referential attenuation—the weakening of links between claims and empirical origins; (2) material accountability as normative anchor; (3) four structural tendencies—referential attenuation, structural opacity, recursive closure, epistemic lock‑in; (4) fifteen axes of epistemic vulnerability across empirical, representational, institutional, and algorithmic layers.

Five diagnostic probes—unattributed recombination, performance without understanding, authoritative posture without accountability, synthetic drift, recursive reinforcement—indicate these mechanisms are operational in micro‑form within research‑adjacent workflows. Analysis identifies three propagation mechanisms (amplification, accumulation, structural coupling) and three threshold conditions (empirical dilution, validation saturation, recursive dependence) as monitorable indicators of when vulnerabilities become self‑reinforcing.

The framework offers a diagnostic lens, not a predictive programme, illuminating structural pressures shaping scientific knowledge as algorithmic systems integrate into its epistemic architecture.

title: Mobile Instant Messaging as a Customer Relationship Management Tool: Evidence from Fashion Retail on Sales Conversion and Customer Engagement
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Ibirapuera University

detail.title: Mobile Instant Messaging as a Customer Relationship Management Tool: Evidence from Fashion Retail on Sales Conversion and Customer Engagement
detail.abstract: Mobile instant messaging (MIM) platforms have emerged as critical channels for customer relationship management (CRM) in retail, yet empirical evidence on their direct impact on sales conversion remains limited. This study examines how salesperson-initiated WhatsApp messages are associated with purchase behavior among existing customers in the fashion retail industry. Drawing on Uses and Gratifications Theory, Relationship Marketing Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, we develop and test hypotheses linking MIM-based CRM contact to sales conversion. Using secondary data from a CRM technology platform encompassing 8,247 customers of a Brazilian men’s fashion retailer, we employ logistic regression and propensity score matching to assess the relationship between WhatsApp messaging frequency and purchase outcomes. Results demonstrate a significant positive association between message receipt and sales conversion (OR = 2.34, p < .001), with effects moderated by customer engagement level and message frequency. Customers receiving 3-5 messages showed optimal conversion rates (32.7%) compared to no-message controls (14.2%). Sensitivity analyses indicate results are robust to moderate unobserved confounding (Gamma = 1.8). Findings contribute to digital CRM literature by demonstrating MIM’s effectiveness as a relationship marketing channel and offer practical guidance for retailers implementing mobile messaging strategies. The study advances understanding of how digital touchpoints predict customer engagement and conversion in omnichannel retail environments.

title: Quantum-Fractal Neurosymbolic Governance (Q-FENG): A Cybernetic Architecture for Ontological Friction Mitigation in Sociotechnical Systems of Critical Infrastructure

detail.title: Quantum-Fractal Neurosymbolic Governance (Q-FENG): A Cybernetic Architecture for Ontological Friction Mitigation in Sociotechnical Systems of Critical Infrastructure

detail.abstract: The deployment of AI systems in critical public infrastructure-from healthcare resource allocation to regulatory compliance-has produced a systemic governance crisis that current frameworks fail to address. This crisis, which we formalize as Ontological Friction, arises from the structural incompatibility between the stochastic, inductive logic of deep learning models and the deterministic, deductive logic of institutional norms. Existing governance approaches-including risk management frameworks (NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001), static guardrails, and post-hoc auditingintervene only after the system's behavioral possibility space has already been constituted, rendering them structurally incapable of ex-ante normative control. This paper introduces the Quantum-Fractal Neurosymbolic Governance (Q-FENG) architecture, a cybernetic control framework that resolves Ontological Friction by formalizing the interference between neural prediction vectors and symbolic norm vectors as a superposition in Hilbert space. Grounded in Stafford Beer's Viable System Model (VSM), Quantum Decision Theory (Busemeyer & Bruza, 2012), and Differentiable Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (dPASP), Q-FENG operates as a fractal governance structure-invariant across Macro (regulatory), Meso (institutional), and Micro (algorithmic) scales-with a cybernetic Circuit Breaker that collapses action probability to zero when destructive interference (θ ≈ π) is detected between what an AI system predicts and what it ought to do. We demonstrate the architecture through an applied case in Brazil's Unified Health System (SUS), using real data from DATASUS to show how Q-FENG would have detected and mitigated both constructive interference (the 2021 Manaus oxygen crisis) and destructive interference (regional concentration bias in specialized healthcare). The Markovian extension of the Ontological Friction angle (θeff) with planning horizon across budget cycles (PPA) constitutes an original contribution to the field.

title: Evaluating Oracle's Native AI SQL Generation on TPC-H Benchmark
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Evaluating Oracle's Native AI SQL Generation on TPC-H Benchmark
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of Oracle Database's native AI SQL generation capabilities using the 22-query TPC-H benchmark. We measure three critical dimensions: semantic correctness, latency breakdown (LLM generation vs database execution), and complexity correlation. Baseline evaluation reveals 63.64% semantic match rate with 100% syntactic success. Importantly, validated prompt engineering experiments demonstrate that schema context and domain hints alone can improve accuracy to 86.36%, achieving a +22.73 percentage point improvement without model fine-tuning. These findings expose addressable patterns in AI comprehension failures and establish a clear, validated path to production-ready accuracy through practical prompt optimization. The Enhanced strategy is statistically significant, particularly for medium (+25%) and complex (+30%) queries.

title: Recentering Public Values In AI Governance: Examples From The Biden Administration
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - School of Law and University of California, Berkeley - School of Information

detail.title: Recentering Public Values In AI Governance: Examples From The Biden Administration

publicationDetails.detailsText: Berkeley Technology Law Journal , Volume 40, No. 4, pp. 1135-1183 (2026)

detail.abstract:
This Article situates key Biden-Harris Administration AI initiatives within a “governance-by-design” framework—an approach we previously developed that centers public values, sectoral expertise, and participatory policymaking in decisions to regulate through technology. Governance-by-design argues for reorienting AI governance around three core principles: (1) privileging human and public rights by empowering domain-specific agencies while building a shared set of tools and approaches for risk assessment; (2) expanding agencies’ technical expertise through public hiring and multisector collaboration; and (3) preserving the publicness of policymaking through designs that foreground embedded values and embedding stakeholder engagement and impact evaluation throughout AI system development and deployment.
The Article uses three examples to illustrate how key Biden-Harris Administration AI actions reflect these governance-by-design principles:
• the Administration’s layered regulatory strategy that empowers sectoral agencies to safeguard human rights and public safety in AI use;
• the expansion of AI and rights-based expertise within government and the establishment of collaborative structures for risk management and evaluation; and,
• the institutionalization of practices that surface and interrogate the normative assumptions embedded in AI systems, while scaffolding public participation throughout their lifecycle.
We argue that together these initiatives offer an alternative to prevailing AI governance debates—particularly the dichotomy between risk-based and rights-based approaches, and the call for a centralized AI regulator. Instead, such governance-by-design provides a field-centric model that leverages existing institutional capacities, protects democratic norms, and re-centers the public in the often-private domain of AI development. It offers a durable, epistemically responsible framework for regulating AI systems in a way that supports both human rights and legitimate democratic governance.

title: When Bigger Is Worse: Semantic-Lexical Mismatch in Legal Entity Retrieval

detail.title: When Bigger Is Worse: Semantic-Lexical Mismatch in Legal Entity Retrieval
detail.abstract: Neural embedding models have achieved state-of-the-art results across many information retrieval tasks, leading to widespread adoption in legal technology platforms. This paper presents evidence that these models systematically underperform traditional lexical methods for a critical class of legal queries: named entity retrieval. Evaluating BM25 against multiple neural embedding models on 1,000 real UK Gazette insolvency notices, statutory announcements published under the Insolvency Act 1986 covering practitioner appointments, liquidations, and creditor meetings, we find that BM25 achieves 82% precision at rank 1 compared to 2% for the best general-purpose neural model (MPNet, 110M parameters) and 50% for domain-adapted LEGAL-BERT. All The practical recommendation is unambiguous: for legal search applications dominated by proper noun and identifier queries, traditional lexical methods provide superior accuracy (6-20x improvement), dramatically lower latency (160x faster), and reduced infrastructure costs. These findings have direct implications for legal technology platforms, compliance systems, and any domain where queries primarily target named entities rather than semantic concepts.

title: Distinguishing Governance from Compliance Evidence: A Framework for Post-Incident Reconstruction

detail.title: Distinguishing Governance from Compliance Evidence: A Framework for Post-Incident Reconstruction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
Background: When automated decision systems fail, post-incident investigations repeatedly discover that formally compliant organizations cannot reconstruct the decision process from the available evidence archive. Existing accountability frameworks treat all documentation as interchangeable, conflating two structurally distinct evidentiary categories: compliance evidence (demonstrating that a process was followed) and governance evidence (enabling reconstruction of whether the decision-making process was adequate to the risks it addressed).

Objective: This paper formalizes the governance-compliance evidence distinction through three jointly necessary properties – reconstructability, evaluability, and contemporaneity – and develops a diagnostic framework for identifying which evidence gaps specific system architectures produce.

Methods: Through abductive case analysis of seven documented system failures and one boundary case across financial trading, social welfare, autonomous vehicles, and IT operations, and comparative analysis of seven regulatory governance frameworks, the paper derives a six-property Decision Event Schema (DES) and maps architectural conditions to predicted evidence degradation patterns.

Results: Three architectural properties – velocity, scale, and opacity – are identified as drivers of structural accountability collapse (SAC), the condition in which governance evidence degrades while compliance artifacts persist. A five-type degradation taxonomy specifies which architectural configurations produce which evidence gaps. Four testable propositions with falsification thresholds and out-of-sample predictions operationalize the framework for empirical validation.

Conclusion: The governance-compliance evidence distinction provides practitioners with a diagnostic basis for assessing evidence architectures before incidents occur, and researchers with testable mappings between architectural configurations and predicted evidence gaps. The five out-of-sample predictions – spanning programmatic advertising, multi-cloud orchestration, criminal-justice risk assessment, medical imaging, and banking fraud detection – provide independently falsifiable tests of the framework’s central claim.

title: Maps and Territory: Designing Alternatives - Systems Design Frameworks for Equitable Talent Recognition and Capability Building Systems
affiliations: Human Resonance Systems Research Collective

detail.title: Maps and Territory: Designing Alternatives - Systems Design Frameworks for Equitable Talent Recognition and Capability Building Systems
detail.abstract:
Current talent systems solve a problem effectively: they perpetuate external dominance while appearing to develop nationals. But this is a problem worth solving differently.

This paper shows how. Building on diagnostic evidence from Papers 1-3 revealing policy gaps, organizational suppression mechanisms, and individual invisibility, Paper 4 designs systems aligned with stated purposes: developing nationals and building regional capability.

The core argument: systems accomplish what they are designed to accomplish. Current systems are designed according to principles of perpetuation and external dominance. Different design principles produce different outcomes. By identifying five alternative principles—capability development, authentic meritocracy, knowledge systematization, organizational autonomy, and regional innovation—and applying them systematically, organizations and policies can design systems that accomplish stated purposes rather than perpetuate unexamined patterns.

The paper provides three-level design frameworks. Assessment system redesign measures authentic capability rather than conformity bias. Organizational redesign distributes authority, systematizes knowledge transfer, and builds decision-making capability. Institutional redesign enables nations to implement frameworks aligned with development goals.

The paper grounds design in feasibility. Comparative development research documents that Singapore and South Korea successfully transitioned from external dependency to capability leadership through similar mechanisms. Real-world organizational examples show assessment, organizational, and policy alternatives working in practice.

Implementation is achievable within realistic timelines. The paper specifies a 5-year phased pathway: foundation building (year 1-2), acceleration with piloting (year 2-3), integration across systems (year 3-5). Proof-of-concept results are possible within 2-3 years. Success is measurable through seven outcome indicators.

The paper answers the strategic question: if current systems are designed, and we understand their design, what would we design instead?

title: Early Detection of VaR Model Deterioration: A Cantelli-Bound Ratio Approach for Proactive Risk Management

detail.title: Early Detection of VaR Model Deterioration: A Cantelli-Bound Ratio Approach for Proactive Risk Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Financial institutions often face a critical challenge in the silent failure of Value-at-Risk (VaR) models, whose performance is typically assessed through ex-post backtesting such as unconditional coverage and independence tests—which tends to detect problems only after violations and losses have occurred. To address this gap, this paper introduces the VaR Efficiency Ratio (VER), defined as the ratio of model-based VaR to a Cantelli-implied VaR computed from the same conditional mean and variance. Using S&P 500 returns from 2000–2025 with rolling five-year estimation windows across multiple confidence levels and forecast horizons, empirical results indicate that lower VER values systematically precede VaR exceedances, providing early-warning signals for model recalibration before traditional backtests detect deterioration. VER declines sharply at deeper tail confidence levels, remains largely invariant across forecast horizons, and exhibits persistent behaviour during major market stress periods. VER is easy to implement and complements standard backtesting by tracking VaR conservatism in real time.

detail.abstract: By March 2026, Israel's multi-front campaign against the Shi'a axis (Iran, Hezbollah, proxy networks) and the Sunni Islamist and jihadist coalition (HTS/al-Jolani, Turkey, Qatar, Hamas) was confronting two mutually reinforcing structural constraints: the systemic saturation of its multilayered air and missile defense architecture, and the institutional exhaustion of its armed forces. This paper argues that these constraints are not tactical deficiencies amenable to operational remediation but institutional thresholds with self-reinforcing dynamics, such that additional pressure on either constraint produces disproportionate increases in cost and disproportionate decreases in operational effectiveness. The paper extends the analysis of the U.S.-Israeli delegated-order architecture undertaken in Finkel & Kamynnik (2026) and focuses on the operational limits of that architecture: the condition of missile defense systems, the military manpower deficit, Hamas's reassertion of administrative control in the Gaza Strip, and the leverage that third-party actors exercise through the West Bank. Three scenarios are developed, differentiated by the rate and configuration of structural overload, and their implications for the bargaining positions of key regional and external actors are assessed. The central finding is that the primary risk is not military defeat on any single front but institutional collapse. This is understood here as the moment at which the simultaneous convergence of manpower exhaustion, interceptor depletion, and a domestic legitimacy crisis renders the continuation of the campaign politically untenable precisely when U.S. diplomacy is offering a settlement on the least favorable terms.

detail.abstract:
The global Pay TV market has shed over 25% of its subscriber base since 2017, and OTT delivery has become the dominant medium for video consumption worldwide. This structural shift has transformed encoding infrastructure from a back-office cost centre into a first-order competitive variable — one where the wrong decision translates directly into tens of millions of dollars in avoidable CDN expenditure, degraded viewer experience, and technical debt that compounds with every hour of content ever encoded.

The economic stakes are stark. A 3-year total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis presented in this paper demonstrates that purpose-built ASIC-based encoding deployments achieve up to 99% cost reduction per channel compared to managed cloud solutions such as AWS Elemental MediaLive — not through compromise, but through intelligent infrastructure alignment. The crossover inflection point between next-generation chip-based systems and legacy appliance architectures has already been crossed for AV1 live encoding, and is arriving for VVC offline VOD in 2026.

Artificial intelligence is the defining force reshaping this landscape. Machine learning has moved from experimental overlay to production requirement across every layer of the encoding pipeline: VMAF-guided rate-distortion optimization delivers 20% bitrate reduction at equivalent perceptual quality; content-adaptive bitrate laddering uses ML complexity analysis to generate per-title and per-scene encoding profiles; reinforcement learning ABR algorithms optimize Quality of Experience in real time; and neural codec architectures are achieving compression efficiency 20-40% beyond VVC on select content categories. The transition from QoS-centric to QoE-driven service performance assessment [3] is redefining the very metrics against which encoding systems are evaluated.

To navigate these converging forces, this paper introduces the Codec-Infrastructure Alignment Matrix (CIAM) — a four-dimensional engineering decision framework mapping encoder technologies across performance throughput, feature richness, AI integration readiness, and economic profile. detail.abstract: This paper provides a behavioral analysis of the post-pandemic transformation of work, using a dataset of approximately 41 billion mobile geolocation records from 73.5 million individuals in the five largest U.S. metropolitan areas from the pre-to post- pandemic periods. By tracking movements between corporate headquarters, residences, and other points of interest, we document a structural shift in work patterns. Office based workdays declined from 42% in 2019 to 20.7% in 2022, before settling at 29.1% in 2023, a new equilibrium significantly below pre-pandemic levels. A "midweek mountain" peak of office attendance on Tuesdays through Thursdays, emerged as a robust new phenomenon post-pandemic. The nature of remote work has also changed: both in and after the pandemic, employees working from home allocated significantly more time to non-work locations like parks and malls during the workday. These findings indicate that the pandemic catalyzed a lasting transformation not just in work arrangements but also in the integration of personal and professional life, with implications for corporate policy, urban economics, and the future of work.

Yet this labor force is entirely invisible to the economic infrastructure humanity has built to measure work. No standard unit of measurement exists. No index tracks machine labor output over time. detail.abstract: I propose a new boundedly-rational trader-behavior model for the continuous double auction, fit in the general equilibrium (GE) framework. detail.abstract:
This working paper establishes the fourth pillar of the Network-Enabled Market Optimization (NEMO) framework: government as systematic participant rather than passive regulator or discretionary funder. Conventional government involvement in poverty reduction programs reproduces structural fragility by positioning public budgets as appropriations competing annually against alternative expenditure priorities. The NEMO Government Participation Framework proposes automated percentage allocation from existing tax revenue streams (Value Added Tax, Corporate Income Tax, Personal Income Tax, Employee Provident Fund, and Employee Trust Fund), transforming government contribution from discretionary expenditure into an inherent component of revenue collection.

The paper presents mathematical architecture for the government pillar across six operational domains: tax allocation automation protocols, EPF and ETF monthly distribution calculations, daily Participation Value Credit (PVC) price reduction algorithms, SME formalization incentive structures, actuarial Social Impact Credit (SIC) distribution modulation incorporating winning history, age, and geographic factors, and zero-value PVC economic implications. Each domain receives rigorous treatment through De Bono's Six Thinking Hats methodology (Nadhir, 2026a) ensuring analytical completeness across factual, emotional, risk, benefit, creative, and synthesis dimensions.

The central finding demonstrates that automated tax allocation at 2 percent of specified revenue streams produces daily government contribution of approximately LKR 24.66 million under Sri Lankan fiscal conditions, sufficient to reduce PVC prices by 34 to 35 percent across all three tiers daily while maintaining actuarially sound SIC distribution. The formalization incentive analysis shows SME formalization under NEMO access generates revenue increases offsetting 61 percent of income reduction from tax compliance costs, with full break-even achievable when merchant network density reaches threshold scale. This creates a self-reinforcing fiscal cycle: government contribution incentivizes formal participation, formal participation expands the tax base, expanded tax base increases government contribution capacity.

The paper situates these mechanisms within public finance theory (Musgrave and Musgrave, 1989; Stiglitz, 2000), behavioural economics of participation (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008; Kahneman, 2011), and development economics literature on cash transfer sustainability (Banerjee et al., 2015; World Bank, 2025). It concludes that automated allocation represents a structurally superior mechanism by removing NEMO from annual budget competition, creating explicit fiscal incentives for government success, and generating formalization feedback loops that increase contribution capacity over time.

detail.abstract:
Introduction and Objectives: Rationality is a fundamental concept in philosophy, natural sciences, and social sciences that plays a role in both theoretical and applied dimensions. “Reason” has undergone a transformation in its historical course from theoretical reason in the “Platonic-Aristotelian tradition” to modern instrumental reason. The concept of rationality as one of the central concepts in the humanities has complex dimensions and is derived from the French language (Arastekho, 2002, p. 681); however, “rationality” or “rational aspects” has many derivatives, all of which are derived from this word. Rationalization is a process by which realities and activities are placed within the scope of the dominance of reason. In fact, rationality is considered to be meaningful in a specific context (Turner, 2006: 145). Therefore, it can be said that a rational act is an act that convinces and convinces the power of reason or human reasoning; In this sense, reasoning is based on thinking and is different from feelings and emotions (Danaeifard et al., 2010; quoted by Snellen). One of the major challenges that researchers and theorists in this field face is the lack of a unified understanding of the concept of rationality and its related aspects. In general, the main question of this research is: “What is rationality and the aspects related to what has characteristics?”; The purpose of this research is to provide the audience with a better understanding of various aspects of rationality by relying on the study and collection of literature and theoretical background in the field of social sciences.

Research Method: In the field of applied research, there are several methods, each of which may be assigned different names depending on the characteristics of the research questions and the specific situations and conditions of the study. The most important of these studies are: case studies, historical, descriptive, exploratory, longitudinal and cross-sectional, field, laboratory, experimental and post-event, correlational and congruent, real and quasi-experimental. Descriptive research method is one of the most basic forms of research. This research, at the bottom of the research hierarchy pyramid and with a descriptive-analytical approach, examines rationality in terms of its application in social sciences. The fact that descriptive research is at the bottom of the research pyramid does not mean that it is unimportant, unscientific or worthless. This type of research describes phenomena in our world. These descriptions can be about basic information, activities, behaviors and fundamental changes in phenomena. The present research is of a descriptive-analytical type and has attempted to examine the concept of rationality and the issues and phenomena related to it with a systematic approach. In this direction, the views and opinions of prominent scholars in this field and their analysis and classification have been the researchers’ approach in this research. The main goal of this research is to accurately describe the concept of rationality, the opinions and views of experts in the field of rationality and related concepts.

Research findings: First, different categories of rationality were presented, which were defined in different ways, depending on the differences in symbols, values, and culture of different societies.

title: Restoring the First Rule: Structural Distance in Problem-Driven Organizational Search
affiliations: and ESSEC Business School

detail.title: Restoring the First Rule: Structural Distance in Problem-Driven Organizational Search
detail.abstract: The Carnegie School proposes that problem-driven organizational search follows two simple rules of locality: search begins where the problem first occurred and close to the prior solution. While the literature has extensively examined the latter, the former dimension of search remains largely unexplored. The question we tackle in this paper is whether it matters where in the organizational structure search occurs, or only what solutions are explored. We formally examine the performance implications of structural distance, which is the distance between where the problem originated in the organization and where search occurs, and compare them to those of solution distance, which is the degree to which a new solution differs from the prior one. We find that, from a search efficacy point of view, structural distance is often more consequential than solution distance, and the relative importance of each depends critically on the pattern of task interdependence. As interdependence increases, structural distance becomes increasingly important and can even substitute for insufficient solution exploration, while the converse does not hold. We also explore conditions under which exploration on both dimensions benefits search. These findings suggest that the dominant focus on solution distance may have overlooked a comparably important dimension of organizational search, with implications for how we understand the internal dynamics of problem-driven search and the relationship between organizational structure and adaptation.

detail.abstract: Transformer-based agentic AI is rapidly being deployed on major platforms to help users shop, watch, and navigate content with less effort. While these systems can deliver impressive performance, a key concern is whether they may be less reliable than they appear. We ask a simple but fundamental question: whether the mechanisms that make transformer-based agents effective can also induce systematic biases or distortions? We study this question through a theoretical analysis of transformer-based generative recommenders, in which the next user interaction is generated sequentially from a user's history. Focusing on how the model allocates attention across historical evidence, we identify four bias channels: (i) Positional bias: stronger positional encoding shifts influence toward recent history, improving responsiveness but potentially reducing stability and long-term diversity; (ii) Popularity amplification: small frequency differences in data can be magnified into disproportionate exposure, contributing to Matthew effects and echo chambers; (iii) Latent driver bias: when important drivers of user choices are not directly observed, the model can place overly concentrated weight on a small subset of past events, creating overconfident attributions. (iv) Synthetic data bias: when users increasingly follow AI suggestions and platforms retrain on model-shaped synthetic logs, outputs can concentrate over time, and long-tail alternatives can disappear first. Our analysis highlights mechanism-level reliability risks that may not be visible in offline performance metrics. The four bias channels indicate that large-scale deployment may systematically distort exposure and choice. For managers, the immediate implication is to treat these as operational risk factors and to monitor concentration and drift over time, rather than assuming that performance gains alone guarantee reliability.

title: When Adding Livestreaming Pays Off: Human-AI Recommendation under Reselling and Agency Channels

detail.title: When Adding Livestreaming Pays Off: Human-AI Recommendation under Reselling and Agency Channels
detail.abstract: E-commerce platforms increasingly integrate automated recommendation systems with livestream-based human interaction. While AI-only recommendation is scalable and cost efficient, livestreaming enhances service quality through real-time demonstration and engagement, but at additional operating costs whose profitability depends critically on channel structure. We develop a tractable equilibrium model in which recommendation mode is an endogenous service technology jointly determined with the selling channel. We study two recommendation modes (AI-only and AI augmented by livestreaming) under two channel structures (reselling and agency), and characterize equilibrium prices, quantities, profits, and consumer surplus across all four regimes in closed form. We derive sharp threshold conditions governing both livestream adoption and channel choice. Under reselling, adoption is driven by a transparent tradeoff between service-induced demand expansion and internally borne service costs. Double marginalization does not affect this margin, as it applies symmetrically across recommendation modes. Under agency, commission payments distort the effective marginal cost of human expertise, generating a nonlinear adoption condition and making commission design the central governance lever for sustaining human-AI complementarity. We further endogenize commission rates and show that the platform optimally balances margin extraction against adoption incentives. The optimal commission either coincides with the unconstrained profit-maximizing level or adjusts to the boundary that induces manufacturer adoption of livestreaming, providing a theoretical rationale for commission differentiation across products and selling formats. Our analysis yields a unified adoption map that partitions the parameter space into regions in which each regime is optimal. The framework explains observed heterogeneity in platform governance and recommendation intensity, and provides explicit decision rules for aligning recommendation technology, channel structure, and commission policy.

detail.abstract:
Strategy execution failure is widely acknowledged but poorly measured. The most commonly cited statistic, that roughly 70% of strategies fail, has no verifiable empirical source (Hughes, 2011). Existing research measures only post-adoption outcomes, capturing what happens after an organisation decides to act on a strategic recommendation. It does not capture non-adoption: recommendations that are assessed, deprioritised, or shelved before implementation begins.

This paper introduces TRUE LOSS, a dual-funnel methodology that measures both non-adoption and post-adoption failure across the complete strategy consulting engagement lifecycle. Using a proprietary analytical model calibrated against 180+ peer-reviewed and industry sources and encompassing 40,344 qualified firms across five regions and 30 countries, we find that 65% of strategy consulting investment fails to translate into realised value, representing approximately $135 billion in annual value destruction globally.

The loss decomposes into two compounding funnels: 47% non-adoption and 18% post-adoption failure. Three structurally distinct segment profiles emerge: government programmes (75.8% TRUE LOSS), large private enterprise (52.8%), and SMEs (58.0%), each driven by different combinations of five universal failure patterns. The methodology converges at 89.6% with Mankins and Steele's (2005) independent estimates, validating the measurement approach. The findings suggest that strategy execution requires lifecycle measurement infrastructure rather than post-hoc performance assessment.

title: How does your AI Model Make Decisions? Behavioral Fingerprinting of Foundation AI Models and Organizational Culture Alignment

detail.title: How does your AI Model Make Decisions? Behavioral Fingerprinting of Foundation AI Models and Organizational Culture Alignment
detail.abstract: Foundation AI models are trained on vast corpora of human-generated text and refined through reinforcement learning from human feedback-processes that necessarily encode the values, reasoning styles, and decision logics of the people involved. Yet the cultural dispositions embedded in these models are neither measured nor reported, leaving enterprises without visibility into a consequential property of the systems they adopt. We introduce Decision Culture: the embedded assumptions a system brings to decisions about who holds authority, what constitutes a legitimate reason, how risk should be weighed, and whose interests are centered. We present the AI Culture Audit, a behavioral fingerprinting protocol assessing ten major foundation models across 18 cultural dimensions, distinguishing Native Behavioral Tendency (what a model does) from Cultural Knowledge Retrieval (what it knows). Applying the same framework to 18 global organizations enables direct model-organization alignment analysis across 3,168 scored responses. Three findings emerge: all ten models exhibit a universal distributeddecision tendency regardless of provider or architecture; models diverge meaningfully on norm enforcement, with direct implications for compliance-sensitive deployments; and a systematic behavioral-knowledge gap produces an AI Cultural Baseline that clusters all frontier models in a narrow zone of cultural space while organizations span the full spectrum. We discuss implications for enterprise AI governance, model selection, and the emerging regulatory landscape under the EU AI Act.

title: Ethical Debt in AI Systems: Organizational Risk and Strategic Product Implications

detail.title: Ethical Debt in AI Systems: Organizational Risk and Strategic Product Implications
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital products and enterprise systems has created new forms of organizational risk that extend beyond traditional concerns of technical performance and reliability. While responsible AI principles and governance guidelines have been widely discussed in recent years, organizations continue to face ethical failures arising from biased datasets, opaque decision-making, and poorly governed automated systems. This paper introduces the concept of ethical debt in AI systems, defined as the accumulated socio-technical risk that emerges when ethical considerations-such as fairness, transparency, accountability, and user autonomy-are deferred or inadequately addressed during the design, development, and deployment of AI-enabled products. Similar to the concept of technical debt in software engineering, ethical debt builds incrementally through product decisions and system design choices, eventually creating long-term organizational exposure. Despite growing attention to AI ethics, existing research largely focuses on high-level principles or regulatory compliance, with limited emphasis on how ethical risk accumulates across the AI product lifecycle and how product management practices contribute to this process. Addressing this gap, this study develops a conceptual framework that explains the formation and accumulation of ethical debt through five key stages of AI product development: problem framing, data representation, model automation, user experience design, and governance oversight. Building on this model, the paper proposes a lifecycle-based mitigation framework that integrates strategic governance, ethical risk identification, responsible system design, deployment safeguards, and continuous monitoring mechanisms. The framework also introduces a conceptual Ethical Debt Index (EDI) to support the measurement and monitoring of ethical risk within organizations. The findings highlight the strategic role of product managers and AI development teams in preventing ethical debt through responsible product decisions and governance practices. By reframing AI ethics as a form of accumulated organizational risk embedded in product development processes, this research contributes a practical and theoretically grounded approach to managing ethical challenges in AI systems. The proposed framework offers organizations a structured pathway for embedding ethical safeguards into AIdriven products while supporting sustainable innovation and long-term institutional trust.

detail.abstract:
The stem article argues that theory-testing research is inherently generative because it relies on abductive reasoning both when translating theory into testable hypotheses (a priori) and when interpreting empirical results (a posteriori). By treating theories as conjectural rather than axiomatic, theory-testing studies not only corroborate or disconfirm propositions but also extend domains, refine constructs, and shift emphases (for example, from transaction costs to total costs and value in transaction cost economics), thereby gradually transforming bodies of knowledge. A priori “theoretical‑model abduction” extends existing theories into new empirical contexts, while a posteriori “inference to the best explanation” uses surprising or anomalous findings to revise or elaborate theoretical claims.
​
The commentaries converge on this generative view but stress different implications. Aguinis translates the epistemological argument into an eight‑step, evidence‑based playbook for making theory contributions, emphasizing cumulative evidence, effect sizes, competing explanations, and reframing anomalies as theory signals. Makadok calls for a realistic “engineering science” of study design and interpretation that explicitly manages tradeoffs, calibrates the protective belt around theories, and tempers perfectionist expectations. Swink highlights operations management’s phenomenon‑driven, practice‑rooted character, warning that much supposed “testing” is mere framing and advocating more space for competing explanations and nascent theory work. Bendoly and Oliva extend the argument to intervention research and process‑rich OM contexts, stressing structured, high‑quality abduction and the need to allow studies to move from deductive framing to abductive sensemaking within a single project.

detail.abstract: This study examines the instrumentalization of criminal law in the governance of unregistered Protestant house churches in China during the period 2015–2025. The study asks how prosecutorial actors deploy multiple criminal provisions to construct a system of governance through criminal law, and what judicial application patterns reveal about the functional role of courts within this system. Drawing on a database of approximately 113 legal documents—including approximately 40 religious cases and 65 non-religious control cases—assembled through the author’s professional practice as a criminal defense attorney and through a professional network of Chinese legal practitioners, providing access to materials unavailable to external researchers through conventional research channels, the study develops the concept of criminal compliance architecture: a system of overlapping criminal provisions (Articles 225, 293, 266, and 300 of the Criminal Law) that, when deployed interchangeably against religious organizational activity, render legal compliance structurally impossible. The empirical findings document five principal patterns: the dominance of Article 300 at approximately 63 percent of primary charges; multi-charge prosecution rates of 55 percent (compared to 20 percent in the control group); compliance-signaling sentencing in which suspended sentences are conditioned on organizational renunciation; temporal concentration in the post-2018 period; and geographic clustering with province-specific charge preferences. The legal analysis documents patterns consistent with courts functioning as processors of compliance outcomes rather than as independent adjudicators. The study further demonstrates that the compliance architecture possesses a self-concealing property that systematically suppresses the information flows on which international monitoring institutions depend. The study carries implications for USCIRF, the U.S. Department of State, consular services, and American religious organizations operating in China.

detail.abstract: Is deplatforming effective in reducing toxicity on social media? To answer this question we study a policy change on Reddit in June 2020 which led to a simultaneous ban of thousands of forums containing hateful content, but not the users of these forums. We use data on the near universe of comments left on Reddit to examine the impact of the ban on user behaviour in a differences-indifferences design. We find that the most active users of banned subreddits comment more after the policy change and substitute to new forums in the weeks after the ban. The increase in activity persists in the long run, but is not associated with higher toxicity: instead, the comments left by affected users outside banned subreddits contain 20% fewer instances of hate speech. We do not find evidence that the policy leads to lower quality of engagement, negative spillover effects or recreation of banned subreddits elsewhere on the platform. Overall, the results suggest that moderation targeting toxic digital spaces can be effective in combating hate speech without lowering user engagement, and thus can be aligned with platforms' incentives.

This article examines the state of China's tax litigation mechanism and describes the current pilot reform programmes: the Xiamen Model and the Shanghai Model. The Xiamen Model centralizes jurisdiction and adjudication of three types of tax-related cases (civil, administrative, criminal) within a specialized “tax collegiate panel” of a district-level court in Xiamen. In contrast, the Shanghai Model sets up the specialized tax tribunals within two courts, which centrally handle all first-instance and appellate tax administrative cases across Shanghai. Regarding whether China should establish a tax court, the article presents a dialectical perspective suggesting China, as a low-tax litigation jurisdiction, should carefully assess the cost-effectiveness of resource investment needed.

title: Before Invention

detail.title: Before Invention

publicationDetails.detailsText: Texas Intellectual Property Law Journal, Volume 34 (forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract:
This Article is the first comprehensive historical account of a foundational doctrine of U.S. patent law: conception. Conception supplies the meaning of invention at the root of the patent system. It is a mental act, the formation of the idea of an invention before it is made. Considered “the touchstone of inventorship,” conception can determine who receives a patent, awarding credit and title, and governs employee inventions and federally funded research. Despite conception’s import, courts inconsistently state its doctrinal standard while insisting on its deep historical continuity, and scholars exclude it from studies of patent law’s practice, theory, and history. Carefully reading nearly two centuries of cases and treatises, the Article details the doctrine’s development, reveals its causes and tectonic effects on the patent system, and proposes a new test. Due to conception’s influence across other doctrines, the test transforms the meaning of invention holding aloft the system’s whole architecture.

The conventional wisdom is that the meaning of conception is well-settled, “unchanged for more than a century.” But this Article argues the doctrine has oscillated between a “mentalist” tradition, privileging a general idea in the mind at an early stage of the inventive process, and a “materialist” one, privileging a detailed idea formed amidst the physical work of experimentation. The doctrine developed in three phases, crafted in the nineteenth century with a mentalist theory equating conception with invention; turned materialist in the twentieth, breaking that equation; and, near the twenty-first, reverted to mentalism, albeit unsteadily. Heedless of these conflicting traditions, scholars and judges pick and choose among their divergent doctrinal standards. The result is a modern doctrine as convoluted as its history. Clarity requires understanding the development of the doctrine’s oscillating preferences for ideation and work.

The Article draws two takeaways from this history. First, conception has long provided the meaning of invention underwriting the patent system. This claim counters popular belief in patent law’s early materialism and recasts the modern system as the triumph of conception’s doctrinal development. Conception is thus not only temporally before making an invention, but also ontologically before the very notion of invention—the first principle of the entire edifice. This conclusion provides a basis for a foundational theory of invention that traverses the many doctrines shaped by conception’s doctrinal development.

Second, conception must be reworked to bring back the materialist turn, grounded in experimental labor. The mentalist tradition is flawed, designed to exclude that labor. The Article proposes a new test synthesizing elements from the materialist case law. While scholars have advocated materialist approaches to other doctrines, primarily related to inventorship and a patent application’s disclosure, those doctrines were largely shaped by conception’s development and should incorporate versions of the proposed conception test, harmonizing divergent theories of invention with their source. The test resolves controversies over federally funded research and artificial intelligence, and the thorny case law on disclosure, the basis of the modern system.

title: Mechanics of Dynamic Markets

detail.title: Mechanics of Dynamic Markets
detail.abstract: This monograph develops a rigorous, unified framework for understanding information asymmetry, price discovery, and hidden liquidity in dynamic financial markets. Beginning with the classical foundations of market microstructure, from the Arrow-Debreu general equilibrium and the Grossman-Stiglitz impossibility theorem to the CAPM and adverse selection models of Akerlof and Stiglitz-Rothschild, this work establishes the theoretical necessity of strategic information-based trading. The central analytical engine is the Kyle (1985) sequential game, treated first in its canonical single-period form and then extended to multi-period and continuous-time settings following Back (1992). We characterize the unique linear equilibrium, derive closed-form expressions for trading intensity, price impact, posterior variance dynamics, and informed trader profitability, and provide intuition for the distinctive invariance property whereby a single trading round always reveals exactly half of the prior fundamental variance.The monograph then introduces two original contributions. The first is the Multidimensional Latency Tomography (MDLT) framework, a probe-based active inference mechanism for recovering hidden liquidity in electronic limit order books. Motivated by the sonar analogy of active measurement under uncertainty, MDLT deploys sequentially timed probe orders and invokes a conservation law of queue dynamics to isolate latent iceberg volume. This yields the Iceberg Density Coefficient and the MDLT Priority Metric, a corrected queue position estimator that eliminates the Hidden Latency Bias endemic to naive execution algorithms. The second contribution extends the analysis to liquidity kinematics via a variational and stochastic action framework, incorporating a Bernoulli Market Hypothesis for hydrodynamic liquidity flows, a Least Liquidity Action principle, and an Onsager-Machlup functional interpretation of order book path probabilities. Together, these constructions provide statistically orthogonal tools: spatial iceberg detection at a fixed instant via MDLT, and temporal anomaly detection over intervals via stochastic action, enabling rigorous inference of hidden market structure. The entire framework is grounded in tick-by-tick order book data and admits calibration via maximum likelihood on standard exchange feeds.

detail.abstract: Expectations are central to models of economic and financial decision-making. Yet in practice, individuals are often inattentive and, when asked, report fragile, context-dependent expectations that are only weakly linked to decisions. This raises the question to what extent they hold such expectations in the first place. Against this backdrop, we ask two questions: When people think about an economic issue, can they build on expectations they formed before? And does it matter if they cannot? We develop and validate a survey measure that distinguishes between individuals who can recall expectations formed in the past and those who must form expectations from scratch. We show that while many households have expectations about key economic variables, a large share of households do not-even among those close to decisions for which the expectation should be relevant. This matters: individuals without a previously-formed expectation (i) express expectations that are more context-dependent, (ii) update expectations more strongly but less persistently in response to new information, (iii) report expectations that are less relevant to decisions, and (iv) rely more on heuristics that do not require expectations when making economic decisions.

detail.title: A Country of Two Theories: Coexistence of Collusion and Efficiency Hypotheses
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between market concentration, labor productivity, and real output, evaluating the efficiency and collusion hypotheses. We develop an oligopolistic model showing that, under technological progress, a positive concentration-output relationship arises in large and competitive markets, such as internationally exposed sectors, implying that the efficiency and collusion hypotheses can coexist within an economy. Using Taiwanese census data, we find that concentration reduces output in locally-oriented service sectors despite rising productivity, while it increases output in manufacturing sectors. These findings reveal sectoral heterogeneity and suggest that uniform antitrust enforcement may lead to over-deterrence risk in Taiwan's manufacturing sector.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates features of performance persistence in actively managed mutual funds, when fund performance is measured relative to both funds' self-reported benchmarks and peer groups. Using a novel benchmark-and peer-group-adjusted performance model (MMT), we evaluate 735 US Large Cap Growth funds from 1990 to 2018. Our findings show that MMTidentified winner funds deliver persistent outperformance across 6-, 12-, and 24-month holding periods, with the strongest results for shorter rebalancing intervals. Crucially, this persistence holds across market regimes-including crisis periods-and survives realistic transaction cost estimates, supporting the model's practical feasibility. Outperformance is not limited to the select few top funds; even diversified portfolios of MMT winners generate superior returns. The MMT model's strength lies in its ability to isolate persistent fund manager skill by adjusting for benchmark misalignment and peer-group dynamics, offering a robust alternative to traditional alpha-based models.

detail.abstract: We study whether frontier large language models (LLMs) exhibit prospect-theoretic framing patterns in risky choice and how their "risk posture" compares with-and impacts-humans in business-relevant contexts. We conducted two between-subjects discrete-choice experiments in which a panel of 18 LLMs and human participants evaluated four numerically equivalent gain-loss framing scenarios, chose between a "certain" option and a probabilistic one, and provided a brief justification. The majority of frontier "reasoning" or chat LLMs favored certainty across frames and contexts between 87-100% of the time, substantially attenuating the classic human-like gain-loss reversal. In contrast, lighter-weight models exhibit greater human-like sensitivity to framing and, in some cases, extreme risk-seeking. In the second experiment, human data reproduce the classic gain-loss framing effect, with modest variation across scenarios. However, when presented with a "committee of advisors" recommendation from AI models in the first experiment, human decisions shift dramatically toward conservatism in both domains, suggesting adherence to AI advice in all scenarios. The probability that subjects chose the certainty option increased by between 8 and 15.5 percentage points in the gain frame, and between 25 and 37 percentage points in the loss frame, controlling for risk preferences and other factors. AI topic modeling of justifications suggests that humans emphasized fairness, responsibility, and moral concerns, whereas LLMs uniformly justified choices by minimizing uncertainty. Our findings suggest that LLM integration is not a neutral upgrade but an implicit implementation of specific organizational risk preferences, with significant implications for AI governance and human-AI collaboration.

title: SupplyQual: An Approach for using Customer Reviews for Evaluating Last-Mile Delivery Performance

detail.title: SupplyQual: An Approach for using Customer Reviews for Evaluating Last-Mile Delivery Performance
detail.abstract: As e-commerce platforms scale, the volume of unstructured customer feedback has outpaced the ability of logistics providers to extract actionable insights. Traditional evaluation methods often rely on explicitly seeking numerical ratings of delivery performance. However, it fails to capture the nuances of last-mile delivery failures, such as distribution center bottlenecks or delivery partner related inefficiencies. We propose SupplyQual, a novel framework that transforms customer feedback into a structured knowledge graph, enabling sophisticated multi-hop queries via an agentic framework. By integrating a Model Context Protocol based access, our framework allows LLM based agents to perform grounded natural language querying over this data. We evaluate our approach using a dataset of 124 queries, demonstrating that the graph-based agentic system achieves a 5.7% improvement in faithfulness and a 2.3% increase in context precision over standard RAG based baselines. Our results suggest that SupplyQual provides a scalable and reliable method for automating qualitative assessments in high-growth, fragmented logistics environments like India.

detail.abstract: Organizations operate in conditions of non-equilibrium in which generative AI compresses feedback cycles and increases strategic variance across decision episodes. While dynamic capabilities explain how firms sense, seize, and transform, they specify less clearly how strategic direction is governed when cognition is distributed across human actors and AI systems. This paper extends dynamic capabilities theory by introducing trajectory coherence, defined as the bounded regulation of strategic variance over time to preserve directional continuity. We conceptualize strategic calibration as the governance process through which organizations align feedback cadence, regulate variance thresholds, and structure interpretive oversight under AI-mediated feedback. The framework proposes that AI intensity amplifies strategic variance, while governance mechanisms moderate this relationship and enable trajectory coherence. The model is falsifiable through longitudinal measurement of directional continuity, variance dispersion, and governance architecture, offering a foundation for empirical research on strategy in AI-mediated environments.

title: Big in Japan -A Case Study on IKEA
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Big in Japan -A Case Study on IKEA
detail.abstract:
Background and Purpose: Japan is a difficult market for foreign companies to stay alive in; something of which IKEA has first-hand experience. While largely successful globally, IKEA had to withdraw from the Japanese market in 1986 after 12 years of struggle. However, on the 20th anniversary of its failure, IKEA made a second attempt at the Japanese market by opening two stores, and further expanded in 2008 with three additional stores. In this thesis, I describe and explain how IKEA entered the Japanese market, why it took two decades before the second try, what was done differently to ensure market survival and to what extent the IKEA concept was adapted to local preferences.

Method: The thesis is written in the form of a descriptive case study, grounded in a variety of sources. Theory was mostly found in text books and academic journals, while empiric data was collected from articles and official web sites. An interview with a project leader at the Swedish Trade Council was also conducted.

Conclusions: The reason why IKEA failed to penetrate the Japanese market in the 1970s can mostly be attributed to factors regarding timing and commitment. During the absence from the Japanese market, IKEA gained extensive international experience and established a global production and distribution network. In addition, the Japanese customers changed to become more receptive to the IKEA concept. During the second attempt, large investments were carried out which signaled market commitment. It also enabled IKEA to control every aspect of its operations in detail. This all-out approach was made possible by the private ownership structure of IKEA that allows for ambitious projects that will take decades to break even. Regarding localization, the products themselves keep to IKEA's highly standardized concept. By this, IKEA can realize economies of scale and be highly competitive in pricing. The adaptations that have been carried out have mostly been centered on the in-store experience. However, stores are decidedly IKEAn even in Japan. Measures were also taken to ensure that IKEA keeps to the original concept internally, by employing Swedish people to management positions.

title: Superintelligent Counsel and the Bargaining Theory of War: information symmetry, commitment floors, and adversarial coevolution

detail.title: Superintelligent Counsel and the Bargaining Theory of War: information symmetry, commitment floors, and adversarial coevolution
detail.abstract: Fearon's rationalist model of war rests on two central mechanisms: private information with incentives to misrepresent and credible commitment problems. This paper asks what happens to that logic when states rely on machine advisers capable of modeling counterparties with superhuman fidelity. Does diplomacy become trivially solvable because uncertainty disappears, or do machine advisers instead intensify strategic competition by exposing commitment problems and by shifting competition toward the determinants of future bargaining power? I answer this question in a Bayesian dynamic bargaining model with an explicit machine-intelligence parameter. As advisory capability rises, private information is progressively eliminated in the Blackwell sense, so information-driven bargaining failures vanish. But the limiting war probability does not generally converge to zero. It converges to a commitment floor : the set of states in which no self-enforcing peaceful bargain exists. I then show that superintelligent counsel does not generically collapse diplomacy to a single equilibrium. Unique convergence requires restrictive conditions-a singleton peaceful bargaining set together with a common and unique selection device. In decentralized interaction, the relevant limit object is instead a setvalued equilibrium correspondence, consistent with results on correlated, communication, and Bayes correlated equilibrium. Finally, I extend the model to allow investments in future power, strategic opacity, and commitment technologies. In that meta-game, commitment infrastructure is underprovided while relative-advantage investments are overprovided. Moreover, when the meta-game is supermodular, the smallest and largest equilibrium leverage profiles rise weakly with machine capability. The upshot is conditional but sharp: superintelligent counsel removes epistemic fog, leaves commitment failures intact, and can make agreement structurally harder unless institutions for verification, mediation, and enforcement improve alongside intelligence.

detail.abstract: We examine how gossip about peers' performance, a form of informal communication, influences employees' performance manipulation. Gossip can be a salient social cue that signals social evaluation and activates social image concerns. In response, employees may choose to inflate their performance to alleviate these concerns and protect their image. We predict that this effect will be weaker for employees with higher self-monitoring, as they are more adept at tailoring their behavior to social cues and managing their image. Using data from two field surveys and an experiment, we find support for our predictions and evidence that employees with lower self-monitoring engage in greater performance manipulation to address social image concerns triggered by negative peer performance gossip. We contribute to the accounting literature by uncovering a social motive for performance manipulation, and highlight a reason for firms to manage gossip about peer performance.
