detail.abstract:
Every year, millions of preventable deaths in the Global South could be averted with timely access to affordable medicines. While achieving equitable pharmaceutical access is widely recognized as a critical global health challenge, the mechanisms for doing so remain contested. Prevailing debates focus narrowly on reconciling R&D incentives with access, overlooking deeper structural and political determinants. This paper argues that the misalignment between innovation incentives and public health needs is a systemic outcome of an innovation regime in which large pharmaceutical corporations allocate resources based on financialized business models designed to maximize shareholder value (MSV). We term this "predatory value extraction" (PVE) governance and argue that addressing the access challenge requires structural reform oriented toward "progressive value creation" (PVC) governance as its antithesis. 

The paper surveys the structural shortcomings behind persistent medicine access gaps in the Global South, then examines how PVE governance has undermined governments, international agencies and other stakeholders working on access initiatives. By tracing the financing of global health initiatives, we show how fragmentation, limited coordination, and donor funding dependencies entrench PVE-driven agenda-setting and exacerbate misaligned priorities in global health. We conclude by outlining steps that policymakers can take to shift the pharmaceutical industry's dominant corporate governance model from PVE toward PVC.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: As the operational boundaries between two-sided platforms increasingly blur, we examine the strategic implications of pricing schemes on platform compatibility agreement. Specifically, a dominant platform with awareness advantage may open a compatible interface for a competitive niche platform. In this setting, the niche platform strategically selects between a unified or a differential pricing scheme for the compatible channel relative to its exclusive channel.

Methodology/results: We develop stylized game models to examine the co-opetition interaction between the dominant and niche platforms. First, we find that compatibility does not always induce price reductions by either platform. Compatibility softens competition under unified pricing but intensifies it under differential pricing, where the niche platform charges a lower compatible channel price while increasing its exclusive channel price. Second, compatibility can be sustained as an equilibrium under unified pricing only when the niche platform’s awareness is high and the compatibility-induced convenience gain is limited. In contrast, under the differential pricing scheme, compatibility becomes unstable as adverse profit redistribution erodes the dominant platform’s incentive to participate. Third, comparing the effects of the two pricing schemes, we find that differential pricing provides the niche platform greater leverage and shifts profits toward the compatible channel, whereas unified pricing mitigates competition and preserves a balanced channel structure. Last, compatibility affects stakeholder welfare differently, redistributing benefits across consumers, providers, and platforms rather than uniformly increasing total surplus.

Managerial implications: Our study provides guidance on the conditions under which platform firms profitably pursue compatibility. The strategic essence of compatibility decision lies in the redistribution of surplus, which shapes the participation incentives of platforms. Managers are advised to calibrate compatibility agreements based on relative awareness advantages and the convenience gains associated with the compatible channel.

title: The Original Email that Started Occupy Wall Street

detail.title: The Original Email that Started Occupy Wall Street
detail.abstract: Occupy Wall Street began on September 17, 2011, when thousands gathered in New York’s Zuccotti Park to protest inequality and corporate power. The movement originated with Adbusters editors, whose call for action—amplified online by Anonymous—sparked a global wave of grassroots activism. This article’s central contribution is the presentation of the original Adbusters email that ignited the movement, revealing how a single message helped catalyze a historic shift toward decentralized, participatory protest against financial-political dominance.

title: The Replication Renaissance: Why Science Starves for What It Won't Serve
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Replication Renaissance: Why Science Starves for What It Won't Serve
detail.abstract: The replication crisis is not a scandal of bad actors. It is a failure of physics. In any information-processing system, when the reward for signal novelty outpaces the structural penalty for noise, the system hallucinates. Science is no exception. Recent text-mining of epidemiology and psychology literature (2024-2025) confirms a non-random spike in p-values between 0.045 and 0.049-the physical fingerprint of interpretive variance overwhelming experimental constraint. We formalize the crisis using the Coordination Invariant (S = C/V), derived from Shannon entropy: Scientific Stability = Constraint / Variance. When V grows without proportional increase in C, mutual information between published claims and reality collapses exponentially. At current incentive ratios, replication project data converge on 70-80% of "significant" findings in high-impact journals being statistically indistinguishable from noise. The fix is not better scientists. It is better physics. We propose three architectural interventions: (1) a Verification Score (Vs) weighting citations by independent replication status; (2) Registered Reports as default publication infrastructure; and (3) a Live Literature Protocol in which every paper carries a real-time stability designation. Registered Reports already publish null results at dramatically higher rates (54% vs. 21% in traditional workflows)-not because they fail, but because they finally report what is actually there. The Renaissance does not require moral reform. It requires constraint. Build the C. Let the truth emerge.

detail.abstract: This submission shows that when the European Commission said in its draft Technology Transfer Guidelines that: “it can be analysed whether after the agreement there will be a sufficient number of competing research and development projects left for effective competition in innovation to be maintained” it confirmed that it protects competition in Future Markets.  Research and development projects only compete against each other when they are trying to make the same future product; in other words the research projects compete only if the products they are trying to develop compete in a Future Market.  And whenever any competition authority analyzes competition in a Future Market it must determine if, after the relevant transaction, a sufficient number of firms will compete in that market.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Published in Computer Law & Security Review, Vol. 61, issue 106306, 2026.

detail.abstract: The ever-increasing reliance on AI systems in courts and its associated risks prompt the question whether there is a need for clearer frameworks to safeguard adherence to the right to a fair trial and the rule of law. Although some frameworks are being developed-mainly in the form of guidelines, strategies or ethical charters-they often remain vague, relying on high-level principles rather than concrete standards. This article proposes an innovative approach to strengthen the regulatory framework for AI in courts by drawing inspiration from existing frameworks for judicial experts. In fact, judicial AI systems may be considered "judicial experts" in cases when judges depend on them in ways similar to how they rely on traditional experts. By examining the obligations imposed on judicial experts, this article explores which of these could be extended or adapted to judicial AI systems. After all, if AI is employed in a similar capacity, why should it not be subject to the same, or even stricter, requirements?

detail.abstract: The 2022 European energy crisis exposed the central role of supply substitution in natural gas markets, as disruptions to Russian pipeline flows were accompanied by a sharp surge in liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports. This paper revisits the fundamentals of the European natural gas market by explicitly distinguishing between pipeline gas and LNG supplies. Using a Bayesian Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) identified through sign and elasticity restrictions, the analysis jointly identifies the contemporaneous elasticities of natural gas prices, supply by source, inventories, and euro area industrial production. The results reveal pronounced heterogeneity across supply channels: pipeline gas is highly price inelastic, whereas LNG serves as the primary adjustment channel on the supply side. Although both supply shocks affect prices, pipeline disruptions generate sharp but short-lived inflationary effects, while LNG supply shocks exert more persistent influences on price dynamics. More broadly, the dynamics of gas prices exhibit a clear horizon-dependent structure, with short-run fluctuations driven by supply shocks and inventory behavior, and medium-to long-run movements increasingly shaped by aggregate demand forces. Counterfactual scenarios of the 2022 energy crisis quantify the stabilizing role of LNG availability and demand adjustment, highlighting how supply composition critically shapes energy price dynamics in Europe.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2605

detail.abstract: Private equity funds play an increasingly important role in financial systems. Yet the impact of monetary policy on their activity has been little explored so far. In this paper, we analyse the transmission of monetary policy through private equity (PE) deals, focusing on the impact on: (i) the volume of private equity deals; (ii) the use of leverage; and (iii) the pricing of those deals. We find that contractionary monetary policy shocks at the short end of the yield curve tend to dampen private equity activity, by reducing deal volumes, the use of leverage and deal prices. A credit channel of monetary transmission seems to affect deal volumes and the use of leverage, while a valuation channel appears to drive the transmission to deal pricing. Monetary policy shocks at the long end of the yield curve have weaker effects on PE activity.

title: Opportunity Zones and the Housing Supply: Do Place-Based Tax Subsidies Create Net New Construction?
affiliations: University of South Carolina

detail.title: Opportunity Zones and the Housing Supply: Do Place-Based Tax Subsidies Create Net New Construction?
detail.abstract: I study whether the Opportunity Zones (OZ) program, the largest place-based developer subsidy in U.S. history, generated net new housing supply or merely redistributed construction across space and time. Using a quarterly panel of residential address counts for all U.S. census tracts from 2012 to 2022, I estimate inverse-probability weighted difference-indifferences models using non-OZ tracts at least ten miles from any designated zone as the comparison group, with propensity score weights following Abadie (2005) to balance pre-treatment characteristics between treated and control tracts. A naive baseline comparison yields a marginally positive treatment effect, consistent with headline estimates in prior work, but this estimate reflects two redistribution mechanisms rather than genuine new construction. First, residential address growth slowed in the three quarters immediately preceding QOF opening, as developers apparently waited for formal eligibility before breaking ground, an anticipation effect that artificially depresses the pre-treatment baseline. Second, non-OZ tracts within ten miles of a designated zone experienced a symmetrical decline in address growth after OZs opened, indicating that investment relocated across census-tract boundaries rather than expanding the supply frontier. The net effect of OZ designation on housing supply is statistically and economically indistinguishable from zero once both mechanisms are accounted for, casting doubt on the efficacy of the proposed expansion of OZ-style incentives in the One Big Beautiful Budget Act for stimulating new housing production absent complementary zoning or infrastructure reform.

detail.abstract: Using monthly state-level U.S. house price data from 1975 to 2026, this paper studies how housing-cycle timing is organised across space at different cyclical frequencies. A time-frequency analysis identifies two prominent cycle bands in the regional panel: a medium-frequency band around 8-10 years and a longer band around 11-14 years. Both bands exhibit substantial time-varying cross-state synchronisation and clear spatial organisation, implying that the aggregate visibility of housing cycles depends not only on their presence across regional markets but also on how closely those regional cycles align in time. Their spatial character, however, differs sharply. The longer cycle is smooth and low-dimensional, organised around a large-scale spatial gradient and well summarised by a leading smooth spatial mode. The shorter cycle is also spatially organised, but in a less smooth, more regional, and more time-varying way. The results therefore reveal scale-specific spatial organisation in U.S. housing cycles. More generally, the findings show that important structure in housing fluctuations is missed by aggregate series and contemporaneous co-movement measures alone, and becomes visible only when regional cycles are examined at the appropriate cyclical scale.

detail.abstract:
The Federal Reserve is headed by Governors whom the President can remove "for cause." President Donald Trump invoked this provision to remove Governor Lisa Cook.  The U.S. Supreme Court granted review to address whether that removal comports with the "for cause" provision.  

This brief offers addresses the separation-of-powers implications of the Federal Reserve, including: (i) the unique constitutional history of the Federal Reserve; (ii) the statutory history of the term "for cause" as used for the Federal Reserve; and (iii) how Congress can preserve a measure of independence for the Federal Reserve through use of the anti-removal power. The brief takes no position on any case-specific facts but instead offers a conceptual framework to understand the Federal Reserve through the lens of Article II of the U.S. Constitution.

title: Girl-Child Education and Human Capital Development: A Path to Sustainable Development
affiliations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University - Department of Economics, Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka Nigeria and Nnamdi Azikiwe University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Girl-Child Education and Human Capital Development: A Path to Sustainable Development
detail.abstract:
A girl child is a young female individual from birth to the end of adolescence, typically under 18 years old, who is entitled to fundamental human rights and protection. The term "girl child" specifically highlights this demographic and often refers to the empowerment and challenges they face globally, including issues of education, early marriage, and gender bias. The main objective of this chapter is to examine the role of girl child education in human capital development and how it serves as a pathway to achieving sustainable development. It derived the objective for conceptualizing that girl-child education should not only be among the critical drivers of human capital development, but also one of the fundamental pathways to sustainable development.
Its framework integrates theories such as human capital theory (Becker, 1964; Schultz, 1961); the capability approach models of (Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2011) and the Heckman's Life-Cycle Theory (2006) all having their core emphasis on human capital and girl child education. This chapter also incorporated the sustainable development theory that further situates girl-child
education as not only an enabler of sustainable development but also economic, social and environmental sustainability, (World Commission on Environment and Development(WCED, 1987).
At the core of this chapter is the framework that predisposes that access to quality education for a girl child enhances their knowledge, skills, health awareness, empowerment and opportunities. These
capital assets through education translate into human capital development outcomes that will not only improve labor productivity, reduce infertility rates, better maternal and child health and enhance
innovation capacity but will in turn, become fundamentals keys for sustainable development, particularly by advancing poverty reduction, gender equality, inclusive growth, and inter-generational
progress which align with the sustainable development goals (SDGs).

detail.abstract: This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in rural public schools and its implications for teacher quality and educational equity in the Philippines. AI adoption in education promises enhanced instructional efficiency, personalized learning, and automated assessment; however, disparities in access and digital literacy threaten equitable outcomes. Using a mixedmethods approach, quantitative data were collected from 100 teachers, complemented by key informant interviews and focus group discussions. Results indicate that AI significantly improves instructional practices and teacher performance, but unequal access to technology exacerbates existing educational inequities. Teacher training, digital literacy, and institutional support were identified as critical factors for successful AI integration. The study proposes a framework for equitable AI adoption, emphasizing capacity-building, policy support, and infrastructure enhancement. Findings contribute to educational policy and technology-driven teaching reform in rural settings.

keywords: Practical Emotional Intelligence Framework for Trauma Recovery

detail.abstract:
Abstract

Emotional intelligence research has significantly expanded understanding of emotional awareness, emotional perception, and emotional regulation. However, a persistent gap remains between emotional awareness and consistent behavioral application in real-world environments such as education, leadership, addiction recovery, and crisis response.

This paper introduces the R.E.A.L. Method (Recognize → Explore → Align → Lead), a structured framework designed to translate emotional awareness into responsible behavioral action. The framework introduces the concept of Applied Emotional Functioning, defined as the capacity to recognize emotional experiences, explore emotional meaning, align responses with personal values, and lead behavior through intentional action.

The model integrates principles from trauma-informed psychology, self-regulation theory, behavioral psychology, and cognitive behavioral approaches. The framework is supported by an ecosystem of reflective tools including guided workbooks, emotional reflection exercises, and real-time emotional regulation practices designed for use in educational, recovery, leadership, and crisis intervention environments.

To support empirical research, this paper introduces the R.E.A.L. Scales, a proposed measurement instrument designed to assess applied emotional functioning across four domains corresponding to the stages of the R.E.A.L. Method. The paper outlines the conceptual structure of the scale and proposes a validation methodology including exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and reliability testing.

The R.E.A.L. Method contributes to emotional intelligence research by providing a structured pathway connecting emotional awareness with behavioral leadership and responsible decision-making. Future research directions include empirical validation of the R.E.A.L. Scales and evaluation of the framework's effectiveness across educational, recovery, and organizational settings.

title: Socio-Cultural Challenges and Inclusive Education in Nigeria
affiliations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University - Department of Economics, Nnamdi Azikiwe University - Department of Economics and Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka Nigeria

detail.title: Socio-Cultural Challenges and Inclusive Education in Nigeria
detail.abstract:
Sociocultural challenges is refer to as difficulties and obstacles that arise from the interaction of social and cultural factors within community or society. These challenges can impact individuals, groups and broader society. Nigeria faces numerous sociocultural challenges that impact its development and citizens well-being. The goal of inclusive education on the other hand is to guarantee that all person may access, participate in, and gain from educational environments, irrespective of their socioeconomic background, gender, race, language, handicap, or other variety (UNESCO, 2020). The Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 4, which strives for inclusive and equitable quality education for all) and international human rights law (such as the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities) serve as the foundation for this idea (UNESCO, 2015; UN General Assembly, 2015). The legal and policy frameworks in Nigeria have changed to reflect this dedication: the Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act of 2018 for instance seeks to safeguard the rights of people with disabilities, and the National Policy on Education contains provisions for special and inclusive education (UNESCO, 2020). 
In Nigeria, sociocultural issues are one of the obstacles preventing marginalized groups from participating fairly and achieving equitable learning outcomes. Children with impairments are stigmatized, their enrolment is discouraged, and they may even be hidden or neglected as a result of beliefs that, for instance, frequently attribute impairment to supernatural causes, curses, or family shame (Project Enable Africa, 2024; Glory Ifezue Foundation, 2025). Social norms and girls’ education, GCI, 2022; “The Challenges and Opportunities of Inclusive Education in Nigeria,” (Angwaomaodoko, 2023). 
Gender norms also play a significant role. In many communities, girls are expected to help with household chores or marry young. When trade-offs must be made (due to poverty, distance, or resource constraints), families typically prioritise the education of boys. Ethnic, religious, and linguistic diversity can further amplify exclusion: children whose first language differs from the language of instruction, or those from minority religious or ethnic groups, often find the curricula culturally distant or inaccessible, which negatively affects both attendance and learning (Angwaomaodoko, 2023; Centre for Disability & Inclusion Africa, 2024).
Cultural standards are intricately linked to poverty and communal expectations, which further solidifies exclusion in reality. Indirect expenses including books, uniforms, transportation, and even assistive technology provide significant obstacles even in circumstances where education is officially free, especially for low-income households or those living in remote locations (Angwaomaodoko, 2024). Thus, while policy frameworks and good intentions exist, without addressing these sociocultural challenges inclusive education in Nigeria will continue to fall short of its promise.

detail.abstract:
Digital platforms have democratized access to commerce but introduced a new form of financial precarity: Platform Extraction. This paper introduces the Extraction Index (EI), a quantitative framework for measuring the structural risk of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) operating within digital enclosures like Amazon FBA.

Drawing on post-colonial economic theory, this research argues that modern platform ecosystems function as "Digital Company Towns," where high fees, information asymmetry, and lack of data sovereignty create a "Double Extraction Loop" that mirrors historical sharecropping. We propose a multivariate formula—weighted for Platform Dependency (D), Fee Burden (F), Information Asymmetry (A), and Exit Difficulty (E)—to predict business fragility.

Validated against a definitive FY2025 dataset of 78,078 SBA 7(a) loan applications (representing $37.2 billion in deployed capital), the EI demonstrates that traditional metrics fail to account for platform dependency. This failure is particularly devastating among Black-owned businesses, who currently capture a mere 4.2% of federal loan dollars despite record lending volumes.

Furthermore, this updated framework addresses the $700 billion AI infrastructure inversion currently underway. We hypothesize and demonstrate that the mass deployment of enterprise AI agents is accelerating platform capture, converting fixed software costs into variable inference burdens, and transforming Exit Difficulty from expensive to existential. This framework offers lenders, regulators, and founders a standardized metric to assess "Digital Sovereignty" and mitigate systemic risk before AI-driven dependencies permanently calcify.

title: Anticipatory AI Governance within the Provincial Council of Gipuzkoa: Action Research for a Digital Inclusion Strategy in the Basque Country
affiliations: Ikerbasque Foundation UPV/EHU and University of the Basque Country - Gipuzkoa Campus

detail.title: Anticipatory AI Governance within the Provincial Council of Gipuzkoa: Action Research for a Digital Inclusion Strategy in the Basque Country

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how subnational governments can operationalise anticipatory AI governance to advance territorial digital inclusion while safeguarding democratic accountability, human digital rights, and institutional legitimacy. Focusing on the Provincial Council of Gipuzkoa in the Basque Country, the study develops an action-research approach that connects AI governance with a territorial digital inclusion strategy. The paper argues that AI governance should be understood not only as a regulatory challenge but also as a matter of institutional capability, democratic innovation, and mission-oriented public action.

Methodologically, the research applies a mixed-methods design combining qualitative action research with quantitative evidence from an online survey of 911 citizens. The qualitative component involved multi-stakeholder engagement with six civil society organisations, seven provincial directorates, and eleven municipalities, structured through an eight-step action-research cycle carried out between 2024 and 2026. This process included alignment with the II Diversity Plan, collaboration with the NGO network Aniztasunaren Sarea, inter-municipal engagement through ElkarBizi, media dissemination, and international academic exchange.

A central outcome of the research is the co-produced “Digital Inclusion and Generative AI Decalogue,” which identifies ten dimensions grouped into four blocks: digital divide, algorithmic bias, data divide, and digital futures. Findings show that digital inclusion is a structural governance challenge rather than a merely technical one; algorithmic risks are recognised differently across stakeholder groups; and persistent data divides continue to limit inclusive policymaking. At the same time, stakeholders converge around the need for ethical, transparent, and inclusive AI governance frameworks.

The survey results reinforce the urgency of anticipatory governance: 74% of respondents had already used AI tools, 62% reported weekly use, 47% expressed concerns about privacy and data protection, and 44% perceived risks of technological dependence. These findings suggest that AI has already become a social and cognitive infrastructure, making the design of territorially grounded, democratically accountable governance models increasingly urgent. Overall, the paper contributes a replicable framework for anticipatory AI governance at the city-regional level, showing how public institutions can align innovation with inclusion, participation, and rights-based oversight.

title: Customer Satisfaction as a Social Construction: Norms, Expectations, and Contradictions in the Discourse of Telecommunications Users in Senegal
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Customer Satisfaction as a Social Construction: Norms, Expectations, and Contradictions in the Discourse of Telecommunications Users in Senegal
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the satisfaction of telecommunications service customers in Senegal not as an objective fact, but as a complex social construction. Drawing on the theoretical framework of social constructivism and a critique of quantification, we examine how norms, expectations, and contradictions structure the discourse of users of Sonatel, the historical and dominant operator. The study of the protest movements reveals a deep gap between the company's marketing discourse, the regulatory frameworks, and the lived experience of consumers. We argue that quantitative approaches to satisfaction, by seeking to reduce it to numerical indicators, mask these tensions and primarily serve to legitimize the company's power. By favoring a qualitative analysis of user discourse, this article highlights the eminently political dimension of satisfaction and the role of collective mobilizations in redefining service norms.

title: How AI Aggregation Affects Knowledge
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, Columbia University - Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research (IEOR), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and

detail.title: How AI Aggregation Affects Knowledge
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) changes social learning when aggregated outputs become training data for future predictions. To study this, we extend the DeGroot model by introducing an AI aggregator that trains on population beliefs and feeds synthesized signals back to agents. We define the learning gap as the deviation of long-run beliefs from the efficient benchmark, allowing us to capture how AI aggregation affects learning. Our main result identifies a threshold in the speed of updating: when the aggregator updates too quickly, there is no positive-measure set of training weights that robustly improves learning across a broad class of environments, whereas such weights exist when updating is sufficiently slow. We then compare global and local architectures. Local aggregators trained on proximate or topic-specific data robustly improve learning in all environments. Consequently, replacing specialized local aggregators with a single global aggregator worsens learning in at least one dimension of the state.

title: From Chicago to Malatya: Building Soul of Post-Earthquake Cities
affiliations: Catholic Theological Union, Chicago

detail.title: From Chicago to Malatya: Building Soul of Post-Earthquake Cities
detail.abstract:
This article analyzes the large-scale post-earthquake reconstruction process in Türkiye following the Feb. 6, 2023 earthquakes, moving beyond a purely technical narrative of success to interrogate the distinction between “building a city” and “cultivating its soul.” While recognizing the construction of over 450,000 housing units within a remarkably short period as an unprecedented administrative and engineering mobilization, the paper argues that the provision of physical shelter alone is insufficient to render a city truly “alive.” The “On-Site Transformation” model is therefore conceptualized not merely as a spatial redevelopment strategy but as a form of social rehabilitation aimed at preserving neighborhood continuity, collective memory, and local identity. In doing so, the article reframes post-disaster reconstruction as an interplay between infrastructural capacity and cultural sustainability.

The second axis of the article emphasizes the transition from reconstruction to cultural cultivation. It proposes the establishment of “Living Libraries” as strategic nodes of social infrastructure designed to foster communal solidarity, intergenerational dialogue, and social integration within newly built housing zones. Drawing on the author’s experience in Chicago and integrating the Anatolian tradition of imece (collective labor), the model seeks to bridge technical rebuilding with social revitalization. Ultimately, the article contends that the true measure of post-disaster success lies not in the quantity of housing delivered, but in the creation of social harbors capable of transforming newly constructed residences into enduring homes embedded within a resilient urban culture.

detail.abstract: Labour welfare has always been an essential component of socio-economic development in India. With rapid industrialisation, technological transformation, and the expansion of informal and gig employment, the traditional labour law framework required reform. In response, the Government of India consolidated 29 existing labour legislations into four comprehensive labour codes: the Code on Wages, 2019; the Industrial Relations Code, 2020; the Code on Social Security, 2020; and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. These reforms aim to simplify labour regulations while ensuring better protection for workers. This research article examines the role of these new labour laws in protecting labourers, particularly focusing on health, safety, and social security provisions. The study concludes that the new labour codes represent a significant step towards improving workers’ welfare, although effective implementation remains crucial.

title: Can Personal Access to Medical Expertise Overcome Vaccine Hesitancy?

detail.title: Can Personal Access to Medical Expertise Overcome Vaccine Hesitancy?
detail.abstract:
Using data on applicants to Dutch medical schools and their older relatives (i.e., parents, aunts, and uncles ages 60+), we estimate the effect of personal access to medical expertise on vaccine hesitancy. Leveraging variation in lottery outcomes that determine admission to medical schools, we find that having a physician in the family increases the likelihood of complying with government recommendations that anyone over the age of 59 receive a second booster dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. Our estimated effects are strongest for having a female physician in the family, suggesting important gender-based differences in how medical expertise is communicated.

title: Why Do Americans No Longer Work So Much More Than Non-Americans?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Research Division, University of Minnesota - Minneapolis and Government of Canada - Bank of Canada

detail.title: Why Do Americans No Longer Work So Much More Than Non-Americans?
detail.abstract:
In the 1990s, Americans used to work much more than non-Americans. Nowadays, about half of the gap in hours worked has reversed. To evaluate the convergence of working hours, we develop a tractable model of labor supply enriched with multiple sources of heterogeneity across individuals, an extensive margin of participation, multi-member households, and an elaborate system of taxes and benefits upon non-employment. Using detailed measurements from micro-level and aggregate datasets, we identify model parameters and sources of heterogeneity across individuals for various countries. We run a horse race between competing explanations and find that U.S. hours per person declined after 2000 owing mainly to the rise of government health benefits provided to the non-employed. Non-U.S. countries have generous benefits for the non-employed, but this generosity has not changed as much over time as in the United States, and public health coverage does not depend on employment status or income levels. For these countries, the rise of labor supply is generally accounted for by a mix of factors, such as the rise of wages and the falling disutility of work.

title: Constituencies of Conflict and Opportunity: Land Rights, Narratives and Collective Action in Darfur
affiliations: and University of Khartoum

detail.title: Constituencies of Conflict and Opportunity: Land Rights, Narratives and Collective Action in Darfur
detail.abstract: Grievance-based narratives are a primary component of civil wars. While present among the general population affected by conflict, the variants held by the segment of the population most proximate to the armed factions-constituencies-play a primary role in the development and conduct of a conflict. Such narratives can coalesce around specific volatile issues and enable non-combatant constituencies to participate in the conflict through the use of specific 'legalities' or legal precepts. These legalities facilitate the engagement of sets of collective action that are opposed to those derived by constituencies of the opposing side. However such constituencies and their narratives are also where potential opportunity resides for peace-building, both during and subsequent to hostilities. This article looks at the case of Darfur to examine these ingredients, with a focus on land rights as the volatile set of issues around which narratives have developed. In Darfur, opposed narratives which maintain how and why groups claim and deserve access to land and territory, and how groups were unjustly displaced or excluded from lands (and hence power), became solidified and acted upon prior to the conflict to become a primary driver in the current war. In certain cases however narrative change has led to interaction between members of opposed constituencies for the purpose of exploring cooperative arrangements.

title: Tariffs, Global Value Chains, and the Incidence of Protection: Evidence from US Automobiles
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research (CEEPR) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Tariffs, Global Value Chains, and the Incidence of Protection: Evidence from US Automobiles
detail.abstract:
In many modern industries, firms compete in differentiated-product markets while relying on complex global value chains for intermediate inputs. In such settings, trade policies such as tariffs on vehicles and parts operate not only through consumer substitution and firm pricing, but also through firms’ cost structures and sourcing decisions. We develop a structural model of the U.S. automobile market that integrates random-coefficients demand, multiproduct firm pricing, and a flexible supply-side framework in which shocks to the cost of imported parts transmit imperfectly into manufacturers’ marginal costs. The model is disciplined by novel model-level data on imported-parts exposure and exploits exchange-rate variation to identify cost pass-through. Our counterfactual analysis quantifies the effects of alternative tariff policies on prices, profits, and welfare. First, tariffs on imported vehicles alone reallocate demand toward domestically assembled products and increase U.S. producer surplus, generating a gain of approximately $1 billion for U.S.-headquartered firms, while reducing consumer surplus by about $14 billion. Second, extending tariffs to imported intermediate inputs fundamentally alters these effects: consumer surplus losses roughly double, and producer surplus for U.S.-headquartered firms declines by about $2.6 billion. These aggregate effects mask substantial heterogeneity: firms with greater exposure to imported parts experience losses, whereas those relying more on domestic inputs are better able to increase profits. Overall, the results show that tariff incidence depends critically on firms’ exposure to global value chains and cannot be inferred from final assembly locations alone.

detail.title: How Responsive are Durables Expenditures to Transitory Income Shocks?
detail.abstract:
We estimate how expenditures on durable goods respond to transitory income shocks using variation from the Economic Stimulus Act of 2008. The estimated responses are large: Households spent about 80 percent of their stimulus payment within three months of receiving the income transfer on durables alone. Most of this spending was on motor vehicles, either financed, used, or both, and about 20 percent of the total durables response was on smaller items. To purchase motor vehicles the average household levered up by 40 cents on the dollar using vehicle loans. Our findings suggest that durable goods and their financing are key to understanding the link between current income and spending.

title: AI Patents in the United States and China: Measurement, Organization, and Knowledge Flows

detail.title: AI Patents in the United States and China: Measurement, Organization, and Knowledge Flows
detail.abstract:
We develop a high-precision classifier to measure artificial intelligence (AI) patents by fine-tuning PatentSBERTa on manually labeled data from the USPTO’s AI Patent Dataset. Our classifier substantially improves the existing USPTO approach, achieving 97.0% precision, 91.3% recall, and a 94.0% F1 score, and it generalizes well to Chinese patents based on citation and lexical validation. Applying it to granted U.S. patents (1976–2023) and Chinese patents (2010–2023), we document rapid growth in AI patenting in both countries and broad convergence in AI patenting intensity and subfield composition, even as China surpasses the United States in recent annual patent counts. The organization of AI innovation nevertheless differs sharply: U.S. AI patenting is concentrated among large private incumbents and established hubs, whereas Chinese AI patenting is more geographically diffuse and institutionally diverse, with larger roles for universities and state-owned enterprises. For listed firms, AI patents command a robust market-value premium in both countries. Cross-border citations show continued technological interdependence rather than decoupling, with Chinese AI inventors relying more heavily on U.S. frontier knowledge than vice versa.

title: Which U.S. States Suffered a Greater Great Depression and Why?

detail.title: Which U.S. States Suffered a Greater Great Depression and Why?
detail.abstract:
Aggregate real U.S. GDP fell by roughly 26 percent between 1929 and 1932, yet the severity of the Great Depression varied dramatically across states: CPI-deflated income per capita declined by 15 percent in Maryland but by 48 percent in South Dakota. To analyze this heterogeneity, we digitize Slaughter’s (1937) panel of state-by-sector production income for all 48 U.S. states and construct a novel set of sector- and state-specific deflators, allowing us to separate movements in physical quantities produced from the large relative price changes that occurred during the Great Depression. We then discipline a three-sector, 48-region dynamic spatial stochastic general equilibrium model and recover sequences of sector-state productivity shocks that exactly reproduce the observed sector-state quantity paths. The choice of deflators proves central, as correct deflation shifts the aggregate contraction away from agriculture and toward manufacturing while preserving idiosyncratic income variation across agricultural-dependent states. We further show that narratives based on common or even sector-specific shocks are inconsistent with the observed evolutions of state-level quantities and relative prices. Explaining the geography of the Great Depression therefore requires a high-dimensional sector-state shock structure.

title: Subjective Earnings and Employment Dynamics
affiliations: CEMFI, Yale University, University of Torino - Dipartimento di scienze economico-sociali e matematico-statistiche, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, University College London, Economics Dpt. and European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research

detail.title: Subjective Earnings and Employment Dynamics
detail.abstract:
We develop a new approach to estimating earnings, job, and employment dynamics using subjective expectations data from the NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations. These data provide beliefs about future earnings offers and acceptance probabilities, offering direct information on counterfactual outcomes and enabling identification under weaker assumptions. Our framework avoids biases from selection and unobserved heterogeneity that affect models using realized outcomes. First-step fixed-effects regressions identify risk, persistence, and transition effects; second-step GMM recovers the covariance structure of unobserved heterogeneities such as ability, mobility, and match quality. We find lower risk and persistence of the individual productivity component than in prior work, but greater heterogeneity in ability and match quality. Simulations show that reduced-form estimates overstate persistence and volatility on individual-level productivity due to job transitions and sorting. After accounting for heterogeneity, volatility declines and becomes flat across the earnings distribution. These results underscore the value of expectations data.

title: Climate Change, Deforestation, and the Expansion of the Global Agricultural Frontier

detail.title: Climate Change, Deforestation, and the Expansion of the Global Agricultural Frontier
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how global warming affects deforestation and agricultural land use. Using high-resolution satellite data on global temperature, deforestation, and land cover from 2001 to 2019, we find that extreme heat shocks to agricultural productivity cause large and persistent forest loss on the world’s agricultural frontier. This effect is strongest in the tropics, in areas growing the most temperature-sensitive crops, and in regions with the most inelastic demand for agricultural products, and it does not seem to be offset by international spillovers. Moreover, we show that deforestation in response to extreme heat can be explained almost entirely by cropland expansion. We corroborate these findings using agricultural census data from Brazil, where we find evidence for a mechanism whereby heat reduces yields and raises local agricultural prices, driving cropland expansion but little land use or input adjustment along other margins. Our estimates imply that extreme heat has driven substantial forest loss and that projected warming through 2100 could lead to an additional 28 million hectares of deforestation. Our findings challenge the view that reallocation will soften the environmental consequences of climate change, suggesting instead that farmers double down and expand cropland locally when productivity falls.

title: Pharmaceutical Advertising in Dynamic Equilibrium

detail.title: Pharmaceutical Advertising in Dynamic Equilibrium
detail.abstract:
Direct-to-consumer advertising (DTCA) of prescription drugs may expand treatment access but also risks promoting overuse and business stealing without generating welfare gains. Among developed nations, only the United States and New Zealand permit DTCA, whereas detailing - promotion aimed at prescribers - is widely practiced. This paper analyzes the impact of DTCA on profits by modeling a counterfactual environment in which DTCA is banned. This is implemented through a dynamic equilibrium framework that adapts the Experience-Based Equilibrium (Fershtman and Pakes, 2012) for empirical analysis. EBE incorporates constraints on the cognitive abilities of decision-makers and mitigates researchers’ computational concerns. Using data from four therapeutic markets, we first validate the EBE’s ability to replicate observed advertising patterns, then simulate counterfactual DTCA bans. Both the data and our empirical work indicate that DTCA and detailing are strong complements, and our results illuminate the need to account for this when evaluating the ban. The ban leads firms to reduce detailing and has a negative effect on profits in all markets, but the magnitude of the effect varies from under 5% in the market for Ulcer to 27.5% for Asthma medications.

detail.title: Skill Formation, Child Labor, and the Schooling Consequences of the World War I Agricultural Boom
detail.abstract:
We examine how the World War I agricultural commodity price boom affected human capital accumulation during the early decades of the high school movement in the United States. First, based on newly collected county-level enrollment data, we show that enrollment and average daily attendance fell sharply at the peak of the boom. Second, using linked census data between 1910 and 1940, we find that greater exposure during teenage years reduced completed schooling by 0.27 to 0.47 years, with the largest effects concentrated in high school. For younger children, the net effect of increased household resources depends on local child labor intensity: the positive effect of higher parental income on completed schooling is offset in counties where child labor was prevalent. Our results are consistent with dynamic complementarities in skill formation whose effects on lifetime schooling are mediated by the opportunity cost of child labor.

title: Real Effects of Nominal Interest Rates

detail.title: Real Effects of Nominal Interest Rates
detail.abstract:
Nominal interest rates have real effects. Residential mortgages and other real world debt contracts require a sequence of constant nominal payments. Combined with payment-to-income constraints, these nominal payments force borrowers to take on less debt when nominal interest rates rise, regardless of the behavior of the real interest rate. Survey data shows that conditional on the real rate, higher nominal mortgage interest rates reduce home buying sentiment. And increases in nominal mortgage rates reduce mortgage origination more in cities where payment-to-income constraints are more likely to bind. We explore the macroeconomic implications of payment-to-income constraints in a new Keynesian model modified to include a credit good. The payment-to-income constraint amplifies the effect of current short-term nominal interest rates on output and inflation, making the model less forward-looking than the standard new Keynesian model.

detail.title: A Gender Quota for Top Executives: Diversity without Disruption
detail.abstract:
We study Germany’s landmark quota requiring major public companies to include at least one woman on their top executive teams. The quota increased female representation among top executives by about two-thirds. Firms largely recruited women from outside their networks and without prior public-company top-executive experience, choosing them over male candidates with similar profiles. Most were appointed to HR or niche roles, and there was no increase in female CEOs. We find no significant effects on the female share of managers in lower ranks, policies promoting gender equality, firm value, or performance. Overall, the quota boosted diversity without causing much disruption.

title: Liquidity-Driven Growth Cycles in Small Open Economies

detail.title: Liquidity-Driven Growth Cycles in Small Open Economies
detail.abstract:
While standard sudden-stop models explain well the sharpness of financial crises, it remains challenging to account for the persistent growth stagnation that typically follows credit-driven capital account liberalizations in emerging markets. This paper presents a small open economy model with endogenous growth and borrowing constraints to ex- plain this phenomenon. The model highlights a valuation optimistic growth expectations, fueled by foreign credit with perfectly elastic supply, raise asset prices and relax liquidity constraints, inducing investment that validates the initial optimism. This positive feed- back loop generates multiple balanced growth paths and self-fulfilling cycles. However, in closed economies or with only FDI inflows, funding supply for investment is limited by consumption smoothing, dampening this feedback and leading to a unique growth path. Belief-driven regime switches can replicate crisis dynamics, including sharp drops in asset prices and growth. The framework also exhibits periodic orbits, producing endogenous deterministic fluctuations under perfect foresight. Countercyclical macroprudential measures can disrupt the detrimental feedback loop, while policies prioritizing FDI over credit prevent bad equilibria altogether, guiding the economy toward a stable, high-growth trajectory.

detail.title: Adversarial Selection
detail.abstract:

We study environments with two adversarial parties whose preferences over the selected items are commonly known and opposed. We propose the Quantile Mechanism: one party partitions the population into k disjoint subsets, and the other selects one item from each subset. We show that this procedure is optimally representative among all feasible mechanisms, and illustrate its use in jury selection, multi-district litigation, and committee formation.

title: The Influence of Human Psychology on Financial Markets and Risk Management: A Behavioral Finance Perspective
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Influence of Human Psychology on Financial Markets and Risk Management: A Behavioral Finance Perspective
detail.abstract: Traditional financial theory is grounded in the assumption of rational agents who maximize utility with complete information. Empirical evidence, however, consistently demonstrates that human psychological factors significantly influence financial decision-making, resulting in systematic deviations from rationality. This paper examines the role of psychological elements in shaping financial markets and risk management practices from a behavioral finance perspective. Drawing on Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979) and major cognitive biases—such as overconfidence, loss aversion, herding, anchoring, and confirmation bias—the analysis illustrates how these factors contribute to market anomalies, asset mispricing, and suboptimal risk strategies. The study integrates a review of foundational literature with illustrative cases, including the 2008 global financial crisis, cryptocurrency market volatility, and exchange-rate fluctuations in the Turkish lira. In the domain of risk management, psychological biases are shown to impair the effectiveness of conventional tools such as Value-at-Risk models and portfolio optimization frameworks. The findings suggest that behavioral interventions can enhance decision quality. This paper contributes to the literature by synthesizing theoretical and empirical insights and offers practical recommendations for investors, risk managers, and regulators. It concludes that a deeper understanding of human psychology is essential for developing more resilient financial systems.

title: Amortized Inference for Correlated Discrete Choice Models via Equivariant Neural Networks
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: Amortized Inference for Correlated Discrete Choice Models via Equivariant Neural Networks
detail.abstract:
Discrete choice models are fundamental tools in management science, economics, and marketing for understanding and predicting decision-making. Logit-based models are dominant in applied work, largely due to their convenient closed-form expressions for choice probabilities. However, these models entail restrictive assumptions on the stochastic utility component, constraining our ability to capture realistic and theoretically grounded choice behavior—most notably, substitution patterns. In this work, we propose an amortized inference approach using a neural network emulator to approximate choice probabilities for general error distributions, including those with correlated errors. Our proposal includes a specialized neural network architecture and accompanying training procedures designed to respect the invariance properties of discrete choice models. We provide group-theoretic foundations for the architecture, including a proof of universal approximation given a minimal set of invariant features. Once trained, the emulator enables rapid likelihood evaluation and gradient computation. We use Sobolev training, augmenting the likelihood loss with a gradient-matching penalty so that the emulator learns both choice probabilities and their derivatives. We show that emulator-based maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal under mild approximation conditions, and we provide sandwich standard errors that remain valid even with imperfect likelihood approximation. Simulations show significant gains over the GHK simulator in accuracy and speed.

The q5-cost of equity is precise at the industry level and aligned with average factor premiums. Factor models perform poorly in out-of-sample tests. Gradient-boosted trees improve on cross-sectional regressions, but not reliably.

title: Capital in the Capitol: Congressional Trades Resemble Uninformed Retail Trading

detail.title: Capital in the Capitol: Congressional Trades Resemble Uninformed Retail Trading
detail.abstract:
Do elected officials exploit informational advantages for personal financial gain? This question has attracted heightened attention amid increased scrutiny of congressional stock trading, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic. Prior research finds little evidence that legislators outperform the market, but existing studies rely on limited time periods and offer limited insight into the mechanisms underlying trade timing. We revisit this question by constructing a novel dataset covering the stock trading activity of all U.S. members of Congress and their immediate families from 2012 to 2023. We find that, on average, legislators’ portfolios underperform or, at best, match market benchmarks after the STOCK Act. What explains this mediocre performance? We show that legislators’ positions track financial professionals’ recommendations, and that their timing largely reflects prevailing market sentiment, estimated from retail investors’ social media posts, rather than anticipating future price changes. Together, these results suggest that legislators’ observable trading behavior is more consistent with public-signal-following than with systematically profitable use of private information.

We examine the differential effects of minimum wages on immigrant and native workers in the United States. We find that minimum wage increases lead to reduced hours of work among immigrants with no effect on their employment. The effects are concentrated among recently-arrived, likely-undocumented workers in high turnover industries. Native workers show no such response, even when examining native subgroups with similar characteristics to the most affected immigrants. We conclude that affected immigrant labor markets feature low-surplus, low-investment employment relationships with flexible hours, but they are embedded in labor markets where replacement is unusually costly.

title: Land Re-Adjustment Among Arab Society in Israel

detail.title: Land Re-Adjustment Among Arab Society in Israel
detail.abstract: Israeli Arab citizens constitute approximately 21% of the Israel's population. Due to prolonged neglect by planning institutions, numerous Arab localities face inadequate infrastructure, underdevelopment, and a significant housing crisis. In the previous decade, in response to substantial criticism regarding discrimination against the Arab minority in Israel, planning institutions have initiated the promotion of master plans for Arab localities. A central mechanism in this process has involved land readjustment plans designed to reorganize the private lands of Arab landowners. Ultimately, these plans facilitate the allocation of new plots for housing, commerce, transportation, green spaces, and public needs. Planning institutions in Israel assert that the purpose of these plans is to develop modern neighbourhoods. However, considerable opposition has arisen among Arab landowners and stakeholders concerning these plans. This study examines the conflict between planning institutions and landowners regarding land readjustment mechanisms and includes an analysis of approximately 1,780 objections filed by landowners against various plans across multiple sites. This article elucidates the primary concerns of landowners, their protective aspirations, and the responses of planning institutions to their arguments. Furthermore, it reveals the planning and cultural tensions intrinsic to advancing land readjustment for private lands within Arab society.

title: Intermediation without Intermediaries
affiliations: Aston University - Aston Business School

detail.title: Intermediation without Intermediaries
detail.abstract: This paper proposes to investigate whether algorithmic financial intermediation escapes the economic forces that finance theory identifies as sources of financial fragility. The research combines reduced-form econometrics for causal identification, structural estimation of strategic complementarity, and a calibrated model for counterfactual analysis. Using on-chain data that provides cleaner identification than traditional banking studies, it tests whether established fragility mechanisms operate in algorithmic lending markets. The findings will inform regulators assessing the applicability of systemic risk frameworks to decentralised finance and guide protocol designers seeking to minimise fragility. As traditional financial infrastructure increasingly adopts algorithmic execution, automated margining, and real-time transparency, the fragilities identified here may also emerge in conventional markets.

title: Epistemic Failure and Methodological Reform in Financial Machine Learning: A Systematic Review of the Generalization Crisis (2015-2026)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Epistemic Failure and Methodological Reform in Financial Machine Learning: A Systematic Review of the Generalization Crisis (2015-2026)
detail.abstract: Financial machine learning aspires to convert highdimensional market data into repeatable predictive advantage, yet reported backtest performance often fails to translate to live deployment. This paper argues that the resulting "generalization crisis" is less a limitation of computational capacity than a limitation of epistemic and statistical rigor. By synthesizing evidence from over 150 primary sources and drawing parallels to the replication crisis in psychology and to Feynman's cautionary notion of "cargo-cult" scientific form without corresponding self-correction, we show that several common research practices are systematically misaligned with the causal and non-stationary structure of markets. We identify three recurrent sources of failure: the information-theoretic redundancy of purely price-derived technical indicators, the compression of high-dimensional fundamentals into low-dimensional linear ratios, and the inappropriate application of IID validation protocols to dependent time series. We further analyze failure modes in Large Language Model (LLM) pipelines arising from look-ahead bias and training-data contamination. We conclude that progress requires a pragmatic "causal turn" toward Automatic Feature Engineering (AFE), Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM), and Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV), aligning modeling practice with the realities of non-stationarity, dependence, and implementability.

title: Measuring Organizational Capital
affiliations: Columbia Business School, Columbia University in the City of New York and Columbia University

detail.title: Measuring Organizational Capital
detail.abstract:
Prior research has pointed to differences in organizational capital as a reason for the persistent performance discrepancies among otherwise similar firms. In this paper, we develop and validate a new measure of organizational capital. Based on over a million crowd-sourced employee reviews scraped from Glassdoor, we construct the measure of organizational capital at the firm-year level using the word embedding model and ChatGPT-generated synthetic reviews. Our measure varies over time in accordance with macro trends, and differs both across and within firms, reflecting firm heterogeneity and major internal changes. We validate our measure by testing empirical predictions of the properties of organizational capital discussed in prior literature. Our findings suggest that this measure captures a slowly evolving intangible asset that is significantly associated with firm performance and top management’s influence, aligning with the conceptualization of organizational capital by Dessein and Prat (2022). We further showcase applications of our measure in accounting, economics, finance, and management literature. Taken together, the paper provides implications for various stakeholders who are interested in assessing and managing firms’ organizational capital.

title: Human Capital, Ancestry, and Skill Composition
affiliations: Miami University

detail.title: Human Capital, Ancestry, and Skill Composition
detail.abstract: A central regularity of US economic geography is the spatial correlation between local human capital and the skill intensity of local industries, yet the causal effect of human capital on the skill composition of industries remains unclear. I examine how ancestry-induced shifts in historical human capital shape the contemporary industrial skill distribution of US counties. Exploiting quasi-random variation in ancestry composition for 1970-2010 based on origin-by-destination immigration stocks from 1860-2010, I generate plausibly exogenous variation in the skill structure of local working-age populations. The findings show that exogenous increases in medium-and high-skill worker shares raise the employment and establishment shares of high-skill industries and reduce those of low-skill industries. Adjustment is asymmetric across sectors: nontradables expand, consistent with stronger local demand, whereas tradables contract as relative scarcity of low-skill labor increases local costs. A model with imperfect substitution across skill types rationalizes these patterns and implies partial yet systematic reallocation toward skill-intensive economic activity following shifts in the labor force composition. The results identify a key mechanism through which long-run, demography-driven human capital shocks reshape regional production structure, informing local economic development and education policies.

title: Political Ideology and Durable Spending
affiliations: Belk College of Business, UNC Charlotte, Georgetown University, McDonough School of Business, Texas Tech University, Rawls College of Business and Georgetown University

detail.title: Political Ideology and Durable Spending
detail.abstract: We study political ideology as a driver of heterogeneous durable spending. Research in psychology suggests that conservatives' personality traits lead them to focus on the investment properties of durables, whereas liberals focus on consumption value. Combining U.S. voter registration records with housing transactions, which capture both consumption and investment motives, we show that conservatives transact more frequently, especially in secondary properties, which do not necessarily provide any consumption value. Conditional on transacting, conservatives more often trade down and realize capital gains, while liberals trade up and increase housing consumption. Conservatives' transactions, but not liberals', respond more strongly to financial incentives: interest rates, the opportunity cost of housing investments relative to equities, and house-price appreciation. Within households, ideology does not combine linearly: mixed-ideology couples transact less than ideologically homogeneous ones of either color, and their choices align more closely with the man's ideology.

title: Triadic Logical Structures as Coordination Layers in Artificial Intelligence Architectures

detail.title: Triadic Logical Structures as Coordination Layers in Artificial Intelligence Architectures
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence into critical infrastructure exposes a structural limitation in the bivalent logic underlying automated decision-making. While probabilistic reasoning models allow systems to process gradients of certainty, their execution phases almost inevitably collapse into a binary threshold (true/false, permit/deny), forcing high-ambiguity transactions into fragile permissive or restrictive states. This research investigates the architectural viability of triadic logical structures as a coordination layer between probabilistic inference and deterministic verification in precision-critical AI environments. Specifically, this analysis examines the hypothesis proposed by Lev Goukassian's Ternary Logic (TL) and Ternary Moral Logic (TML) frameworks, which introduce a formalized third state known as the "Epistemic Hold" or "Sacred Pause." This third state serves as a mandatory deliberative phase, explicitly decoupling high-speed statistical inference from deterministic governance and accountability. Through a comprehensive review of historical three-valued logic systems, unstructured multi-agent architectures, and hardware implementation constraints, this report demonstrates how triadic coordination layers can prevent hallucination cascades and provide deterministic triggers for human-in-the-loop oversight. While significant technical challenges remain regarding multi-valued logic hardware emulation and cryptographic overhead, the theoretical alignment with modern decision theory suggests that transitioning from bivalent execution models is necessary to ensure the safety, auditability, and cognitive integrity of future autonomous systems.

detail.abstract: Climate change, as rightfully depicted as one of the most pressing issues in our world today, carries with it impacts beyond mere scientific problems. With increased climate change comes a social crisis that directly or indirectly affects people’s livelihoods and health in a socio-cultural dimension. The economic and infrastructural disadvantage of developing states inadvertently aggravate these impacts which, as this research seeks to find, are rooted in systems of domination. Women, who are already targets on inequality, especially in developing countries, bear a heavier burden of climate change as merely carrying out their daily domestic duties has been seen to become more strenuous. From a constructivist perspective of climate change and gender subjectivity, patriarchal, capitalist system simultaneously exploit the natural world and subordinate women, thereby resulting in a disproportionate impact on women’s lives, health, and livelihood. This paper therefore seeks to suggest the need for actual implementation of the legal frameworks that have been put in place, as well as adoption of mitigation measures that take into consideration the active role women play.

title: Income Fluctuations and Life Satisfaction: A Gain-Loss Asymmetry Perspective Evidence from the German Socio-Economic Panel
affiliations: and Tekirdag Namik Kemal University

detail.title: Income Fluctuations and Life Satisfaction: A Gain-Loss Asymmetry Perspective Evidence from the German Socio-Economic Panel
detail.abstract: The primary aim of this paper is to explore the impact of real-life income fluctuations on individuals, focusing specifically on "gain-loss asymmetry"-a phenomenon where losses exert a more pronounced psychological effect than equivalent gains. By analyzing data from the German SocioEconomic Panel (SOEP), this study evaluates the effects of actual income changes on experienced utility, distinguishing between real income variations and anticipated changes. Self-reported life satisfaction is used as a proxy for experienced utility, with income changes determined by comparing current net real household income to that of the previous five years. Employing an ordinary least squares model with a two-way fixed effect estimator, our findings reveal that income losses significantly and negatively affect life satisfaction compared to equivalent gains, with the exception of the first lag. Beyond the first lag, losses exert a significantly greater impact than gains. Notably, the gain-loss asymmetry is more pronounced among middle-income individuals, while categorical losses are more impactful for higher-income groups.
