title: Pricing Prediction Markets: Risk Premiums, Incomplete Markets, and a Decomposition Framework

detail.title: Pricing Prediction Markets: Risk Premiums, Incomplete Markets, and a Decomposition Framework
detail.abstract: Prediction markets—binary contracts on real-world events, with annualized trading volumes exceeding $50 billion across major platforms as of early 2026—lack the pricing infrastructure available to every other major asset class. This paper proposes a three-layer pricing and decomposition framework for prediction markets—the first, to my knowledge, to formally separate physical event probability from risk premium in this asset class. The framework consists of: (i) a log-odds state variable that maps bounded contract prices to an unbounded state space amenable to standard stochastic tools; (ii) a jump-diffusion dynamics specification in log-odds space, building on Dalen (2025); and (iii) a Wang (2000) probability distortion that decomposes observed market prices into a physical probability component p * and a risk loading λ: p mkt = Φ(Φ-1 (p *)+λ). The framework is motivated by the observation, formalized here but rooted in Manski (2006) and Harrison and Pliska (1983), that prediction market contracts are structurally equivalent to cash-or-nothing binary options operating in incomplete markets where the risk-neutral measure is not unique—so observed prices necessarily embed both event probability and a risk premium that no-arbitrage reasoning alone cannot separate. I document that log-odds levels exhibit the same stylized facts as equity log-prices—random-walk behavior (unit root in x t), fat tails (kurtosis 6-12 in increments), and volatility clustering—supporting the diffusion-based dynamics layer. The decomposition framework yields two testable predictions: (i) λ > 0 generates the well-documented favorite-longshot bias as a direct mathematical consequence, and (ii) cross-platform price differences between Polymarket and Kalshi reflect different risk loadings (λ K ≠ λ P). Contract-level calibration against 2,460 resolved Polymarket contracts yields λ MLE = 0.176 (SE = 0.027, p < 10-10), consistent in sign and order of magnitude with catastrophe bond markets (λ ≈ 0.45, Wang 2004) and significantly different from zero. The risk loading is not uniform: it vanishes in high-volume and sports/politics markets, increases with contract duration, and is concentrated in illiquid, longer-horizon contracts—suggesting that competitive trading competes the distortion toward zero. Cross-platform validation across N = 291,309 contracts from Polymarket (2025-2026), Kalshi (2021-2026), Metaculus, Good Judgment Open, INFER, and Manifold confirms a positive, significant λ on all real-money platforms, with a pooled estimate of λ = 0.183 (SE = 0.003, p < 10-15). Manifold, a play-money platform, exhibits λ =-0.22 (p < 10-11), consistent with overconfidence absent financial stakes. A novel finding is that the risk premium is time-varying: it is statistically significant at market opening and decays toward zero as the event approaches resolution, consistent with information-driven convergence.

title: On the Macroeconomic Dynamics of the Circular Economy: A Stock-Flow Consistent Model
affiliations: Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: On the Macroeconomic Dynamics of the Circular Economy: A Stock-Flow Consistent Model
detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic ecological-macroeconomic model of the circular economy that integrates the core strategies of reducing, reusing, and recycling within a unified intertemporal framework. The model treats produced capital, material stocks, and waste liabilities as physically interconnected state variables subject to strict material-balance constraints. In doing so, it departs from conventional growth theory, where capital depreciation is typically modeled as a loss of productive services rather than as a physical transformation into residual matter. We show that once depreciation is recognized as a source of future waste generation, the optimal growth problem changes systematically. Two macroeconomic mechanisms emerge from the analysis: a circular capital discount, reflecting the shadow cost of future residuals embodied in current investment, and a waste-liability drag, through which depreciation-related and production-related residuals lower the effective intertemporal return to capital and reduce sustainable consumption relative to a linear benchmark. We show analytically that these mechanisms imply a liability-adjusted golden rule of capital accumulation and a lower socially optimal steady-state capital stock than in the standard neoclassical model. The paper also shows how the planner’s allocation can be mapped into a system of circular Pigouvian incentives, derives a circularly adjusted accounting identity for comprehensive wealth, and provides stylized comparative-dynamic illustrations of how reducing, reusing, and recycling operate through distinct macroeconomic margins. More broadly, the paper offers a stock-flow consistent macroeconomic foundation for the material-balance perspective in ecological economics.

title: Geopolitical Risk and the Limits of Modern Portfolio Praxis

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and the Limits of Modern Portfolio Praxis
detail.abstract:
The pricing canon of modern finance—the CAPM and its extensions—rests on institutional preconditions that it does not model: stable property rights, investor-invariant payoff functions, and an exogenous loss distribution that is in principle estimable from observable data. When an expert advisory council to the Norwegian government uses the word confiscation in its first report on the Government Pension Fund Global, it signals that these preconditions can no longer be assumed for the jurisdictions where the Fund holds the vast majority of its assets. This collection develops the formal apparatus for a class of risk that the pricing canon does not address: risk that is endogenous to the investor’s own exposure, specific to the investor’s identity, and strategically produced by actors who profit from institutional destruction.

The collection is organised around five research questions:
1. Under what conditions does an external financial asset become a liability? (Essays I–II)
2. Does there exist a principled concentration limit when the targeting hazard is endogenous? (Essay III)
3. What happens when the enforcement apparatus itself is endogenous to the targeting actor’s choices? (Essay IV)
4. Is the resulting barrier reversible? (Essay V)
5. Does the asset-pricing canon contain an implicit institutional postulate, and what happens when it fails? (Essays VI–VII)

title: Towards a mitigation behavioral framework for indoor wildfire smoke exposure: the Response to Indoor Pollution Exposure (RIPE) Model
affiliations: Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) - Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester Polytechnic Institute and Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) - Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering

detail.title: Towards a mitigation behavioral framework for indoor wildfire smoke exposure: the Response to Indoor Pollution Exposure (RIPE) Model
detail.abstract: During wildfire smoke events, people are instructed to stay indoors, where they already spend 90% of their time. However, wildfire smoke can infiltrate indoors, and there is currently no behavioral model on human responses to indoor air pollution. We examined older populations’ wildfire smoke threat perceptions and behaviors in the Western United States through semi-structured interviews. We propose a novel framework, the Response to Indoor Pollution Exposure (RIPE) Model, to explain individual decision-making and smoke mitigation behaviors (SMB) during smoke events. Guided by the Health Belief Model and the Protective Action Decision Model, the RIPE model displays how sensory reinforcement in the indoor environment shape mitigation efficacy perceptions and consequently threat and susceptibility perceptions. Reflective thematic analysis identified five themes: (1) health risks and emotional responses drive SMB adoption, (2) indoor environments shape exposure and mitigation experiences, (3) participants are dissatisfied with current stakeholder smoke mitigation efforts and communication (4) financial, logistical, and knowledge related barriers constrains SMB adoption (5) participants obtain wildfire smoke information through multiple sources and sensory cues. While participants recognized wildfire smoke risks and were willing to adopt SMB, cost and low comprehension of mitigation behaviors remained major barriers. Respondents in self-reported leakier homes experienced stronger negative sensory reinforcement, highlighting the built environment as a critical determinant of exposure and mitigation efficacy. Results also suggest the utility of wildfire councils, and future policy should focus on providing clearer guidance on how to implement SMBs correctly rather than emphasize health risks. ​

detail.abstract: Food insecurity and malnutrition have been on the rise in Africa since 2014. While initiatives to increase agricultural production via exogenous technologies and fossil fuel inputs have frequently been framed as hunger alleviation strategies, this approach is deeply colonial and fails to address the multiple aspects of malnutrition. We argue that it is time for a paradigm shift. Agroecology represents a more decolonial approach that better addresses the six dimensions of food security.

detail.abstract: Since 2008, the persistent failure of covered interest parity (CIP) has become a central puzzle in international finance. Although "balance-sheet costs" are widely cited as a key driver, the specific mechanisms through which these costs transmit to market prices remain unclear. We develop a general equilibrium model showing how Basel III regulations generate CIP deviations through the Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI) channel. In our framework, mark-to-market fluctuations in Availablefor-Sale (AFS) securities directly affect Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital and Liquidity Coverage Ratios (LCR). Under certain conditions, AFS losses constrain banks' intermediation capacity in FX swap markets, even in the presence of clear arbitrage opportunities. Our model predicts that a 25 bp term-premium shock widens CIP deviations by approximately 12 bp, with a response amplified by a factor of 2.5 relative to the pre-crisis regime. Panel regressions for G-10 currencies (2001-2022) confirm our predictions: AFS losses erode CET1 capital and reduce the pledgeable collateral banks deploy in FX markets, causing CIP deviations to widen significantly in the post-crisis era.

title: Holy Work: How Religiosity Shapes Local Labor Market Outcomes
affiliations: Miami University and Colby College

detail.title: Holy Work: How Religiosity Shapes Local Labor Market Outcomes
detail.abstract: We utilize a novel identification strategy to quantify the impacts of religiosity on US local labor markets. Exploiting the quasi-random variation in historical immigration from 1850 to 2010 and origin-specific religiosity, we isolate exogenous variation in the religious composition of US commuting zones for 1940-2010. We find that, relative to the religiously Unaffiliated share, an exogenous increase in Protestant, Orthodox Christian, and "Other" religious shares decreases employment and marriage shares, whereas Jewish share increases employment and college education shares along with mean income in commuting zones. The share of married women in the workforce falls with all religious shares except Jewish share. Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity by gender. We demonstrate both the causal effect of religiosity and the heterogeneous impacts of different faiths.

detail.abstract: The sewage sludge (SS) from swine slaughterhouses has the potential to replace chemical fertilizers in rice production, but the knowledge regarding its effects on the qualities of soil and rice has been limited. The objectives of this study aim at investigating the effects of SS on soil qualities, evaluating the effects of SS on rice growth, nutrient uptake, and accumulation of toxic elements, and determining the economic benefits of SS application in rice production. The pot experiment contained four treatments, including (1) no chemical fertilizer and SS (CT), (2) the chemical fertilizer application (CF), (3) application of chemical fertilizer (CF) with SS to replace 50% of nitrogen (N) requirement (SS50), and (4) application of CF with SS to replace 100% of N requirement (SS100). The SS application decreased soil pH and soil redox potential but increased CEC. The SS100 provided the highest TOC, C stock, mineral N, and exchangeable Ca. Whereas the SS50 had the highest soil available P. Both SS50 and SS100 did not affect soil toxic elements level and enhanced the height, tiller number, and fresh weight of grain, husk, straw, and root biomass, and total N, P, and K uptake. The SS application did not increase the level of toxic elements in grain. Both SS rates increased the net benefit of rice production. The most cost-effective treatment is the SS50, with the net benefit higher than the SS100 and chemical CF, indicating that the SS from swine slaughterhouses can replace chemical fertilizers in sustainable rice production.

title: Systemic Stability in Macroeconomic Networks: Bridging Differential Geometry and Random Matrix Theory

detail.title: Systemic Stability in Macroeconomic Networks: Bridging Differential Geometry and Random Matrix Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Modern macroeconomic systems are inherently high-dimensional, networked dynamical systems in which localized shocks propagate through complex interaction structures and may trigger systemic crises. Classical econometric approaches, which largely rely on linear aggregation and exogenous perturbations, are fundamentally limited in capturing the endogenous, topology-driven mechanisms underlying such events.

This paper introduces a unified geometric–spectral framework for the analysis of systemic stability by rigorously coupling differential geometry with Random Matrix Theory (RMT). We represent the macroeconomic system as a correlation-induced Riemannian manifold, where the metric structure is derived from empirical cross-correlations and the network topology is approximated via filtered interaction graphs. Within this setting, structural robustness is quantified using discrete Ricci curvature, while collective dynamics are characterized through the eigenvalue spectrum of the empirical correlation matrix.

We establish a geometric–spectral coupling principle and show that systemic instability corresponds to a phase transition defined by a dual condition: (i) a geometric contraction, manifested as a collapse in average network curvature, and (ii) a spectral concentration, where the leading eigenvalue separates sharply from the theoretical noise bulk predicted by Random Matrix Theory. This joint threshold provides a mathematically consistent criterion for detecting the emergence of macroscopic synchronization and loss of structural resilience.

Numerical experiments demonstrate that periods of systemic stress are characterized by simultaneous curvature decay, eigenvalue inflation, and topological centralization of the network. These findings show that systemic risk is not merely a statistical anomaly but a topological phase transition of the macroeconomic system.

The proposed framework yields a robust and interpretable early-warning indicator for financial contagion, with particular relevance for monitoring structurally evolving systems such as emerging financial markets.

detail.abstract: Biliran Province in Eastern Visayas, Philippines, has demonstrated steady economic growth in recent years, with its economy expanding by 6.6% in 2023, driven by agriculture, fisheries, and emerging tourism sectors. Despite these gains, the province remains highly vulnerable to climaterelated hazards such as typhoons, floods, and landslides, threatening livelihoods and food security. This developmental research aims to assess existing livelihood portfolios, evaluate vulnerability and adaptive capacity, and co-design sustainable diversification strategies linking fisheries, agritourism, and renewable energy applications. Using a mixed-methods approach-including household surveys, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, participatory vulnerability mapping, and technical feasibility studies the study seeks to identify high-return, climate-resilient interventions. Baseline data indicate that agriculture, forestry, and fishing contributed 23.8% to the provincial economy in 2022, while poverty incidence among families dropped from 19.9% in 2021 to 8.5% in 2023, largely due to targeted livelihood support programs. Anticipated outputs include an anonymized household livelihood database, hazard-exposure maps, cost-benefit analyses of interventions, and pilot implementation plans for local government adoption. This research is expected to guide evidence-based planning for inclusive and climate-resilient growth in Biliran Province.

title: Winners and Losers: Firm, Labor, and Crime Responses to China's Coal Capacity Reduction Policy
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, University of International Business and Economics, Peking University and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Winners and Losers: Firm, Labor, and Crime Responses to China's Coal Capacity Reduction Policy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of China's 2016 coal capacity reduction policy on firms, local labor markets, and crime. We find that the policy substantially reduced the asset size and employment of coal firms in treated cities while simultaneously increasing their profitability and lowering debt. Policy-induced layoffs generated adverse spillovers in local labor markets, reducing residents' incomes, worsening public perceptions of job opportunities, and increasing divorce rates. These labor market effects were most pronounced among older and less-educated individuals. Employment also shifted away from the mining sector toward wholesale and retail trade and real estate-related industries. In addition, the policy led to an increase in crime, driven primarily by property offenses committed by individual offenders, while violent crime remained largely unchanged. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that the increase in coal firms' profits exceeded the fiscal resources required for worker resettlement.

title: Thesis Research Report Note

detail.title: Thesis Research Report Note
detail.abstract: This research examines the role of natural gas transportation infrastructure in Nigeria and its significance within the energy trilemma of energy security, energy equity, and environmental sustainability. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines quantitative and qualitative approaches through two survey instruments developed around the energy trilemma framework and supported by literature-based analysis. The findings show that improved access to natural gas is positively associated with employment growth, higher tax revenue, stronger labour income, and broader economic performance. At the same time, the study identifies major barriers, including inadequate and aging pipeline systems, weak investment, security challenges such as vandalism and theft, regulatory instability, and high infrastructure costs. The thesis concludes that stronger governance, sustained infrastructure investment, regulatory transparency, and improved monitoring technologies are necessary if natural gas is to support affordable energy access, economic growth, and environmental responsibility in Nigeria. Its originality lies in linking the management of natural gas transportation directly to Nigeria's energy trilemma and development pathway.

title: AI and Distributive Politics

detail.title: AI and Distributive Politics

detail.abstract: This paper develops a tractable political-economy framework for studying how frontier-expanding Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshapes redistribution, capital accumulation, and welfare. Production is organized over a continuum of tasks, and higher AI capability expands the set of tasks profitably performed by capital-like inputs, raising the automation share and shifting income away from labor. Fiscal policy is a proportional tax on capital income whose revenues finance productive public spending and lump-sum transfers; with heterogeneous wealth, the tax is chosen by majority voting and pinned down by the preferred policy of the median voter. The model delivers an endogenous tax schedule linking automation intensity to redistribution, and compares a constitutional regime with a fixed tax rate to a flexible quasi-static regime in which policy is re-optimized across automation states. The quantitative illustration studies this mechanism through the automation margin: an AI-driven automation shock lowers the politically chosen capital tax, increases steady-state output, and raises disposableincome inequality, implying only partial political insurance against the distributive consequences of AI-induced automation. More unequal economies choose higher taxes at any given automation state, but not enough to fully stabilize inequality. A welfare decomposition across percentiles shows that the long-run gains from AI combine a common capital-deepening component with a distributional component that becomes less favorable to poorer households as automation expands, clarifying why no single fiscal rule dominates along all margins.

title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets and Financial Stability
affiliations: , Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance and Stanford University

detail.title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets and Financial Stability
detail.abstract: We document new evidence on the capitalization, funding structure, and performance of private credit funds using comprehensive fund-and asset-level data covering most of the industry. Private credit funds are highly capitalized, with equity typically accounting for 65-80% of total assetsmore than six times the capitalization of U.S. banks, where equity represents about 10%. Debt usage is moderate and largely reflects bank credit lines used for liquidity management. Fund lives average 10-12 years, while underlying loan maturities are generally shorter, implying little or no maturity mismatch-unlike banks, which fund long-term assets with short-term callable deposits. Private credit portfolios are diversified across industries, geographies, and credit strategies, reducing exposure to correlated shocks. Performance data show positive average net annualized returns with limited downside risk to creditors, as losses are largely borne by equity investors. Overall, private credit funds appear conservatively structured and unlikely to pose systemic risks comparable to traditional banks under their current balance-sheet configurations. We conclude by discussing potential vulnerabilities that could emerge as the sector grows, including governance and disclosure frictions, stress-period dynamics, bank-nonbank linkages, and the transmission of losses through limited partner balance sheets and retail investment vehicles.

title: Memetic Volatility Propagation: Cross-Subreddit Sentiment Contagion as a Leading Indicator of Market Volatility
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Memetic Volatility Propagation: Cross-Subreddit Sentiment Contagion as a Leading Indicator of Market Volatility
detail.abstract: We apply network epidemiology to nancial social media by modeling the propagation of bullish and bearish narratives through Reddit nance communities as a contagion process. Using 18 months of Reddit comment data (January 2024June 2025) spanning approximately 47 million comments across major nance subreddits, we construct temporal interaction graphs and classify users into Susceptible InfectedRecovered (SIR) states based on their expressed sentiment dynamics. We compute time-varying reproduction numbers (R t), entropy measures, network saturation metrics, and cross-community propagation rates. After ensuring stationarity through joint ADFKPSS testing and rst-dierencing 30 of 70 series, we conduct 1,144 Granger causality tests (26 SIR features × 44 market targets, lags 15 days) against a panel spanning 8 instruments (SPY, QQQ, GME, NVDA, TSLA, AMC, VIX, XLF). At the 5% signicance level, 183 tests reject the null (16.0%); applying BenjaminiHochberg false discovery rate correction, 25 relationships survive at q < 0.05. DurbinWatson statistics for top pairs cluster tightly around 2.0 (range 1.902.28), conrming absence of residual autocorrelation. The strongest FDRsurviving results show bearish infection counts and network saturation Grangercausing meme-stock volatility (AMC high-low range, q = 0.013) and VIX dynamics (bear infections → VIX close, q = 0.015; cross-subreddit propagation → VIX absolute returns, q = 0.048). Lead-1-day correlations are modest in magnitude (peak |r| ≈ 0.39), consistent with the social medianance literature. These results demonstrate that cross-community contagion dynamics contain statistically robust, though economically modest, predictive information about market volatility after rigorous correction for non-stationarity and multiple testing.

title: Enhancing Revenue Collection Capacity through Automation: Evidence from a VAT
affiliations: Ashoka University, , University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Enhancing Revenue Collection Capacity through Automation: Evidence from a VAT
detail.abstract: Tax administrations around the world are investing heavily in digitization, creating new opportunities for enforcement. Can low-cost enforcement tools built atop this digital infrastructure increase tax capacity? We study an Indian intervention implementing automated cross-checks to target fraudulent input tax credits. Using administrative data, we show that the policy reduced fraudulent credits and increased tax payments, resulting in a 5 percent reduction in overall evasion at minimal cost. We find little adverse impact on legitimate activity. This type of policy is readily implementable in many developing countries that already have digital filing but are yet to exploit its full potential.

title: The Sethi-Skiba Point: A Structural Taxonomy of Threshold Phenomena in Dynamic Management Problems
affiliations: and Universidad Finis Terrae

detail.title: The Sethi-Skiba Point: A Structural Taxonomy of Threshold Phenomena in Dynamic Management Problems
detail.abstract: Nonconvex dynamic optimization problems often admit multiple locally optimal outcomes, requiring decision makers to choose not only how to adjust but which equilibrium to pursue. The Sethi-Skiba point identifies the threshold state where a decision maker is indifferent between trajectories leading to radically different regimes. While well-known in control theory, its implications for management science remain fragmented. This paper provides a unified review of the theory, computation, and applications of Sethi-Skiba thresholds. We present geometric foundations in capital accumulation models, explaining connections to nonconcave value functions, hysteresis, and global optimality. We then survey numerical methods and their high-dimensional limitations. Building on this, we organize the literature into a taxonomy of managerial archetypes: revitalization traps, preservation thresholds, social contagion, and strategic entry barriers. Identical mathematical structures govern problems in advertising, environmental management, epidemics, and industrial competition. By reframing Sethi-Skiba points as a general theory of strategic thresholds, this review highlights a shift from marginal adjustment to basin selection. Managerial success in nonconvex environments depends less on fine-tuning controls than on correctly identifying regime boundaries. We conclude by outlining directions in behavioral modeling, empirical detection of tipping points, and networked systems.

title: Financial Inflows and Inclusive Development in Sub-Saharan Africa

detail.title: Financial Inflows and Inclusive Development in Sub-Saharan Africa
detail.abstract: In the last decade, sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) has witnessed an influx of foreign cash inflow, which has played a crucial role in financing development projects and stimulating economic growth. However, its impact on inclusive human development in SSA remains a subject of debate. This study investigates the impact of financial inflows on inclusive human development in SSA using annual data from 1990 to 2023. The panel data were analysed using the System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimation technique because of its advantage in taking care of the problem of endogeneity. Inclusive development was captured using the inequality-adjusted human development index to capture adjustments in inequality. The result of the study revealed that foreign direct investments and external borrowing had positive and significant impact on inclusive development in SSA, while remittances and portfolio investments were not significant in explaining inclusive development. The study concludes that foreign direct investments and borrowing have the potential to catalyse inclusive development in SSA. For SSA countries to enhance the developmental impact of financial inflows, the study recommends that financial inflows should be aligned with national development priorities by channelling them towards critical sectors such as education, health and infrastructural investment.

In my remarks, I argued that dominant corporations control our lives with impunity, and that antitrust law is vital to tackling this problem and enhancing the public's economic and political liberty.

title: Instrument Choice in Pre-Contest Investment
affiliations: Tromso University Business School, Oslo Metropolitan University and University of Oslo - Department of Economics

detail.title: Instrument Choice in Pre-Contest Investment
detail.abstract: We study a two-period contest in which two risk-neutral rivals can invest before a subsequent all-pay auction in order to alter the playing field. Pre-contest investments can take the form of a head start, which shifts a player's score additively, or a bias, which raises the productivity of effort multiplicatively. We characterize the subgame-perfect equilibria of the game. In any pure-strategy equilibrium, at most one player invests, and the investor uses at most one instrument. The choice between head start and bias depends only on the rival's valuation: against sufficiently weak rivals, the investor chooses a head start, whereas higher rival valuations induce a switch to bias. Equilibrium existence requires that the chosen investment make both head-start and bias deviations by the rival unprofitable, and we characterize the corresponding thresholds. In a quadratic-cost example, the model generates both reinforcement equilibria, in which the high-value player invests, and preemptive equilibria, in which the low-value player invests. More generally, the analysis shows that allowing multiple investment instruments can fundamentally alter equilibrium existence: the monotonicity property familiar from one-instrument environments need not hold once contestants can choose between distinct forms of strategic advantage.

title: The Gravity-Staggered-Adoption Estimator: A Guardrail Solution to Forbidden Comparisons in Trade Policy Evaluation
affiliations: Dalian University - School of International Business

detail.title: The Gravity-Staggered-Adoption Estimator: A Guardrail Solution to Forbidden Comparisons in Trade Policy Evaluation
detail.abstract: Trade policy evaluations using gravity models have typically addressed staggered implementation through pooled estimators that implicitly use already-treated units as controls. This paper shows that conventional gravity estimates suffer from "forbidden comparison" bias which attenuates estimates towards zero. I develop the Gravity-Staggered-Adoption (GSA) estimator, which embeds Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) cohort-specific restrictions within a structural gravity framework with high-dimensional fixed effects. Applying GSA to sanctions on the Russian Federation (2014-2024), I find that conventional models understate the true effect by 5.8% in relative terms. The GSA estimator yields a weighted average treatment effect of-0.910, implying a 59.8% reduction in Russian trade-an order of magnitude larger than previous estimates. These findings demonstrate that properly accounting for staggered adoption is not just a refinement but a necessity. The GSA estimator provides a blueprint for future research on any trade policy with heterogeneous implementation timing.

title: The Weil Conjectures: The Most Beautiful Story in Mathematics
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: The Weil Conjectures: The Most Beautiful Story in Mathematics
detail.abstract: This paper offers a rigorous and narrative account of the Weil conjectures, with an emphasis on both the mathematical architecture and the remarkable human story. Rather than presenting a merely chronological summary, the exposition is organised around the conceptual mechanisms that connect number theory, algebraic geometry, and topology: the zeta function of varieties over finite fields, the construction of ℓ-adic étale cohomology, the Grothendieck– Lefschetz trace formula, and Deligne’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The narrative interweaves Weil’s prison letter, Dwork’s unexpected p-adic tour de force, Grothendieck’s visionary programme, and the dramatic tension between Grothendieck’s architectural philosophy and Deligne’s pragmatic brilliance. The aim is to present these ideas in a polished, readable form that highlights both the internal coherence of the theory and its long-range influence across modern mathematics.

title: The Tongue as a Moral Force: Speech, Consequence, and Responsibility in Talmudic Thought
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business

detail.title: The Tongue as a Moral Force: Speech, Consequence, and Responsibility in Talmudic Thought
detail.abstract: In an era of social media and pervasive online harassment, the ethics of speech has never been more urgent. Western culture offers little systematic guidance for restraining the tongue. This paper argues that the Talmud contains a sophisticated and modern philosophy of communication deserving serious scholarly attention. Drawing on primary sources, the paper examines four interrelated principles. These include the idea that articulating an ominous possibility can help bring it into being, the injunction against inviting misfortune through reckless speech, the teaching that blessings and curses carry real weight regardless of the speaker's status, and the belief that an undeserved curse boomerangs upon its source. The paper situates these principles within the broader framework of biblical speech ethics, including the prohibitions of malicious speech, verbal oppression, and public shaming. Together, these teachings establish a coherent ethical discipline where words possess moral weight irrespective of intent. Speakers are held responsible for unanticipated consequences. This makes restraint in speech a binding ethical and spiritual obligation, not merely a social virtue. The paper concludes by drawing connections between these ancient teachings and contemporary concerns in business ethics and organizational behavior. It suggests that Talmudic speech ethics offers a rich and underutilized resource for modern ethical reflection.

title: The Same Mistake Twice: Informational Herding and the Limits of Cross-Platform Efficiency in Latin American Election Markets

detail.title: The Same Mistake Twice: Informational Herding and the Limits of Cross-Platform Efficiency in Latin American Election Markets
detail.abstract:
Prediction markets have been lauded as efficient aggregators of dispersed political information. This paper argues that cross-platform price convergence --- increasingly cited as evidence of market efficiency --- can instead reflect informational herding: multiple platforms processing the same distorted input, producing correlated errors rather than independent assessments. We examine three recent Latin American presidential elections traded simultaneously on Polymarket and Kalshi --- Peru (April~12, 2026), Ecuador (April~13, 2025), and Chile (December~14, 2025) --- spanning a liquidity range of more than two orders of magnitude (USD2.5M to USD 86.1M).

The central finding is platform-invariance of mispricings: mean cross-platform price divergences are below 3 percentage points in all three countries, despite important differences in trading volume and fundamental differences in regulatory regime and user base. Both Polymarket and Kalshi assigned 65% win probability to the losing candidate in Ecuador; both correctly tracked the winner in Chile; both persistently overprice the polling frontrunner in Peru by 33 percentage points. This invariance rules out platform-specific explanations and implicates a shared informational deficit: internationally-oriented traders on both platforms processed the same English-language polling signals while systematically underweighting local structural factors --- incumbency dynamics, vote-transfer base rates, and coalition arithmetic --- not encoded in internationally circulating information.

Using Kalshi bid-ask spread and open interest data, we show that limits to arbitrage are directly measurable rather than merely theoretical: Ecuador's half-spread (2.0pp) equaled the PM--KA price gap (2.1pp), and informed traders who held 65% of open interest on the correct side lacked sufficient capital to overcome the order book's resistance. We introduce the Market-Poll Gap (MPG) and Base Rate Adjusted Poll (BRAP) as diagnostic tools, and propose a two-factor taxonomy: informational errors (platform-invariant, driven by herding on distorted international signals) versus structural errors (platform-specific, driven by thin-market dynamics and limits to arbitrage). For practitioners, the implication is that market depth and information source independence must be evaluated jointly: high volume provides liquidity but not accuracy when the underlying information set is systematically distorted.

title: Media Censorship Backfire
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Media Censorship Backfire
detail.abstract: This paper utilizes a game-theoretical model to present a comprehensive framework for understanding the causes and consequences of media censorship backfire. The model examines two state censorship tactics: manipulating media biases and manipulating the citizens' cost of accessing news. The findings reveal that the commonly cited factors in existing literature-impaired media credibility, deteriorated citizen beliefs in the state, and decreased citizen responses to the media-only capture one type of censorship backfire. Manipulating media biases can generate conditions diametrically opposed to those mentioned above and backfire. Additionally, manipulating the citizens' cost of news access can backfire without changing their beliefs. This tactic may also impact the level of media bias, yielding outcomes similar to those resulting from media bias manipulation. Based on my model, these various types of censorship backfire operate on essentially similar mechanisms and can coexist under specific conditions.

title: The Accountability Dilemma in Mass Purges
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: The Accountability Dilemma in Mass Purges
detail.abstract: Despite expectations that large-scale anti-corruption campaigns would enhance governance, they often lead to bureaucratic inefficiencies and economic decline, as seen in China and Vietnam. This paper examines these purges as a top-down accountability mechanism in authoritarian regimes. Through a game-theoretic model, we demonstrate that systemic corruption traps rulers in a persistent trade-off between social productivity and political stability. Whether rulers incentivize informants, distinguish between ideologically congruent and non-congruent agents, prioritize profit or survival, or base purges on corruption or performance, the core dilemma remains-and often becomes more intricate. Our findings challenge the effectiveness of mass purges as a sustainable governance strategy.

title: The Everydayization of Injustice: Functioning, Adaptation, and the Deferred Crisis
affiliations: Rabindra Bharati University

detail.title: The Everydayization of Injustice: Functioning, Adaptation, and the Deferred Crisis

detail.abstract: I argue, in this article, that injustice often persists not because people believe in it, but because they learn to live around it. Calling this process everydayization, I distinguish it from ideological normalization. Everydayization operates through adaptation, fatigue, and constrained survival-through habits that no longer feel like choices, and through small calculations made in systems that offer few real alternatives. People may not consent to injustice, but they navigate it, accommodate it, even tactically weaponize it. Injustice, in this account, functions not as rupture but as routine. Crises, I suggest, don't erupt from nowhere. They arrive when these quiet mechanisms of endurance finally collapse. Taking insights from thinkers such as Foucault, Gramsci, Fraser, Scott among others, I examine how everyday functional injustice survives by exhausting resistance. I end by arguing in favour of a politics of counter-functioning, that is, committed and situated practices that interrupt the smooth operation of injustice before it turns into a visible crisis.

title: Income Statement Line Items as Production Factor Cost Shares: Evidence from Macroeconomic Announcements
affiliations: Washington State University, Vancouver

detail.title: Income Statement Line Items as Production Factor Cost Shares: Evidence from Macroeconomic Announcements
detail.abstract: The financial reporting conceptual framework requires that financial statements help investors assess the uncertainty of future cash flows — a requirement whose implications for the discount rate have been largely unexplored. Using macroeconomic announcements as the moments when aggregate factor price shocks arrive publicly, this paper shows that income statement factor cost shares predict differential firm-level return responses through the discount rate channel, not just cash flow expectations. The sample covers 163 FOMC announcements, 252 employment reports, and 251 CPI releases spanning 2005–2024, yielding over 2.3 million firm-event observations across 8,790 independent firm clusters. Tangible and intangible capital consumption have opposite interest rate sensitivities — a firm at the 75th versus 25th percentile of tangible consumption earns 0.10 percentage points lower return per standard deviation of rate surprise (t = −9.2); amortization predicts a positive response (t = 2.3; F = 76.2, p < 0.001) — with aggregation into a single D&A line attenuating the capital channel by approximately 20%. The same cost structure variables produce cross-setting sign reversals consistent with factor price channels: the near-zero CPI result for tangible capital is a deductive consequence of historical cost accounting rather than an inflation hedge; labor consumption reverses sign between rate and inflation settings; and consumer-facing labor-intensive firms respond to wage surprises as a cost shock while non-consumer firms respond as a demand signal. Of twelve predicted signs derived from the production function model, eleven are confirmed simultaneously— a joint pattern inconsistent with fixed firm characteristic explanations.

title: Identity and Provocation: Dynamics of Minority Assimilation
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Identity and Provocation: Dynamics of Minority Assimilation
detail.abstract: This paper formalizes how extremists manipulate an ethnic or religious identity to generate intergroup tension and polarization in society. I argue that Islamic extremists seek to reinforce the Islamic identity of other Muslims. To do so, they launch terror attacks against a majority non-Muslim population as a provocation strategy to trigger a backlash against Muslims. This backlash makes it more difficult for Muslims to assimilate, pulling them away from the mainstream and promoting their in-group solidarity. I find that this strategy of provocation succeeds only if Muslims manage to provide sufficient in-group favoritism to counteract the backlash. If the majority shuns unassimilated Muslims more, or if the Muslim community is more economically unproductive, it is easier to mobilize Muslims, and extremists can induce more Muslims to stop assimilating. The efficacy of provocation increases if the government adopts a policy to exclude the Muslim community and, surprisingly, decreases when the Muslim community is more extreme or more homogeneous.

title: When is Intergroup Herding Beneficial?
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) University

detail.title: When is Intergroup Herding Beneficial?
detail.abstract: We develop a population dynamics model to explore the benefits of intergroup herding. We consider a society composed of two groups-one autonomous and the other open, i.e., learning from outsiders indiscriminately-and analyze the joint evolution of their technology adoption and population sizes. When the autonomous group converges to an inferior steady state, it can, under some conditions, drag the open group down with it. However, if the autonomous group converges to the superior steady state, the open group always ends up in the superior steady state, even if technology adoption is very difficult for its members. When the open group learns from multiple autonomous groups, the advantage of intergroup herding is more salient. However, if population is bounded, or if adopting the inferior technology generates a negative externality on the other group, intergroup herding becomes less beneficial.

title: When Manufacturing Matters Most: Structural Transformation and Productivity Growth Trajectories in Developing and Emerging Economies
affiliations: , University of Palermo and Asian Development Bank

detail.title: When Manufacturing Matters Most: Structural Transformation and Productivity Growth Trajectories in Developing and Emerging Economies

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 840

detail.abstract: Structural transformation is a central driver of economic development, yet recent challenges such as premature deindustrialization have raised critical questions about whether low-income economies can still follow traditional growth paths that rely on manufacturing expansion to drive productivity gains. Building on a theoretical model that incorporates learning-by-doing mechanisms, sectoral employment reallocation, and factor accumulation, we examine labor productivity growth trajectories using a panel of 31 developing and emerging economies over 1960–2019, detecting a data-driven structural break in 1982 that fundamentally altered productivity growth dynamics. To account for the potential heterogeneity in how structural transformation affects different types of economies, we employ quantile-based techniques to examine effects across different segments of the productivity growth distribution, moving beyond conventional approaches that focus on average effects and may obscure important distributional patterns. The unconditional quantile regression results identify manufacturing expansion as a key driver of productivity growth, with employment reallocation in this sector delivering twice the productivity benefits for slower-growing economies compared to high performers. The quantile decomposition further shows that observable characteristics and unobservable factors became increasingly important determinants of productivity performance following the structural break, with substantial heterogeneity across the distribution. Moreover, we construct counterfactual scenarios to investigate what outcomes low-performing economies could have attained had they adopted the characteristics, returns to factors, and unobservable capabilities of top performers. These scenarios unveil substantial untapped growth potential, with bottom-quartile economies potentially achieving average productivity growth improvements of up to 2.7 percentage points.

title: Toward a Simple Economic Framework for Analysis of Business Ecosystems
affiliations: Kelley School of Business, Indiana University

detail.title: Toward a Simple Economic Framework for Analysis of Business Ecosystems

declarations.funderStatement: International Center for Law and Economics

detail.abstract: This chapter develops a progression of frameworks to analyze economic organization for both single- and multi-product production, culminating in a framework for studying business ecosystems. The first stage draws on transaction cost economics, focusing on how governance affects the costs of transactions. The second incorporates transaction value economics, highlighting how interactions can create value through mechanisms such as knowledge sharing. The third extends these perspectives by integrating insights from property rights economics, along with additional insights from transaction value economics, to account for how governance influences the value of future transactions via its impact on investment and innovation, with a particular focus on the latter. This progression provides a structured, economically grounded approach for analyzing coevolution and other defining features of business ecosystems within an antitrust-relevant framework - analysis that has become especially relevant and important with the proliferation of digital business ecosystems.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Buy the World a Coke Index, a novel global inflation measure that calculates the U.S. dollar cost of purchasing one standardized unit of consumption (a single-serve Coca-Cola) for every living human, repriced annually on December 25. Unlike single-country, single-commodity inflation measures such as the Big Mac Index, this index simultaneously captures three distinct inflationary signals: monetary debasement (the dollar price of the good rises), population growth (more humans to serve), and global purchasing power convergence (emerging-market prices converge toward developed-market levels as economies develop). The paper situates this index within a four-tier framework for measuring monetary debasement since the closing of the gold window in August 1971: Tier 1, M2 money supply growth (~3,434%); Tier 2, the Buy the World a Coke Index (~2,686%); Tier 3, single-country commodity measures such as the Big Mac and domestic Coca-Cola price (~1,187-1,700%); and Tier 4, the official Consumer Price Index (~702%). The systematic divergence between tiers is not noise; each gap has identifiable economic content. The gap between Tier 1 and Tier 2 captures the Cantillon Effect (monetary expansion absorbed by financial assets rather than goods). The gap between Tier 2 and Tier 3 captures population growth and global convergence effects. The gap between Tier 3 and Tier 4 captures the methodological suppression embedded in CPI construction. The paper proposes formalizing this four-tier framework as the Rowles Reality Inflation Index and discusses implications for monetary policy assessment, the Bitcoin valuation debate, and the Vintage Bifurcation thesis.

title: Credit Crunches and the Great Stagflation
affiliations: Wharton School, Department of Finance, New York University (NYU) - Department of Finance and New York University (NYU) - Department of Finance

detail.title: Credit Crunches and the Great Stagflation
detail.abstract: We argue that severe credit crunches in the banking system contributed to the Great Stagflation of the 1970s. The credit crunches were due to Regulation Q, a banking law that capped deposit rates. Under Reg Q, Fed tightening triggered large deposit outflows that led banks to contract lending. The credit crunches line up closely with stagflation in the time series. To explain this, we add Reg Q to a standard model where firms use bank loans to finance working capital. When Reg Q binds and credit contracts, working capital becomes more expensive, leading firms to raise prices and shrink output. The model implies an augmented Phillips curve where monetary tightening reduces aggregate supply in addition to demand. The impact on supply is increasing in the severity of the credit crunches, firms' external finance dependence, and their working capital intensity. We test all three predictions in the cross section of manufacturing industries. In each case, we find that more exposed industries raise prices and cut output relative to others. Our results imply that under severe financial frictions monetary policy affects aggregate supply and not just demand.

title: From Adoption to Retreat: The Rise and Fall of DEI Disclosure
affiliations: University of Scranton - Kania School of Management, Stevens Institute of Technology - School of Business and Gonzaga University

detail.title: From Adoption to Retreat: The Rise and Fall of DEI Disclosure
detail.abstract: This study examines the lifecycle of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) disclosure among U.S. publicly listed firms, from its rapid rise to its abrupt political reversal. Using a large panel of firmyear observations, we show that DEI disclosure expanded quickly in recent years but sharply declined in 2025. We analyze both adoption and exit dynamics. DEI adoption is driven by institutional investor ownership, industry peer effects, and political geography. To study the reversal, we develop a taxonomy of firm responses, distinguishing between firms that maintain DEI language, those that substitute terminology, and those that fully withdraw. Institutional ownership shapes not only whether firms adopt DEI disclosure but also how they adjust when conditions change. In particular, active institutional investors are associated with language substitution, while ownership by the Big Three institutional investors is linked to a lower likelihood of complete withdrawal. Placebo tests confirm that these patterns are specific to DEIrelated disclosure rather than broader reporting trends. Overall, the findings highlight that voluntary disclosure regimes supported by investor governance are highly sensitive to political shocks, yet leave a lasting imprint on firms' disclosure choices during periods of retreat.

title: Does Partial Pay Transparency Reduce Pay Inequality? An Experimental Investigation

detail.title: Does Partial Pay Transparency Reduce Pay Inequality? An Experimental Investigation

contentType.other: It is accepted at Management Science.

detail.abstract: As organizations increasingly adopt pay transparency policies, a key challenge is determining what compensation information to disclose. However, little is known about the effectiveness of disclosing only parts of total compensation, such as salary, while excluding other components, such as benefits. Using an online experiment on Prolific, this paper uncovers a concerning outcome: when decision-makers are incentivized to allocate bonus earnings between workers, partial transparency systematically increases the influence of component equality on the allocation choices. This causes decision-makers to focus more heavily on ensuring equality within the transparent component. This focus is significantly amplified for the transparent component relative to a non-transparent pay component, and this tendency persists even when doing so worsens overall pay inequality. We further show that social preferences play a central role in generating this asymmetry, while monetary incentives for decision makers primarily exert a level effect that shifts allocation behavior without altering the asymmetric pattern. In addition, decision-makers' beliefs about the importance of visible relative earnings differences help explain variation in allocation behaviors. In contrast, this asymmetric focus on achieving component equality disappears when either all or none of the compensation is transparent. Our results suggest that firms implementing partial transparency may inadvertently reinforce pay disparities rather than reduce them. These findings highlight the need for organizations to carefully design transparency policies to avoid distortions in fairness perceptions and pay allocation decisions.

title: State-Action Immunity for Climate Collaborations
affiliations: Yale School of Management and Yale University

detail.title: State-Action Immunity for Climate Collaborations

detail.abstract:
In the absence of sufficient public policy to address the climate crisis, some private-sector companies take on the role of government by collaborating with competitors to collectively adopt pro-climate policies. But these climate collaborations create risk of antitrust liability for participating companies because they can be anticompetitive and can harm consumers in a relevant market. To encourage collective adoption of beneficial private-sector climate policies, state legislatures should leverage an existing doctrinal tool—state-action immunity—to insulate genuine climate collaborators from antitrust liability.

 First we categorize existing climate collaborations and explain the legal risks associated with each type. Second, though current doctrine deters climate collaborations, it also offers a solution. The state-action immunity doctrine allows state governments to immunize private companies—such as colluding shipping carriers and monopolist billboard advertisers—from federal antitrust liability, provided that the state legislature’s intention to displace competition is clearly articulated and the immunized behavior is actively supervised. We argue that this doctrine can also be used to immunize societally beneficial climate collaborations from federal antitrust liability.

 A model for doing so exists in state certificate of public advantage (COPA) statutes, which have until now been used to immunize anticompetitive hospital mergers. States can and should enact Climate COPA statutes that permit state agencies to issue COPAs to societally beneficial climate collaborations. Such statutes could immunize and thus enable collaborations to, for example, restrict environmentally harmful local activities, make packaging more environmentally friendly, and remove environmentally harmful products from state retail outlets. Climate COPA statutes could help protect private industry from the weaponization of federal antitrust laws against climate progress.

title: Economic Policy Uncertainty, Financialization and Stock-Commodity Co-movement
affiliations: Hanyang University - School of  Business, Hanyang University and Hanyang University

detail.title: Economic Policy Uncertainty, Financialization and Stock-Commodity Co-movement
detail.abstract: Commodity Futures Modernization Act (CFMA) allows financial institutions to treat commodities as financial assets and thereby accelerates the financialization of commodity markets. This study investigates how Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) influences the co-movement between stock and commodity markets and how this relationship has evolved with financialization. We find that, following financialization, the impact of EPU on stock-commodity co-movement is not uniform but varies significantly across commodity types. Specifically, gold appears to have lost some of its traditional hedging properties, whereas grains exhibit enhanced diversification effects with stocks in response to EPU shocks.

detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve's monetary aggregates (M1 and M2) were last substantively redefined in May 2020, when the elimination of reserve requirements prompted the reclassification of savings deposits from M2 into M1. Since that redefinition, a parallel monetary channel has grown to material scale: payment stablecoins, dollar-denominated digital instruments issued on distributed ledger infrastructure, now represent approximately $315 billion in circulating float as of Q1 2026. This float is functionally equivalent to demand deposits or money market fund shares but appears nowhere in the H.6 statistical release. This paper documents the historical pattern by which the Fed has redefined its monetary aggregates in response to financial innovation (1971, 1980, 2006, 2020), demonstrates that stablecoins satisfy the same three triggering conditions that prompted each prior redefinition, and proposes the creation of a new standalone aggregate, M(s), to capture regulated payment stablecoin float. The paper argues that the passage of the GENIUS Act (2025) creates both the regulatory predicate and the data infrastructure necessary to implement this measurement, and that failure to do so will cause the Fed to systematically mis-estimate effective money supply as dollar-denominated value migrates to on-chain settlement channels.

title: Equitable Micromobility Deployment Mandates show Benefits only when Spatially Targeted
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business and The University of Texas at Austin, TX, USA

detail.title: Equitable Micromobility Deployment Mandates show Benefits only when Spatially Targeted
detail.abstract: To reduce mobility inequities, governments require private operators to meet minimum visit frequencies, trip counts, or vehicle deployments in disadvantaged neighborhoods. Shared scooters are a case in point: by 2024, 36 United States programs had adopted minimum deployment thresholds. We evaluate 15 programs in 13 cities (2019-2023) with spatial regression discontinuity, analyzing 66 million vehicle snapshots and telemetry from a large operator. Most mandates cover large areas and have null effects on availability-not from noncompliance, but because thresholds rarely constrain deployment. But the two cities that use targeted, pocket-based mandate zones centered on transit stops-Baltimore and Denver-increase availability by +38.38 scooters per km 2 (p < 0.01) and +70.30 scooters per km 2 (p < 0.01), respectively, closing 98% and 85% of the preexisting gap between mandate areas and median central neighborhoods. In Baltimore, where we also observe ridership from a large operator, the mandate causes an additional +26.47 rides per km 2 (p = 0.05), closing 35% of the corresponding preexisting ridership gap.

title: Policy Uncertainty As A Bubble Moderator: AI And Endogenous Investor Participation

detail.title: Policy Uncertainty As A Bubble Moderator: AI And Endogenous Investor Participation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I do not have any funding that could influence this study.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes and tests a theory in which policy uncertainty moderates the amplitude of speculative bubbles around general-purpose technologies by altering the composition of investors in public equity markets. In the model, a new technology generates a cash-flow distribution whose variance narrows over time as markets learn. Bubbles arise because asset prices reflect the beliefs of the marginal participating investor, who is optimistically biased when outcome uncertainty is high. Policy uncertainty raises the cost of participating in public equity markets for risk-averse momentum traders, confining early-stage risk to risk-tolerant venture capital and thereby compressing speculative premia. The delay between venture funding and public listing-the VC-to-IPO gap-is a sufficient statistic for bubble dampening within the model: longer private-market gestation means the technology matures before the broad public investor base is engaged. In the dot-com boom (1995-2001), low policy uncertainty and a median IPO age of four years coincided with a Nasdaq peak of 6.7× its 1995 level. In the current AI cycle (November 2022-present), policy uncertainty exceeds twice the dot-com baseline, median VC-to-IPO time surpasses eleven years, and the Nasdaq Composite has risen approximately 1.69× from its November 2022 level. The participation-filter mechanism is tested empirically using the Liberation Day tariff shock of April 2025 as a natural experiment.

title: The Role of GVC Linkages in Shaping the Impact of Commodity Shocks on Mauritanian Value Added

detail.title: The Role of GVC Linkages in Shaping the Impact of Commodity Shocks on Mauritanian Value Added
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether global value chain (GVC) positioning mediates the transmission of commodity price shocks to sectoral value-added growth in Mauritania, a resource-dependent least developed country whose integration into global production networks is overwhelmingly forwardoriented. Using a 28-year sector-level panel (26 sectors × 28 years, 1990-2017) derived from the Eora26 Multi-Region Input-Output database and IV-2SLS estimation with Bartik-style peer instruments, we identify two asymmetric transmission channels. First, sectors with higher forward linkage capture significantly less of commodity price increases-a value capture trap in which upstream suppliers cannot appropriate rents that accrue to downstream foreign processors. Second, backward-linked sectors face a cost-transmission squeeze during commodity price cycles. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the value capture trap is concentrated in the three primary resource sectors-Agriculture, Fishing, and Mining and Quarrying. These results are robust to outlier exclusion, extended controls, and winsorisation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to apply MRIO-based sector-level GVC decomposition to Mauritania, and the first to test GVC positioning as a transmission channel of the resource curse for any individual West African least developed country. The findings argue for a deliberate shift toward backward integration through domestic processing investment, local content mandates, and targeted manufacturing FDI as the principal structural response for commodity price vulnerability.

title: Firm Creation under DACA
affiliations: Miami University

detail.title: Firm Creation under DACA
detail.abstract: Undocumented immigration remains a central issue within US immigration policy debates, yet little is known about how legalization programs affect firm dynamics and labor market composition. In this paper, I study the impact of a particular legalization reform, Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), enacted in 2012, on establishment and employment outcomes. I exploit variation in pre-treatment exposure to the policy across sectors and commuting zones, using a triple-difference estimator. I find that DACA increases establishment entry by 2.4 percent in more exposed sectors and temporarily reduces exit rates, suggesting market expansion and entrepreneurship amongst formerly undocumented workers. The share of native workers rises by 2.1 percentage points, whereas that of ineligible undocumented workers declines by a similar magnitude, demonstrating labor substitution. Heterogeneity estimates across sectoral skill types reveal that these effects are concentrated in low-and medium-skill sectors. These results have important policy implications such that immigrant regularization can enhance firm dynamism and facilitate labor reallocation, without displacing native workers.

title: The Replacement Fallacy
affiliations: Real Safety AI Foundation

detail.title: The Replacement Fallacy
detail.abstract: This paper identifies a structural pattern we term the Replacement Fallacy: the tendency for technologies introduced as supplements to natural or human systems to gradually displace those systems through a predictable five-phase trajectory of introduction, adoption, degradation, dependency, and lock-in. We demonstrate this pattern through four historical case studies.

title: Towards a New Hybrid Stochastic Model for Enhanced Stock Price Estimation: The Heston-GARCH-Levy Model

detail.title: Towards a New Hybrid Stochastic Model for Enhanced Stock Price Estimation: The Heston-GARCH-Levy Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The primary author is David S.Y. Park. I am the mentor who helped David S.Y. Park understand the mathematics and build the simulations
declarations.funderStatement: The work was funded by a research grant from David S. Y. Park's high school. This work has already been published, and has the following DOI: https://doi.org/10.36838/v8i3.85

detail.abstract: The objective of this paper is to look at a stochastic framework for stock price estimation that builds upon specific advanced structures used in the financial industry. Specifically, we look at and simulate the Heston Model (with correlated Wiener processes with correlation coefficients), and other variants that are considered more accurate with respect to Black-Scholes. Then we look at an improved version of this model with jump conditions and simulate it, then look at the Stochastic Alpha Beta Rho (SABR) model and the Rough Volatility Model. We finally construct a possible Heston-GARCH-Levy Model with Jump Diffusions, which has a Heston Stochastic Volatility, a GARCH for Conditional Heteroskedasticity, as well as Jump Diffusions that introduce discontinuities in the price process, with Levy processes for tailed behavior. This combined model is then analyzed as a Hybrid Stochastic System specifying assumptions, the function spaces and norms needed, existence and uniqueness proofs, handling of hybrid components, regularity and stability bounds, counterexamples when solutions fail, and looking at BIBO stability of the system. Our analysis has resulted in a final stochastic model that has passed conditions for uniqueness and existence of solutions.

title: When Oil Volatility Spikes, Litigation Follows
affiliations: Capital Market Risk Advisors, Capital Market Risk Advisors and Capital Market Risk Advisors

detail.title: When Oil Volatility Spikes, Litigation Follows
detail.abstract:
Volatility in the markets tends to lead to disputes and litigation. Crude oil just experienced one of the most violent price swings in history. The CBOE Oil Volatility Index hit near its second highest level since 2010, surpassed only by COVID. The implications span oil, gas and fertilizer markets and all the customers of those markets.

In our experience advising clients through multiple volatility disputes in the equity, fixed income, sugar, copper and energy markets, extreme price dislocations like this don’t just move markets. They move disputes and litigation typically 6 to 18 months later.

In this research paper, we outline the current situation, the likely avenues for disputes and steps clients can take now to prepare themselves.

title: Non-clinical Service and Liability in Healthcare Credence Goods Markets: Theory and Experiments
affiliations: Nankai University, Shandong University - School of Economics, Shandong University - School of Economics and

detail.title: Non-clinical Service and Liability in Healthcare Credence Goods Markets: Theory and Experiments
detail.abstract: We study how non-clinical service interacts with liability in healthcare credence goods markets. We develop a model in which an informed provider chooses treatment, pricing, and non-clinical service that affects patient experience but not treatment effectiveness. We test the model's predictions in a laboratory experiment, comparing baseline and liability regimes under abstract and healthcare framing. We find that liability increases providers' reliance on non-clinical service as a reputational instrument. Healthcare framing substantially reduces undertreatment in the absence of liability. However, when combined with liability, healthcare framing leads to higher overcharging, which is systematically associated with higher non-clinical service, reallocating opportunistic behavior toward pricing once clinical discretion is constrained. Overall, our findings highlight a trade-off: liability and framing discipline clinical behavior but simultaneously redirect strategic behavior toward pricing and nonclinical service.

title: Lifting Constraints: Venezuelan Oil and Global Market Adjustment
affiliations: Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei (FEEM), University of Milan, Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei (FEEM) and Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei (FEEM)

detail.title: Lifting Constraints: Venezuelan Oil and Global Market Adjustment
detail.abstract: We quantify the contribution of Venezuela's oil sector collapse to changes in global oil market responsiveness after 2007. We extend the multi-country structural model of Baumeister and Hamilton (2024) by modeling Venezuela explicitly and constructing a counterfactual production path that abstracts from the 2007 institutional shift. This counterfactual isolates the mechanical contribution of Venezuelan supply and provides an upper bound on its impact. We document a sharp decline in global short-run supply elasticity and a more than doubling of the oil price multiplier after 2007. Decomposition results show that this increase is driven primarily by a reduction in the effective inventoryrelated adjustment margin, with changes in other producers' supply elasticities accounting for most of the remainder. By contrast, Venezuela's contribution through its production share and contemporaneous supply elasticity is small. Restoring Venezuelan output raises global supply elasticity modestly but has limited effects on price amplification.

title: Predicting LBO Candidate Likelihood in the Post-COVID Era: Evidence from Machine Learning and Interest Rate Regime Analysis
