declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether publicly observable firm-level financial characteristics can predict leveraged buyout (LBO) targeting among US public companies in the post-COVID era. Using a matched sample of 12 completed LBO transactions and 98 industry-and size-matched control firm-years from the SimFin database over 2020-2024, we construct a binary classification framework employing logistic regression and gradientboosted trees (XGBoost) with SHAP-based interpretability analysis. We address multicollinearity by excluding return on assets (VIF = 10.64, r = 0.93 with FCF/Assets) from the logistic regression while retaining it in XGBoost. Debt-to-EBITDA, return on assets, and interest coverage ratio emerge as the three most important SHAP predictors, consistent with Jensen's (1986) free cash flow hypothesis. We document economically large shifts in SHAP feature importance following the 2022 Federal Reserve tightening cycledebt-to-EBITDA +143%, free cash flow yield +178%, while EBITDA margin declined 95% and Tobin's Q declined 96%-although 95% bootstrap confidence intervals overlap across regimes, precluding statistical significance due to the small post-2022 LBO sample (n=2). These findings are consistent with Axelson et al. (2013): when credit becomes expensive, PE acquirers shift focus from static profitability toward dynamic cash generation and leverage capacity.

title: The Limits of Lucas: Health Returns Under Financing Frictions

detail.title: The Limits of Lucas: Health Returns Under Financing Frictions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper uses publicly available secondary data (Nigeria GHS-Panel from World Bank), not human subjects research requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We study when investing in health raises income and when it does not. Using a nationally representative Nigerian panel with 18,142 household-years from 2010 to 2024, we estimate a log-income production function in which health's marginal product depends on out-of-pocket (OOP) health spending. At zero OOP, the implied return matches the Lucas (1988) benchmark, but at observed OOP levels this return falls by more than half at the mean and turns negative for 14.2 percent of households, rising to 29.7 percent among the poor. We explain these "wrong-signed" returns with a model of survival health investment where low-income households use health spending for biological maintenance rather than growth, generating dual thresholds that divide the population into optimization, survival, and catastrophic regimes. Empirically, an OOP threshold near 11 percent of income marks where health returns turn negative, while an income threshold near ₦79,000 marks where OOP switches from raising to crowding out dietary diversity. Below these thresholds, higher OOP increases dietary diversity, reduces labor supply, and shifts diets toward protein-rich foods, consistent with efficiency gains from restored health rather than standard wealth-shock responses. Our framework nests Lucas as the frictionless special case, reconciles macro evidence of high health returns with micro evidence on catastrophic expenditures, and provides an outcome-based rationale for the WHO 10 percent benchmark.

title: The Formalization of Synthetic Data in the Social Sciences: Architecture, Validation, and Epistemic Foundations
affiliations: Independent and

detail.title: The Formalization of Synthetic Data in the Social Sciences: Architecture, Validation, and Epistemic Foundations
detail.abstract: The widespread adoption of computational models such as agent-based simulations or AI-based language generation has led to the emergence of a new class or construct of data artifacts: model-generated digital outputs that represent, among other things, social interactions, institutional dynamics, as well as decision-making processes within computational environments. Although synthetic data are increasingly relevant in the social sciences and practical matters such as policy advice or design, they remain conceptually rather underdefined as well as methodologically underspecified. Hence, this paper presents a systematic methodological framework for synthetic social data. It contends that these artifacts should not be regarded as empirical observations or merely as technical data/ information. Instead, they function as structured epistemic instruments that generate conditional possibility spaces based on explicitly specified assumptions. By drawing on model theory, counterfactual reasoning, and the non-ergodic nature of economic/social systems, this paper clarifies the ontological and epistemic status of these data. The principal contribution is a formal three-layer architectural concept that distinguishes the structural core, calibration layer, and projection layer. Building on this very approach, a multi-dimensional validation framework is proposed that integrates structural, parametric, dynamic, as well as contextual dimensions of assessment. Additionally, the analysis introduces principles of operational quality governance, including reproducibility, documentation, communication, and bias management. By integrating architectural transparency, structured validation, as well as institutional accountability, this paper positions synthetic social data as an emerging methodological paradigm for the production of social knowledge in order to enhance their use for the applied sciences along with practical applications. The scientific value of such data resides not in deterministic predictions, but in the systematic exploration of probable contingencies or scenarios under transparent assumptions. In short, this paper proposes a conceptual framework for the architecture, validation, as well as governance of synthetic social data and positions them as a distinct epistemological category within the social sciences.

title: Greater Autonomy, Better Access? The Causal Effect of Physician Associate Scope-of-Practice Expansions on Healthcare Access and Cost Barriers

detail.title: Greater Autonomy, Better Access? The Causal Effect of Physician Associate Scope-of-Practice Expansions on Healthcare Access and Cost Barriers

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of expanded scope-of-practice laws for physician associates (PAs) on healthcare access and utilization among working-age individuals in the United States. Using a dynamic difference-indifferences approach and nationally representative individual-level data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) spanning 2012 to 2024, we exploit staggered adoption of these laws across states and variation in treatment intensity. We find that expanded PA autonomy reduced cost-related barriers to care by 0.5 percentage points. We find no significant effects on routine checkups, having a personal healthcare provider, or emergency department and outpatient visits. Additionally, expanded PAs autonomy does not affect care quality, as proxied by malpractice payment records. Taken together, these findings indicate that granting greater practice autonomy to PAs could alleviate financial barriers to healthcare access and enhance consumer welfare.

title: Missionary Infrastructure and the Intensive Margin of Ottoman State Schooling

detail.abstract: This paper examines the spatial determinants of state-school expansion in late OttomanAnatolia (1876–1902/08). Using a sanjak-level dataset derived from Ottoman administrative records, I study the relationship between Western missionary main stations and theexpansion of the male rü¸sdiye school system. Sanjaks hosting main stations experiencedapproximately 1.1 additional schools compared to control sanjaks. This coefficient is sta-ble across specifications: Oster (2019) bounds yield δ= 1.1 with an identified set excludingzero, it is robust to inverse-probability weighting (β= 1.03), Poisson count models, andthe exclusion of any individual treated unit or vilayet. A continuous distance specificationconfirms that proximity to main stations predicts greater school expansion. A placebo teston female rü¸sdiye returns a precise null, consistent with a response operating specificallythrough the male bureaucratic-training channel. Statistical precision under clustered in-ference remains limited (randomization p= 0.14). All frontier sanjaks that initially lackedstate schools universally gained provision regardless of missionary presence.

title: Institutional Thresholds and Globalization: Do Strong Institutions Unlock Renewable Energy Transition? Panel Evidence from 180 Countries

detail.title: Institutional Thresholds and Globalization: Do Strong Institutions Unlock Renewable Energy Transition? Panel Evidence from 180 Countries
detail.abstract: Renewable energy transitions remain  persistently uneven across countries  despite accelerating global commitments  to decarbonisation. This paper examines  whether institutional quality moderates  the association between economic  globalization and renewable energy  adoption, arguing that globalization's  impact is fundamentally conditional on  the governance environment in which it  operates. Drawing on a game-theoretic  framework, a theoretical institutional  turning point is derived above which the  government's dominant strategy shifts  from fossil-fuel lock-in to renewable  energy transition. Using an unbalanced  panel of 180 countries over 1996-2022  comprising 3,510 country-year  observations, a composite institutional  quality index is constructed via  principal component analysis of six  World Governance Indicators, and  two-way fixed effects models with  country-clustered standard errors are  estimated. The results reveal that  globalization is negatively and  significantly associated with renewable  energy share across the full  distribution of institutional quality,  but this association weakens  systematically as institutions  strengthen. A turning point is estimated  at an index value of approximately 1.912  on a standardised scale, though this  estimate carries statistical uncertainty  and should be interpreted with caution.  Only five economies - Finland, Denmark,  New Zealand, Switzerland, and Norway -  consistently maintain institutional  quality above this estimate on average,  while 175 countries across all income  groups fall below it, including 55  high-income economies. These findings  suggest that income alone may be  insufficient to unlock globalization as  a channel for renewable transition; the  quality of governance appears to be a  binding constraint. Results are robust  to outlier exclusion, minimum  observation requirements, and  income-group subsamples.

title: Exploring General Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Exploring General Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
detail.abstract: Defining an asset's "allocation density" provides a different perspective on a general equilibrium model of a pure exchange economy. This perspective illustrates key features of that economy while being mathematically straightforward. Calculation of equilibrium asset prices and the transactions required to bring all agents to their equilibrium endowments is simplified. In addition, the special role of assets whose nominal prices are unaffected by changes in asset allocation is highlighted.

title: Trade Network Position and Home-Currency Invoicing

detail.title: Trade Network Position and Home-Currency Invoicing
detail.abstract: This paper studies how global trade network structure shapes countries' invoicing currency choices. Using panel data on trade invoicing and network centrality, we show that countries use more of home currency for imports as importer-side structural network position improves, reflecting the bargaining power of economies that serve as key destination markets in global trade. In contrast, changes in exporter-side network position do not have significant effects on home-currency export invoicing, suggesting that exporters' currency power does not adjust substantially with network position. These findings highlight how asymmetric trade networks sustain dominant currencies through the bargaining power of central importing economies.

title: The Strategy of the Objective: A Hermeneutic Approach to Strategy

detail.title: The Strategy of the Objective: A Hermeneutic Approach to Strategy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rifé Cabos, R. (2026). The Strategy of the Objective: A Hermeneutic Approach to Strategy. Cambridge Open Engage. doi:10.33774/coe-2026-m7g8l-v2.

detail.abstract: Strategic theory has offered innumerable methods for achieving objectives, yet it has largely neglected the objective itself. Although objectives are commonly represented as a desired end state, there exists a relative will on the part of the opposing actor that resists that outcome and therefore also forms part of the final conditions. The objective is therefore intimately linked to the understanding of the other will. To address this complexity, this article proposes a hermeneutic approach grounded in the premise that actors communicate their intentions through the effects their actions imprint upon reality. These effects are changes that, as such, can be measured across the structural variables of modern conflict. In this way, they can be mapped and interpreted within conceptual spaces of competition or conflict, offering a point of departure for identifying and adjusting strategic objectives in line with the evolution of such behaviour.

detail.title: Provenance Over Detection: A Cryptographic Framework for Human Authorship Verification in Music Distribution

detail.abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated music has exposed a structural flaw in how digital streaming platforms govern content authenticity. Current platform responses rely primarily on output-based detection-identifying AI-generated audio after the fact using algorithmic classifiers. These tools are unreliable, slow to adapt, and generate false positives at rates that threaten legitimate artists. This paper argues that detection is the wrong frame entirely. The solution is provenance: cryptographic verification of human authorship embedded at the point of creation and carried through the distribution chain. Drawing on existing standards including C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, 2025), recent advances in audio watermarking (Digimarc, 2025; Ono, 2026), and blockchain-based session verification (Pandey, Singh, et al., 2025), this paper proposes a music-specific provenance framework that addresses AI detection, royalty attribution, rights management, and licensing transparency within a single embedded metadata layer. The framework is designed for DAW-level implementation with distribution-chain readability, adding negligible file overhead while creating a permanent, tamper-evident record of an audio asset's origin, authorship, and modification history.

title: When Silence Harms: Misconceptions About CPR and a Legislative Path Forward

detail.abstract: The law's silence about the effectiveness of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) at various stages of a patient's life creates an illusion of choice where none exists. Nearly ninety percent of Americans overestimate CPR's effectiveness, and many hospitals still initiate it by default-even when clinical evidence shows it to be traumatic and futile for dying patients. This Article contends that CPR's exclusion from informed-consent doctrine represents a systemic form of misrepresentation inconsistent with the Patient Self-Determination Act (PSDA). Drawing on behavioral-economics research, the Article proposes a modified prompted-choice model requiring hospitals, long-term care facilities, and physicians to disclose, upon admission, a patient's default CPR status, the intervention's realistic success rate given their condition, and the option to decline. Embedding this disclosure duty within the PSDA's existing framework would realign clinical practice with legal norms of patient autonomy. The proposal offers a pragmatic legislative mechanism for reducing moral distress among providers, minimizing conflicts with surrogates, and ensuring that care decisions reflect informed, voluntary consent rather than cultural myth.

title: Does FIFA World Cup Participation Move the Macroeconomy? Evidence from Seven Tournaments Across Non-Host Countries, 1998-2022

detail.abstract: Using a stacked difference-indifferences event-study design across seven FIFA World Cup cycles (1998-2022), we estimate the macroeconomic effects of tournament participation on up to 214 non-host countries. We find a modest and statistically significant contemporaneous increase in real GDP growth of 0.56 percentage points (p = 0.040), but no effect on private consumption, no persistent export response, and no differential gain for emerging and developing economies. The effect dissipates within one year. These findings suggest that World Cup participation is macroeconomically neutral at the aggregate level, providing a more realistic benchmark for assessing the economic relevance of international sporting exposure ahead of the 2026 tournament.

detail.abstract: Renewable integration in the United States is increasingly constrained by transmission bottlenecks, rising curtailment, and growing largeload demand. At the same time, major technology firms have committed to ambitious clean energy goals, including 24/7 carbonfree energy and carbon neutrality by 2030. These goals are becoming harder to achieve as AI and data center electricity demand rises rapidly. This paper evaluates a coordinated twolayer framework: first, deploying Grid Enhancing Technologies (GETs) to unlock additional physical transfer capability on the existing grid; second, using renewableaware workload migration, described here as Compute as Virtual Transmission, to shift flexible digital demand toward regions and hours with renewable surplus. With U.S. data center demand projected to reach 450 TWh by 2030, shifting even 20% of flexible workloads could align about 90 TWh of demand with renewable availability. The paper also introduces a new trilemma framing centered on congestion cost, renewable curtailment, and 24/7 clean energy requirements, and presents a simplified twopoint corridor example to show how physical and digital coordination can reduce congestion and improve renewable utilization. The main argument is that the nearterm constraint is not only generation or transmission buildout, but the lack of coordination between infrastructure and flexible demand.

title: Do Retail Investors Drive Lottery-Like Stock Mispricing?
affiliations: Coastal Carolina University and Old Dominion University

detail.title: Do Retail Investors Drive Lottery-Like Stock Mispricing?
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether retail participation explains the underperformance of lottery-like stocks. Prior research links retail trading to attention-driven buying after salient events. In contrast, we examine systematic retail participation. Using weekly Robinhood holdings data, we construct measures capturing persistent ownership and flow dynamics rather than short-lived attention shocks. We study their relation to the MAX anomaly, the negative relation between extreme returns and future returns. Systematic retail participation predicts positive future returns, while the MAX anomaly remains negative and economically significant. Retail participation does not strengthen the MAX effect, indicating distinct sources of return predictability.

title: Assisted Dying in the United States
affiliations: Mitchell Hamline School of Law

detail.title: Assisted Dying in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Chapter 10 in Research Handbook on Voluntary Assisted Dying Law, Regulation and Practice, Edward Elgar 2025

detail.abstract:
The United States was one of the first jurisdictions in the world to legalize assisted dying. Oregon enacted its Death with Dignity Act in 1994. Over the past thirty years, ten more U.S. jurisdictions have authorized assisted dying. All these U.S. laws are internationally distinctive in two ways. First, the United States is a federal system with 56 jurisdictions. Assisted dying is authorized at only the state/territory level, and 45 jurisdictions have not yet authorized it. Second, all U.S. assisted dying laws are restrictive compared to laws in other nations. They are restrictive in terms of the mode of administration, authorizing only assisted dying that is self-administered by the patient through ingestion. U.S. assisted dying laws are also restrictive in terms of eligibility. Assisted dying is available to only those patients with a terminal illness likely to cause death within six months.

But neither the legal framework nor the practice of assisted dying is static. Assisted dying in the United States is evolving. More states are poised to authorize assisted dying. And both new and existing states are breaking away from the traditional model. They are increasingly amending or designing their laws to make assisted dying more accessible. Already, the scope and nature of assisted dying in the United States is materially different from five years ago. It is likely to look even more different over the next five years.

detail.abstract: We penetrate the black box of post-acquisition integration by examining whether business unit leaders (BULs)-executives responsible for integrating and operating acquired targets-shape integration outcomes. Using natural language processing-based measures of realized integration outcomes and financial metrics, we find that BULs' target-industry experience increases (decreases) integration success (failures) through superior realization of transaction synergies. Other BUL attributes are unrelated to integration outcomes. Consistent with the importance of integration for acquisition success, such experience enhances acquisition performance. BULs' target-industry experience improves integration planning and their post-acquisition career outcomes but is unrelated to earlier stages of the acquisition process.

title: Institutional Narrative Risk and the Financial Transmission of Political Uncertainty
affiliations: Florida International University

detail.title: Institutional Narrative Risk and the Financial Transmission of Political Uncertainty
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether narrative signals issued by sovereign authorities are reflected in realized firm-level financial performance. Using official government communications, we construct a measure of institutional narrative risk (NMR) capturing policy signaling across coercion, exchange, and cooperation dimensions. Lagged narrative exposure is related to firm-level liquidity, operating profitability, capital efficiency, and financing conditions in a two-way fixed effects panel of globally significant firms in a capital-intensive, geopolitically exposed industry. Coercion-oriented signals exhibit the strongest associations within one reporting cycle, with economically meaningful effects on liquidity and operating profitability. Capital efficiency responds more weakly, and financing-cost effects are small and specification-sensitive. Comparing origin-based and mentions-based exposure mappings, internal financial adjustment aligns more closely with sovereign authority signals than with narrative mention intensity. These findings extend the political uncertainty literature beyond market-based outcomes by linking primary-source sovereign communications to downstream accounting performance and demonstrating that exposure design materially shapes inference.

title: On the Exact Obstruction to the Jamshidian Decomposition in Multifactor Affine Models

detail.title: On the Exact Obstruction to the Jamshidian Decomposition in Multifactor Affine Models
detail.abstract: The Jamshidian decomposition reduces a European coupon-bond option to a portfolio of zero-coupon bond options through a single deterministic set of component strikes. We study when such a decomposition can hold exactly in a general exponential-affine setting. Our main result shows that within the class P i (x) = A i e-B ⊤ i x , an exact deterministic-strike Jamshidian decomposition exists if and only if all loading vectors {B i } are positively collinear, i.e. lie on a single ray in R d. We then develop a quantitative near-collinearity framework. For a fixed reference direction u, we define the associated transverse dispersion D u and show that the projected deterministic-strike approximation is a pathwise upper bound whose error is confined to a strip around the projected one-factor exercise hyperplane. We also show that the corresponding projected strikes are minimax-optimal for worst-case strip width under the stated criterion. Finally, we discuss several structural extensions. Unrestricted state-dependent strikes trivialize the decomposition problem; numéraire changes leave the exercise geometry unchanged; and a scalar-factor rigidity result shows that, for exponential-affine families, nonlinear scalar reparameterizations do not evade the positive-collinearity obstruction.

title: Cross-Country Macroeconomic Dynamics: Inflation, Growth, and Monetary Policy - India, Singapore, and the United Kingdom

detail.abstract: This paper presents a comparative macroeconomic analysis of India, Singapore, and the United Kingdom, examining how inflation dynamics, monetary policy frameworks, and growth cycles interacted across the post-pandemic period. OLS persistence regressions confirm inflation is highly self-propagating across all three economies (β ranging from 0.95 to 0.99), with the UK exhibiting near-unit persistence (β = 0.99) consistent with unanchored expectations. Pairwise Granger causality tests reveal an asymmetric transmission structure: India's CPI Granger-causes both Singapore (p = 0.028) and UK inflation (p = 0.018), suggesting a sequential emerging-toadvanced economy transmission chain. Singapore's exchange-rate-centred framework produced a comparatively smoother disinflation path, consistent with its direct import price adjustment mechanism. The findings offer insights into the comparative advantages of exchange-rate versus interest-rate targeting frameworks under conditions of recurring global supply shocks.

title: Everybody Knows: A Unitary Theoretical Framework or a Pluralist Toolbox?

detail.title: Everybody Knows: A Unitary Theoretical Framework or a Pluralist Toolbox?
detail.abstract: Real world problems are frequently complex and do not admit of single explanations. By contrast, the social science academic thesis and article writing process has become stultified, locked into a process that involves identifying not just a research question, or hypothesis, but a unitary theoretical framework. This has injurious effects on social science research in a number of ways including distorting and misrepresenting data that does not fit the selected framework. The alternative of using a pluralistic theoretical framework is advanced and defended against potential criticisms.

detail.abstract: This paper provides the geometric and dynamical backbone of a theory of monetary circulation developed across a sequence of works. Building on the semi-Markov path framework of activated money introduced in Paper 1, we develop a rigorous network-geometric theory of trapping, bottlenecks, and regime persistence in monetary circulation. The core contribution is a non-equilibrium, non-stationary theory of confinement: we formalize trapping sets, escape intensities, exit-time bounds, and bottlenecks on directed institutional networks without assuming stationarity, equilibrium, or prices. A central object is a barrier potential defined on the network, which induces an effective landscape governing escape rates in an Arrhenius-type manner. This landscape-based view yields precise criteria for long exit times, hysteresis, and selective de-trapping. We introduce a geometric trapping angle θ(S, t), which quantifies the degree of confinement of circulation in a set S and interpolates continuously between mobile and fully trapped regimes. The angle provides a coordinate-free, scale-invariant summary of confinement and plays a key organizing role for regime classification. Finally, we define productive basins as dynamically accessible regions of the network and establish a structural separation between trapping and production: high activity and irreversibility do not, in general, imply productive circulation. This paper closes the mathematical layer needed to interpret crises, persistent liquidity blockages, and recovery episodes as geometric regime phenomena. Economic interpretation and empirical identification are developed in companion papers. This paper forms the second part of a three-paper sequence and provides the geometric backbone of the theory.

title: A Structural Theory of Monetary Circulation

detail.title: A Structural Theory of Monetary Circulation

detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural theory of money in which macroeconomic outcomes emerge from the activation, circulation, and irreversibility of monetary flows. Rather than modeling prices, preferences, or equilibrium behavior, the framework treats money as a dynamical object whose economic effectiveness depends on where it resides, how long it remains, and how asymmetrically it circulates across an economic network. At the micro level, monetary units evolve according to an activation-weighted semi-Markov process, capturing residence times, routing across agents or sectors, and stochastic circulation paths. At the macro level, we show that long-run economic output can be represented as the timeaverage of activation-weighted entropy production, providing a rigorous micro-to-macro link that does not rely on optimization or equilibrium assumptions. Under ergodic conditions, this yields a unique macro growth rate. When ergodicity fails, the same structural laws generate historydependent macro outcomes, offering a mathematical interpretation of persistent bubbles, crises, and segmented circulation regimes. Policy interventions enter the framework as structural modifications of activation, routing, and residence dynamics, rather than as direct controls over aggregate quantities. This preserves policy relevance while avoiding ad hoc macro closures. The theory deliberately abstracts from welfare and price formation in order to isolate the structural mechanics of monetary circulation. By grounding macroeconomic production in the geometry and irreversibility of money flows, the paper provides a complementary perspective on macroeconomic dynamics, bridging elements of monetary theory, network analysis, and stochastic processes. This paper constitutes the first part of a three-paper sequence on the structural theory of monetary circulation.

title: Urban Air Mobility Ecosystem Readiness in India: A Multi-Dimensional Assessment Framework for Emerging Economies

detail.title: Urban Air Mobility Ecosystem Readiness in India: A Multi-Dimensional Assessment Framework for Emerging Economies

detail.abstract: Urban Air Mobility, or UAM, is no longer a futuristic concept confined to science fiction. With several eVTOL aircraft nearing certification in the United States and Europe, the question for countries like India is not whether this technology will arrive, but whether we are ready for it. This paper proposes a practical assessment tool-the UAM Ecosystem Readiness Index (UAM-ERI)-designed specifically for the messy, complex realities of emerging economies. Unlike existing frameworks that assume a certain baseline of regulatory sophistication and infrastructure maturity, the UAM-ERI accounts for the institutional fragmentation, income disparities, and infrastructure gaps that characterize markets like India. The framework evaluates six interconnected dimensions: Regulatory Maturity, Infrastructure Preparedness, Technological Capability, Economic Viability, Social Acceptance, and Environmental Sustainability. Each dimension is weighted through an Analytical Hierarchy Process involving 18 domain experts. Applying this framework across five Indian metros-Delhi-NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Chennai-the study finds that India's technology talent and market size represent genuine strengths, but regulatory clarity and physical infrastructure lag far behind. Bengaluru scores highest overall (0.548), yet even this puts it squarely in the "developing readiness" band. The paper closes with a phased 2026-2035 implementation roadmap grounded in these findings.

detail.abstract: This study employs an ensemble machine learning method, known as “Stacking,” to forecast corporate bond returns. We find that the Stacking method introduces new features into combination forecasts, increasing the predictive model’s power and generating higher statistical and economic gains across bond ratings and maturities. Moreover, the method is efficient for tackling high dimensionality and achieves the best result when using predictors from corporate bond, Treasury, and stock markets jointly. While the overall performance of different Stacking models is satisfactory, simpler Stacking models appear to outperform others and generate optimal forecasts.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a formal system of fragility metrics within Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT). We define three fundamental quantities: the Local Fragility Index (LFI), the Local Stability Margin (LSM), and the Fragility Field Index (FFI). These metrics provide a minimal and complete structural description of amplification, compensability, and connectivity of fragile regions in liquidity-driven systems. The paper establishes precise definitions and mathematical status of each metric, distinguishing their differential, variational, and topological nature. The proposed triad forms a unified framework for describing local fragility, proximity to compensability boundaries, and structural propagation of instability. The framework is restricted to structural characterization and does not include operational procedures, estimation methods, or applied control mechanisms. These remain within the applied layer of WLRT.

title: The Transnational Effect of Temperature on Remittances

detail.title: The Transnational Effect of Temperature on Remittances
detail.abstract: We study how temperature shocks on both sides of the US-Mexico migration corridor affect remittances. Using quarterly Mexican municipality-level remittance data and Mexican undocumented migrant network data linking communities of origin to US destinations, combined with weather data, we identify two opposing forces. Extreme temperatures in Mexico increase remittance inflows, consistent with an insurance motive. In contrast, temperature extremes in US destinations reduce remittances. These effects operate through migrant labor markets: heat and cold reduce the earnings of immigrants.

title: Gender, Ethnicity, and Justice: Evaluating How Intersectional Hate Crimes Are a Barrier to Gender Equality

detail.title: Gender, Ethnicity, and Justice: Evaluating How Intersectional Hate Crimes Are a Barrier to Gender Equality
detail.abstract: For ethnic minority women who are victims of hate-motivated violence, and gender equality, which is required as Sustainable Development Goal Goal 5 by 2030, remains unachievable. Contemporary domestic and international legal frameworks use a single-axis approach that treats gender and ethnicity as distinct grounds of discrimination, making the compounded damages suffered by women who hold multiple marginalized identities invisible. This paper examines how the existing legal frameworks support substantive gender equality and how much they acknowledge and deal with intersectional hate crimes that target both gender and ethnicity. This paper shows how the legal methods are separated fundamentally and how it fails intersectionally vulnerable women through a comparative examination of international instruments and domestic legal systems in Canada, France, and India. Institutional hierarchies hinder adequate prosecution and punishments as they lack frameworks to identify compounded discrimination, and the current data techniques fail to capture the same. The prime example is Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG) as it portrays how colonialism and patriarchy combine to generate a distinct, tragic vulnerability that cannot be addressed by a single-axis approach. India's Bharatiya Sanhita, while expanding hate crime provisions, is still institutionally underutilized for intersectional protection, France's statutory framework lacks substantive enforcement, and Canada's extensive hate crime provisions are applied inconsistently. This paper bridges the theory and practice as the implementation must be driven by strategic partnership between civil society and the justice system which incorporates institutional accountability mechanisms and performs in line with SDG 5 frameworks.

title: The "Nazi Economic Miracle" Reconsidered: Financial Engineering, Regulation, and the Political Economy of Unsustainable Rearmament (1933-1939)

detail.title: The "Nazi Economic Miracle" Reconsidered: Financial Engineering, Regulation, and the Political Economy of Unsustainable Rearmament (1933-1939)
detail.abstract: Claims of an "economic miracle" under National Socialism usually point to the rapid collapse of mass unemployment and the visible recovery of German output after 1933. This paper argues that these outcomes were produced by a distinctive architecture of finance and control rather than by a uniquely efficient growth model. First, the regime expanded spending while obscuring the true deficit threw off budget instruments, most notably the MEFO bill system, supported by Reichsbank rediscounting. Second, it reconstructed the domestic financial market into a captive savings pool via exchange controls, administrative allocation of credit, and pressures on banks and institutional investors to absorb state paper. Third, it imposed a command administrative layer, wage restraint, price controls, import licensing, and corporatist labor institutions, that contained open inflation by repressing consumption and rationing foreign exchange. The same tools that accelerated employment and rearmament created a deferred crisis: a maturity wall in hidden debt, tightening balance of payments constraints, shortages, and investment distortions that shifted incentives from efficiency toward political access and plan compliance. By 1938-1939 the model relied increasingly on coercive absorption of debt and on expectations of external acquisition to relax real resource constraints. On this reading, the "miracle" was a time buying mobilization mechanism whose internal logic made peacetime stabilization progressively harder without a major reorientation of policy.

title: Economics as a Tool of War

detail.title: Economics as a Tool of War
detail.abstract: Economic sanctions, export controls and financial restrictions have become central instruments of modern statecraft. Rather than replacing military conflict, these tools transform the infrastructure of globalisation—financial networks, trade routes and industrial supply chains—into arenas of geopolitical competition. This paper examines the mechanisms through which economic coercion operates, focusing on three primary channels: resource denial, financial intermediation and network control. Drawing on historical and contemporary cases—including the British blockade of Germany during the First World War, sanctions on Iraq, Iran’s exclusion from SWIFT and the financial measures imposed on Russia after 2022—the paper evaluates the strategic effectiveness and limitations of economic warfare. While such measures rarely produce immediate political capitulation, they can degrade military capacity, disrupt logistics and reshape global economic expectations. The growing reliance on economic weapons, however, is likely to accelerate the fragmentation of global markets and encourage the creation of alternative financial and technological systems. As economic policy becomes increasingly militarised, the distinction between commerce and conflict continues to erode.

title: Estimating Long Run Value at Risk for Wealth Management

detail.title: Estimating Long Run Value at Risk for Wealth Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The portfolio allocation weights used in this study were provided by Randalls Wealth Management as part of a supervised applied dissertation partnership. The underlying market return data was sourced independently from Bloomberg Terminal. The author has no financial relationship with Randalls Wealth Management and the findings of this research reflect the author's own independent analysis.

detail.abstract:
Scaling short-horizon Value at Risk to multi-year investment horizons remains a fundamental challenge for wealth managers and institutional investors. Variance-covariance methods that rely on square-root-of-time scaling break down under the fat tails, skewness, and volatility clustering empirically documented in asset returns. These features are confirmed in this study's dataset of 425 monthly observations spanning January 1990 to May 2025, which exhibits excess kurtosis of 4.13 and skewness of 1.19. This paper provides a comprehensive empirical comparison of simulation-based approaches for estimating long-horizon Value at Risk on a globally diversified multi-asset portfolio.

Two families of methods are evaluated. The first is a moment-matched Monte Carlo engine based on Fleishman cubic polynomial transformations, calibrated window-by-window to reproduce rolling empirical skewness and kurtosis across 150-month estimation windows, with an optional variance-alignment step. The second comprises seven bootstrap designs of increasing sophistication, covering i.i.d., circular block, stationary block, wild, AR-sieve, GARCH, and filtered historical simulation approaches, each targeting different features of return dependence and heteroskedasticity. All methods generate 60-month horizon losses and are evaluated in a rolling back-test framework using 20,000 Monte Carlo paths and 10,000 bootstrap draws per forecast origin. Inference is corrected for the 59-month overlap inherent in rolling 60-month windows using Newey-West HAC z-tests alongside Kupiec unconditional coverage and Christoffersen independence diagnostics.

The moment-matched Monte Carlo engine achieves well-calibrated coverage at both confidence levels, recording a 4.63% breach rate at the 95% VaR level against a 5% nominal target and 0.93% at the 99% level against a 1% target, with no detectable exception clustering in either case. Bootstrap performance is substantially more variable. Naive designs systematically under-cover at the 95% level, with observed hit rates ranging from 10.0% to 24.2%, while all bootstrap variants produce zero breaches at the 99% level, indicating over-conservatism in the extreme tail. A focused head-to-head comparison demonstrates that a properly tuned stationary bootstrap can match Monte Carlo performance under overlap-aware inference. Sensitivity analysis identifies block-length selection and volatility scaling as the two primary governance levers, with stationary bootstrap VaR at the 95% level increasing by 49% as mean block length rises from 6 to 30 months, while Monte Carlo VaR responds near-linearly to the volatility multiplier.

The findings support a pragmatic two-engine risk management workflow in which moment-matched Monte Carlo serves as the primary production engine for long-horizon VaR, with a dependence-preserving stationary bootstrap retained as a documented robustness check. Both engines should be evaluated under an explicitly overlap-robust inference framework. The results have direct implications for strategic asset allocation, risk budgeting, and liability-driven investment in wealth management and pension fund contexts.

detail.abstract: We introduce Epistemic Curvature (EC), a market metrology system that computes the Riemannian curvature of the Fisher-Rao statistical manifold of market-implied probability distributions. The central primitive is the Epistemic Curvature Spectrum-the eigen decomposition {(κ_α(t), v_α(t))} of the Ricci tensor R_ij(θ(t)) at the market's current belief state-which measures, at every timestamp, which dimensions of the market's collective probability beliefs are geometrically fragile (conviction repellers, κ < 0) and which are robust (conviction attractors, κ > 0). A comprehensive prior-art scan across 17+ academic venues confirms zero prior work computing smooth Riemannian curvature of a Fisher-Rao manifold of market beliefs. We establish two new theoretical results: the corrected SPD(d) scalar curvature formula R =-d(d+2)(d-1)/4 (yielding R₀ =-35.0 for d = 5), and the warped product structure of N(μ,Σ) yielding R =-d(d+1)²/4. The MVP build (Phases 1-4 complete, plus rolling lead-lag econometric module and option-implied manifold pipeline) achieves 62/62 unit tests passing and 5/5 pre-registered falsification tests passing on real S&P 500 data. Three parametric families (Normal, NIG, Gaussian Mixture) are implemented with analytic Fisher metrics and JAX automatic differentiation. The option-implied pipeline extracts risk-neutral densities via the Breeden-Litzenberger formula, fits log-normal mixtures, and computes curvature from a 25dimensional cross-asset belief state using exact numerical quadrature of the Fisher metric, confirmed to agree with Monte Carlo fallback within 10%. The rolling lead-lag study establishes that scalar curvature leads VIX with a broad plateau from lag 0-12 days (peak r = +0.081 at lag = 1d), with statistically significant regime-dependent structure (Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.05 across calm, moderate, and crisis regimes): pre-GFC +13d, COVID +2d, recent +0d. Predictive regressions with Newey-West HAC correction establish β < 0 (curvature predicts VIX increases) at horizons h = {1, 5, 10, 21} days, with R² = 0.109 at h = 5d. Option-implied curvature is shown to lead return-implied curvature by approximately 3 trading days, confirming the forward-looking advantage of the options channel. The system emits failure artifacts rather than smoothing over poor identification.

title: Economics as a Tool of War: Mechanisms, Effectiveness, and Political Economy

detail.title: Economics as a Tool of War: Mechanisms, Effectiveness, and Political Economy
detail.abstract: War is frequently analyzed through the lens of military force, yet the modern conduct of conflict is inseparable from economic organization. States mobilize resources, finance armies, and attempt to degrade an adversary's capacity to sustain operations. In contemporary practice, "economics as a tool of war" increasingly denotes the deliberate use of trade, finance, and industrial constraints to generate strategic effects-sometimes as a complement to kinetic operations and sometimes as an attempted substitute. The rise of comprehensive sanctions regimes, the use of export controls on dual use technologies, and the freezing of sovereign assets all reflect an expansion of what Baldwin termed "economic statecraft," the use of economic means to pursue foreign policy goals (Baldwin 1985). This paper develops an analytical account of economics as a coercive instrument in interstate conflict. It pursues three objectives. First, it clarifies concepts and typologies, distinguishing economic warfare from routine economic competition and from wartime mobilization. Second, it synthesizes competing Economic instruments are now central to coercion and conflict management: sanctions, export controls, financial restrictions, aid conditionality, asset freezes, and blockade-like constraints can degrade an adversary's war-making capacity while staying below the threshold of direct kinetic escalation. This article synthesizes research on "economic statecraft" and "economic warfare" and advances an integrated framework that links three channels-resource denial, financial intermediation, and network control-to observable outcomes in modern conflicts. Building on classic debates about sanctions effectiveness and newer work on the interwar invention of sanctions, the paper argues that economic measures function less as a binary substitute for war than as a graduated repertoire that reshapes the battlefield by reallocating production, constraining logistics, and reconfiguring expectations. Case evidence from World War I's maritime blockade, the 1990s Iraq regime, the 2012 disconnection of Iranian banks from SWIFT, and post 2022 measures against Russia illustrates recurrent trade-offs: coercive pressure is strongest when measures target bottleneck nodes, but humanitarian and political externalities accumulate and can undermine legitimacy or catalyze adaptation. The paper concludes by outlining testable implications and likely future trajectories, including supply-chain weaponization, digital payments contestation, and the entanglement of industrial policy with security strategy.

detail.abstract: We introduce the Admissible World Deformation Field (AWDF), a market metrology system that computes the minimum deformation required to map the market-implied world into the nearest jointly admissible world under a structured library of cross-market financial constraints. The deformation field-measured in constraint-dual sigma units-constitutes a new cross-asset state variable that separates structural contradictions (hard admissibility violations carrying nonzero KKT multipliers and non-recoverable with soft slacks) from softer plausibility pressure. The production engine solves a formal quadratic program with KKT-style dual tension extraction, enforcing hard admissibility faces and soft slacks simultaneously; the Active-set anchored solve is the benchmark leader with composite score 1.4842, hard breach 9.6×10⁻⁵, and feasibility gap 2.106. On the live-public evaluation path-21 persisted runs, official FRED-distributed series spanning listed volatility, rates, credit, FX, and macro-the system achieves: falsification pass rate 1.0 across all five pre-registered destruction protocols; stability score 0.963 under bid-ask perturbation; reproducibility 1.0 under pinned configuration; analog top-1 accuracy 0.621 and top-3 accuracy 0.853 on a 95-episode live-public historical library; and a baseline lift of 1.972 over a trivial localvol proxy floor. The current live memo identifies a primary fracture: the 1Y equity tail requires 2.9 sigma of deformation against tail-admissibility, with the binding stack tail-admissibility + crosshorizon-transport at confidence 0.49 and lead tension dual residual 0.1146 against tolerance 0.04 (hard). We demarcate explicitly what the current live-public evidence establishes, what it does not, and what licensed institutional market-stack expansion closes the remaining research gap. The central claim-that the AWDF deformation magnitude and its constraint decomposition constitute a new structural inconsistency primitive upstream of return-space risk measures-is supported by the live-public calibration and falsification evidence but awaits broader empirical validation on a licensed institutional data stack before the claim can be treated as publication-complete.

title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence in Credit Risk Management: A Review of Contemporary Approaches

detail.title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence in Credit Risk Management: A Review of Contemporary Approaches
detail.abstract: Credit risk management has been transformed by machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques that enable more accurate default prediction, automated underwriting, and robust risk assessment. This article synthesizes advances across three complementary streams: (1) uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural architectures that improve model calibration; (2) applications of ensemble methods including random forests and gradient boosting; and (3) the emergence of deep learning for financial risk modeling. We present quantitative comparisons of model performance on standard metrics (AUC, calibration error) and discuss implications for deployment in regulated financial environments. The bottom line: AI doesn't just predict who will repay a loan better than traditional methods—it also catches its own mistakes, flags unfair treatment, and keeps working reliably when the economy shifts, making it the smartest employee in the bank's risk department.

title: Restoring Equivalent Exchange: A Reductive Currency System — Proof of Return

detail.title: Restoring Equivalent Exchange: A Reductive Currency System — Proof of Return

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently and is not affiliated with any financial institution or blockchain project.

detail.abstract:
Everything that humans exchange daily — labor, time, meals, services — is finite and returns the moment it is consumed. Yet the medium designed to exchange these things — currency — has been engineered not to return. This asymmetry has bred hoarding, obstructed circulation, and entrenched a structure in which only those closest to the faucet benefit (the Cantillon effect).

This paper proposes a currency system that resolves this contradiction by embedding return into currency itself. The system comprises three currencies: Base, which guarantees existence; Amortization, which is Base returned through exponential decay upon use; and Creation, which supports creative endeavor. The core is an automated currency issuance and return system driven by an exponential model — decay and recovery as mirror images.

Currency is issued, used, and returned according to natural law. Through the same exponential feedback found in nature — radioactive decay, thermal cooling, ecosystem cycles — issuance and return maintain autonomous equilibrium without human intervention. The entire system is described by just two exponential functions.

Satoshi Nakamoto demonstrated through Proof of Work "a method for reaching consensus without a trusted third party." This paper demonstrates through Proof of Return "a method for exchanging things that return, with a medium that also returns."

title: Making the Host Rule Explicit in Monty Hall-Type Problems: A Pedagogical Note

detail.title: Making the Host Rule Explicit in Monty Hall-Type Problems: A Pedagogical Note
detail.abstract: Monty Hall is easy to state but easy to under-specify. In classroom formulations, the player's choice is usually clear, but the host's rule is often left only verbally sketched, even though different host protocols can imply different posterior probabilities. This pedagogical note presents Monty Hall-type problems as finite Bayesian models with an explicit observation mechanism σ(O | p), so that the host rule is written directly into the update. Once the protocol is fixed, posterior inference is a single finite Bayes calculation, and the standard result appears as a special case. The aim is not to propose a new theorem in probability, but to offer a compact teaching representation in which the role of the host mechanism is explicit at the point where updating is performed.

title: Tax Harmonization and the Repatriation of Risk
affiliations: University of St. Gallen - School of Finance and

detail.title: Tax Harmonization and the Repatriation of Risk
detail.abstract: International tax harmonization can curb profit shifting but may also weaken efficient risk sharing within multinational firms. We study this trade-off in the U.S. property-casualty insurance industry using the 2017 Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT), which raised the cost of cross-border affiliate reinsurance. We exploit a unique institutional feature that allows Bermudian affiliates to elect 953(d) status and be taxed as U.S. corporations while remaining located in Bermuda, effectively decoupling tax status from operational location. Our empirical strategy allows us to separate tax-motivated from risk-motivated internal capital flows: we estimate that about 80% of pre-reform offshore reinsurance was tax-driven and disappeared after the reform, while roughly 20% reflected genuine risk sharing. However, the resulting contraction in the internal risk pooling increased the retained risk of U.S. insurers and revealed a solvency regulation blind spot. That is, even as economic risk increased, the reported capital ratios remained unchanged because regulatory rules favor third-party reinsurance.

title: Disciplinary Typologies and Children’s Socioemotional and Behavioral Difficulties in Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago
affiliations: Syracuse University, Syracuse University and Syracuse University

detail.title: Disciplinary Typologies and Children’s Socioemotional and Behavioral Difficulties in Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago
detail.abstract: BackgroundDisciplinary practices in families often involve a combination of nonviolent strategies, psychological aggression, and physical punishment, particularly in Caribbean contexts.ObjectiveUsing a person-centered approach, this study identified disciplinary typologies and examined their associations with children’s socioemotional and behavioral difficulties during the early stage of middle childhood in Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago.Participants and SettingThe study included 2535 primary caregivers of children aged 5–6 and 7–9 years in Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago.MethodsData were drawn from the 2022 UNICEF Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS6) in Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago.ResultsLatent class analyses identified three common disciplinary typologies across countries: High Mixed, Verbal-Nonviolent Mixed, and Low Discipline. Two additional heterogeneous patterns, Verbal-Physical Mixed and Supportive-Harsh Mixed, were observed among Jamaican children aged 5–6 years. Across both countries, typologies characterized by frequent use of harsh strategies were associated with greater difficulties in behavioral regulation and higher levels of depression, whereas low-discipline patterns were linked to fewer difficulties (e.g., Jamaica: behavioral control χ2(4) = 16.08, p = .018; depression χ2(4) = 9.77, p = .045; similar patterns in Trinidad and Tobago). During the transition to school, mixed but conditionally inconsistent disciplinary patterns were particularly important for children’s behavioral control.ConclusionsThese findings underscore the importance of examining the organization and predictability of disciplinary practices in combination, rather than in isolation, to better understand children’s socioemotional and behavioral adjustment in global majority contexts.

title: Integrity Shocks and Reputation Spillovers in Collaboration Networks: Evidence from Scientific Retractions
affiliations: IESEG School of Management

detail.title: Integrity Shocks and Reputation Spillovers in Collaboration Networks: Evidence from Scientific Retractions
detail.abstract: Integrity failures in collaborative production rarely remain confined to the individual responsible. When output is jointly produced and responsibility is imperfectly attributable, negative signals about one contributor can reshape the incentives and collaboration choices of affiliated partners. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework explaining how integrity shocks propagate through collaboration networks and induce strategic reorganization of partnerships. Exposure depends on prior tie strength and network position, shaping incentives to maintain, dissolve, or reconfigure collaborations and generating second-order dynamics that reorganize collaboration networks. We examine this mechanism in the context of scientific retractions, which provide a clean empirical laboratory with observable collaboration ties and precisely dated integrity shocks. Using detailed data on collaboration networks around the first retraction of highly prolific authors, we show that integrity shocks trigger selective dissolution of collaboration ties, reduce research productivity among more exposed collaborators, and induce strategic repositioning toward higher-prestige partners and outlets. Taken together, the evidence shows that integrity shocks do not merely generate reputational penalties but reorganize collaboration networks through strategic responses to heterogeneous exposure.

title: Sociodemographic Determinants of Vaccine Hesitancy: Evidence from the MENA Region

detail.title: Sociodemographic Determinants of Vaccine Hesitancy: Evidence from the MENA Region
